- Keep total length constant (e.g., 30 nt) while varying distribution of adenines: (i) terminal A-block (A10 + mixed remainder), (ii) periodically spaced A’s (A every 3 bases), (iii) clustered internal A-block, (iv) A-poor control with same length/charge.
- Include T-rich and random controls.
4.2 Coupled kinetics with full mass balance:
- For each DNA, run displacement at fixed DNA:MOF ratios under buffer A and B.
- Measure simultaneously: (i) Thy-L released to solution by LC-MS (internal standard), (ii) DNA depletion/uptake by fluorescence (labeled DNA) with calibration and quench controls, and (iii) solution Zn by ICP-MS at matched timepoints.
- Define stoichiometric benchmarks and acceptance windows: report mol Thy-L released per mol nucleotide adsorbed (or per mol DNA). Target “coupled exchange” signature: Thy-L release scales with A-density/geometry and saturates near a constant ratio (±20%) for the best-matching DNA sequences, while Zn leaching remains below threshold.
4.3 Competition tests to separate Watson–Crick recognition from generic ligand exchange:
- Repeat displacement using the decisive negative control gate (N3-methylthymine-L or 2,4-difluorothymine-L). If displacement is recognition-driven, A-rich DNA should show markedly reduced ability to trigger Thy-L release and uptake relative to true Thy-L, despite comparable coordination installation levels.
- Add soluble acetate challenge (e.g., 5 mM) during DNA exposure: if DNA uptake is primarily via A–T recognition and not simply scavenging Zn–O2CR, acetate should partially suppress Thy-L release without reproducing DNA sequence selectivity.

Step 5 — pH-triggered release deconvolution with stability thresholds and ‘no-DNA’ controls.
5.1 Define quantitative stability thresholds (pre-registered):
- Zn leaching: acceptable ≤1% of total Zn over a full capture→release cycle; caution 1–5%; failure >5%.
- Framework integrity: PXRD peak positions retained; crystallinity loss <20% by integrated intensity comparison; porosity recovery ≥80% of pre-gating BET after reactivation.
5.2 pH-step release with full controls:
- Perform pH steps (7.4 → 5.5 → 4.5) on (i) DNA-loaded Thy-L@KBM-1, (ii) Thy-L@KBM-1 without DNA, and (iii) ungated KBM-1 loaded with DNA.
- Quantify DNA release kinetics (fluorescence), Thy-L rebinding/release (LC-MS), Zn leaching (ICP-MS), and any linker/ligand loss (solution NMR/LC of supernatant and/or digest).
5.3 Dissolution discrimination via competitive ligands at low pH:
- Include parallel samples with added acetate (5–20 mM) at pH 4.5 to test whether release coincides with Zn–carboxylate exchange/dissolution; include phosphate as a destructive control to establish the signature of node dissolution (high Zn leaching + PXRD collapse).
- Interpret release mechanism only if DNA release occurs with Zn leaching below threshold and without linker loss; otherwise classify as framework damage-driven release.

Step 6 — Structural localization: commit to realistic probes and falsifiable alternatives.
6.1 Primary local-structure probe: Zn K-edge EXAFS/XANES across states (KBM-1 → Thy-L@ → DNA-displaced → post-pH). This is prioritized over SCXRD.
6.2 Secondary probes (pre-committed if EXAFS is inconclusive):
- Solid-state NMR using isotopic labeling where feasible (e.g., 15N-labeled thymine derivative or 15N-labeled adenine in the framework if accessible) to detect proximity/interaction changes.
- Fluorescence quenching/FRET: install a fluorophore-tagged Thy-L analog at low fraction to report displacement in situ (validated to behave similarly to unlabeled Thy-L).

Step 7 — Success criteria (revised to reflect mechanistic rigor).
7.1 Mechanistic validation gates:
- Demonstrated competitor-sensitive Thy-L installation consistent with labile Zn coordination (EXAFS + competition).
- Quantified A–T pairing energetics under buffer A/B and observed salt dependence consistent with recognition-driven displacement.
- DNA-library results that match the geometric multivalency criterion: sequences predicted to have higher n_eff show higher cooperativity (Hill coefficient increase and/or induction behavior) and higher selectivity vs A-poor controls.
7.2 Performance metrics:
- ≥2× selectivity (A-geometry-matched vs mismatch) at equal length/charge in buffer A; measurable but reduced selectivity in buffer B (explicitly predicted).
- Stoichiometric coupling within ±20% for best-performing sequences.
- Retained crystallinity and porosity recovery ≥80% after at least two gating/displacement cycles.
- pH-triggered release with ≤1% Zn leaching and no detectable linker loss above background.
Feasibility:
1) Binding-site and exchange feasibility is made chemically explicit and experimentally testable before any ‘toehold-like’ claim: the revised plan treats Thy-L exchange as occurring at a labile Zn coordination environment (terminal aqua/hydroxo and/or defects) rather than assuming open metal sites or framework-linker substitution. Zn K-edge XANES/EXAFS across controlled competitor challenges (acetate/imidazole/phosphate) directly maps whether monocarboxylates bind reversibly without node rearrangement, addressing the coordination ambiguity. The acetate/imidazole dose-response additionally differentiates coordination-driven PSI from nonspecific adsorption.

2) Selectivity is no longer asserted from base pairing alone; it is parameterized by measured A–T pairing energetics under the exact buffer/ionic strength (two regimes) and translated into a falsifiable multivalency/geometry criterion derived from the known density/spacing of accessible Ade WC faces in KBM-1. The DNA library is redesigned to vary A-distribution/periodicity at constant length, enabling a direct test of whether cooperativity arises from confinement-enhanced multivalency rather than simple A-tract affinity.

3) Quantification rigor is upgraded to mass-balance-grade analytics: LC-MS (not HPLC/UV) with isotopically labeled internal standards, matrix-matched calibrations (with/without DNA), and explicit vessel-adsorption corrections ensures Thy-L release is accurately quantified in complex DNA/buffer matrices. Stoichiometric coupling benchmarks (mol Thy-L released per mol nucleotide/DNA) are pre-defined with acceptance windows.

4) The pH trigger is deconvoluted from framework damage by pre-registered Zn-leaching thresholds, no-DNA pH controls, and solution-phase monitoring of linker loss (NMR/LC) alongside porosity recovery. Competitive ligand challenges at low pH (acetate benign; phosphate destructive) provide a diagnostic signature to distinguish designed reversibility from node dissolution.

5) Structural localization risk is mitigated by prioritizing realistic, occupancy-tolerant local probes (Zn EXAFS/XANES as primary; ssNMR or fluorophore-reporter Thy-L as secondary), so failure of SCXRD/PDF does not stall mechanistic adjudication. Together, these changes convert the proposal from an attractive concept into a mechanistically locked, falsifiable coordination/supramolecular program aligned with known aqueous MOF stability constraints and Bio-MOF nucleobase recognition.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-pre-registered proposal that directly confronts the central failure modes of aqueous MOF–biomolecule studies: ambiguous binding sites, conflation of adsorption with coordination, and post hoc mechanistic storytelling. Engineering resolution is very high: the stepwise plan uses state-of-the-art, domain-appropriate tools (Zn K-edge EXAFS/XANES, LC-MS with isotopic standards, ICP-MS mass balance, competitive ligand diagnostics) with explicit acceptance criteria and decision rules. Logical consistency is likewise strong; the hypothesis is mechanistically constrained, falsifiable, and explicitly conditional on identifying a labile Zn coordination environment proximal to adenine WC faces. Importantly, the proposal does not assume ‘toehold-like’ behavior but derives it from quantified A–T energetics translated into a geometric multivalency criterion. Evidence grounding is solid and remains within the Bio-MOF / nucleobase-recognition domain without importing irrelevant paradigms. Minor deductions arise from residual risk that EXAFS sensitivity may be insufficient to resolve low-occupancy Thy-L binding modes, and from the practical complexity of maintaining tight mass balance across so many coupled assays, which could strain throughput and statistical power. Rationale quality is high: the work does not merely apply base pairing to MOFs, but restructures the problem around coordination lability as the bottleneck, representing a genuine conceptual advance rather than an incremental application.

Hypothesis: A sequential, quantitatively verified, site-selective post-metalation of mixed-linker [M2L2P]-type MTV‑SURMOFs can be made falsifiable and robust by (a) operationally defining “pKa-programmed” LPE as a kinetic deprotonation/ligation window controlled by solvent, base-equivalent, and cycle timing (not pKa alone), (b) engineering *bounded* node-adjacent defect pockets at a measured density that preserves orientation/crystallinity, and (c) installing Cu2+ under a ligand/water-activity regime that thermodynamically favors binding to pendant neutral donors (L3) and kinetically suppresses Zn→Cu exchange at carboxylate nodes. Mechanistically, Zn2+ paddlewheel nodes provide an epitaxy-stable scaffold and maintain continuous oriented channels; late-cycle incorporation of low-fraction L3 introduces inward-facing pyridyl/thioether donors that act as high-affinity, non-framework coordination sites; and isolated missing-linker pockets increase local accessibility and residence time for Cu2+ near L3 without creating percolating defects that destabilize Zn nodes. If Cu2+ is delivered as a partially complexed species (Cu–ligand) in low water activity, the dominant pathway becomes diffusion-limited capture at L3/defect pockets rather than transmetalation at carboxylate–Zn sites or precipitation as Cu(OH)x. The resulting architecture produces a cooperative adsorption landscape in which (i) Cu2+ provides isolated open Lewis-acid/π-complexation sites that increase aromatic adsorption enthalpy, while (ii) the Zn2+ framework preserves pore continuity and electrostatic field uniformity, preventing pore collapse and minimizing site blocking. This hypothesis is falsified if (1) per-cycle linker uptake cannot be independently quantified and shown to follow the programmed sequence within defined tolerances, (2) defect density cannot be bounded below a crystallinity/orientation threshold, or (3) Cu2+ installation causes measurable Zn loss/exchange or forms non-chelated hydroxo/oxo deposits while failing to increase enthalpy-normalized adsorption beyond mesoporosity-only controls.
Plan:
Step 0 — Platform selection, substrates, and analytical calibration
0.1 Choose a benchmark [M2L2P] SURMOF system with established LPE recipes and strong diffraction signatures. Primary: Zn2+ paddlewheel framework (Zn2(BDC)2-type analogue within [M2L2P] family) on COOH-terminated SAMs (e.g., 11-mercaptoundecanoic acid on Au) or hydroxylated oxide (e.g., Al2O3/Si) with carboxylate anchoring layer. Rationale: Zn2+ nodes reduce Cu-driven framework redox/ligand exchange during growth.
0.2 Establish thickness/mass calibration for normalization: (i) spectroscopic ellipsometry per cycle, (ii) QCM-D mass-per-cycle on identical substrates, and (iii) AFM step-height (masked growth) for absolute thickness.
0.3 Define absolute composition calibration for IRRA: prepare reference films with known linker ratios (verified by digestion NMR/ICP) to convert IRRA band integrals of each linker’s diagnostic vibrations to mol-fraction.

Step 1 — Define the “pKa-programmed LPE” process window (operational chemistry, not qualitative pKa)
1.1 Linker set (ternary):
• L1: BDC (terephthalate, baseline).
• L2: electron-withdrawing dicarboxylate (e.g., 2,5-difluoro-BDC or 2-nitro-BDC) to shift deprotonation/coordination kinetics.
• L3: BDC bearing a pendant neutral donor oriented into the pore (e.g., 2-(pyridin-3-yl)-BDC, 2-(methylthio)-BDC, or triazole-tagged BDC).
1.2 Measure linker pKa *and* effective deprotonation under growth solvent: determine pKa in water/MeOH and estimate apparent acidity in EtOH/DMF mixtures using titration + conductivity; record solubility limits and aggregation.
1.3 LPE solvent/base-equivalent specification (starting window; to be optimized):
• Metal solution: 0.5–1.0 mM Zn(OAc)2·2H2O (or Zn(NO3)2·6H2O) in EtOH:DMF:H2O = 70:25:5 (v/v/v).
• Linker solutions: 0.25–0.75 mM total linker in same solvent system.
• Base-equivalent control: add triethylamine (TEA) at 0–2.0 equiv relative to total –COOH (or replace with 2,6-lutidine for weaker/basic steric control). Target apparent pH (in the aqueous fraction) 5.5–7.0; record with micro-pH electrode in a matched solvent surrogate (EtOH/H2O) and maintain constant across cycles.
• Cycle timing: 5 min metal exposure → 2× 1 min rinse (solvent) → 5 min linker exposure → 2× rinse; temperature 25–35 °C.
1.4 Programmed sequence definition (example 60-cycle film; adjust to reach 100–300 nm):
• Cycles 1–15 (orientation lock-in): L2-rich (e.g., L2:L1:L3 = 80:20:0) to favor fast deprotonation/coordination at growth front.
• Cycles 16–45 (pore regularization): L1-dominant (10:90:0).
• Cycles 46–60 (Cu-capture seeding): low L3 fraction (10:85:5) to minimize growth poisoning.
1.5 Sequence fidelity measurement (mandatory quantitative):
• In situ QCM-D: record Δm per cycle for metal and linker half-cycles; require stable growth (±10% mass-per-cycle after cycle 10).
• Ex situ IRRA after defined cycle blocks (e.g., after 15, 45, 60 cycles): integrate diagnostic bands for L2 and L3 vs L1; convert to absolute mol-fractions using calibration.
Go/no-go #1 (sequence fidelity): L3 incorporation in the final block must be 3–7 mol% (target 5±2%) and ≤1 mol% in early/mid blocks; L2 must be ≥60 mol% in cycles 1–15 and ≤15 mol% thereafter. If not met, adjust TEA equivalents, linker concentration, and exposure time (kinetic control) until criteria are satisfied.

Step 2 — Quantified defect-pocket engineering with bounded density and identified defect type
2.1 Replace vague “defect pulses” with a modulator-dose protocol embedded in LPE:
• Modulator: benzoic acid or acetic acid (monocarboxylate) introduced only during metal half-cycles at defined pulses.
• Pulse schedule: every 10th metal half-cycle, add modulator at 5–20 mM for 60–120 s (then rinse). Keep all other parameters constant.
2.2 Defect density quantification and defect-type discrimination:
• Film digestion: dissolve SURMOF (e.g., DCl/DMSO-d6 or acidic aqueous/organic mixture validated not to scramble linkers) and quantify linker ratios by 1H NMR using an internal standard.
• Metal content: ICP-OES/ICP-MS on digest to obtain Zn:(L1+L2+L3) ratio.
• Defect metric: define missing-linker fraction fML = 1 − (measured linker equivalents per Zn)/(ideal linker equivalents per Zn in [M2L2P]). Track across pulse intensity.
• Defect-type proxy: XAS at Zn K-edge to detect changes in Zn coordination number consistent with missing-linker vs missing-node; corroborate with XPS (Zn 2p shifts) and, if available, PALS to detect free-volume changes consistent with defect pockets (optional but recommended).
2.3 Bounding “isolated, non-percolating” defects in thin films:
• Structural retention constraints: GIWAXS/XRD must retain (i) the same out-of-plane orientation peaks and (ii) FWHM broadening ≤25% relative to defect-free film.
• Leakage/lability constraint: no measurable Zn loss during modulator pulsing (Zn in rinse solutions by ICP-MS below 1% of total Zn content per 100 cycles).
Go/no-go #2 (defects): Acceptable defect window is fML = 0.5–3.0% with crystallinity/orientation criteria met. If fML >3% or orientation degrades, reduce modulator concentration/pulse time or pulse frequency.

Step 3 — Engineer Cu2+ selectivity: precursor chemistry, water activity control, and time-resolved kinetics
3.1 Cu2+ precursor/ligand environment (to suppress Zn→Cu exchange and hydroxo deposition):
• Use Cu(OTf)2 or Cu(NO3)2 at 0.1–1.0 mM in MeCN:EtOH = 80:20 with controlled water content ≤0.5 vol% (Karl Fischer verified).
• Add a competing, *moderate* chelator that stabilizes Cu2+ against carboxylate exchange but still allows substitution by pyridyl donors: 2,2′-bipyridine (bpy) or acetonitrile-rich solvation; starting condition: Cu:bpy = 1:0.5 (mol/mol). Alternative if L3 is thioether: avoid strong N-chelation; use Cu(OTf)2 in dry MeCN without bpy.
• Add a non-nucleophilic base is avoided to prevent Cu(OH)x; maintain low water activity; no carbonate buffers.
3.2 Diffusion-limited installation protocol:
• Immerse films in Cu solution under N2, 25 °C, static (no stirring) for controlled times (5, 15, 30, 60, 180 min).
• Rinse in dry MeCN/EtOH and perform a “locking” step: brief solvent exchange with dry MeCN containing 1–5 mM of the free L3-analog (small-molecule pyridine) to strip weakly physisorbed Cu and leave strongly bound Cu at donor sites (optimize to avoid stripping desired Cu).
3.3 Prove selectivity and rule out transmetalation/precipitation (time-resolved):
• XPS vs time: quantify Cu 2p/Zn 2p ratios and Cu satellite features; require monotonic Cu uptake with constant Zn signal (±5%).
• XAS (Cu K-edge): determine coordination environment; require spectra consistent with N/S-ligated Cu2+ (and not CuO/Cu(OH)2). Compare to reference Cu(OTf)2, CuO, and Cu–pyridine complexes.
• EPR: confirm isolated Cu2+ signatures (g||, A||) consistent with mononuclear sites; absence of signals typical of clustered Cu(II) oxo species.
• ICP-MS of metalation bath and rinses: Zn leaching ≤0.5% of total Zn per metalation (hard limit).
Go/no-go #3 (selective metalation): (i) Zn loss ≤0.5%, (ii) no CuO/Cu(OH)2 signatures by XAS/XPS, and (iii) Cu uptake saturates with time consistent with diffusion/finite site density (plateau by ≤3 h). If violated, reduce water content, lower Cu concentration, increase chelation (bpy ratio), or shorten exposure.

Step 4 — Adsorption testing with rigorous normalization and transport/enthalpy decoupling
4.1 Film normalization (mandatory):
• Determine areal mass loading (QCM-D) and thickness (ellipsometry/AFM). Report uptake as (i) mg analyte per g framework and (ii) mol analyte per mol total metal, and (iii) per accessible pore volume.
• Accessible pore volume proxy in films: combined ellipsometric porosimetry (EP) with a non-coordinating probe vapor (e.g., toluene or cyclohexane) and/or Kr adsorption on scraped film (if feasible). If EP available, use it to quantify mesopore contribution.
4.2 Adsorption measurements:
• QCM-based vapor sorption for benzene/toluene/xylene at multiple temperatures (e.g., 298/308/318 K) to extract isosteric heat via Clausius–Clapeyron on matched coverage regions.
• Complement with vapor sorption isotherms (gravimetric or volumetric if sufficient material can be harvested; otherwise QCM across RH-controlled partial pressures).
4.3 Controls to decouple access vs binding (as required):
• Control A (mesoporosity-matched, no Cu): create mesopores via the same pause/rinse and defect window, but omit L3 and omit Cu metalation.
• Control B (Cu-loading matched, minimal mesopores): L3 present and Cu-metalated, but grown without pause/rinse and at lowest defect density (fML ~0.5%).
• Control C (L3 present, no Cu): isolates effect of donor tags alone.
• Control D (conventional MTV-SURMOF): one-pot mixed-linker LPE (constant linker mixture each cycle) with same overall linker ratios and thickness.
4.4 Success metrics (quantitative):
• Primary performance: at matched film mass and matched accessible pore volume (±10%), Cu-metalated L3+defect films must show ≥30% higher aromatic uptake at P/P0 = 0.1–0.3 and ≥20% higher isosteric heat at low coverage than Control A.
• Site-efficiency: uptake increase per incorporated Cu (Δmmol arene / mmol Cu) must exceed that of a Cu-only SURMOF benchmark by ≥2×.
• Stability: after 50 adsorption/desorption cycles and 24 h at 50% RH, retain ≥90% of initial uptake and preserve GIWAXS orientation peaks (intensity loss ≤20%).
Go/no-go #4 (mechanistic attribution): If uptake gains correlate only with increased mesopore volume (EP) and not with increased Qst or Cu site density, the “enthalpy-driven cooperative landscape” claim is rejected and the project pivots to optimizing access/transport rather than bimetallic binding.

Step 5 — Mechanistic closure experiments
5.1 Competition adsorption: benzene vs cyclohexane to isolate π/Lewis-acid contributions (cyclohexane is non-π). A larger benzene/cyclohexane selectivity in Cu-metalated films supports Cu–π interactions.
5.2 Poisoning test: dose pyridine vapor at low coverage to reversibly block Cu Lewis sites; a corresponding drop in aromatic uptake (with minimal pore volume change) links uptake enhancement to Cu sites.
5.3 Spatial distribution verification: ToF-SIMS depth profiling and cross-sectional STEM-EDS to ensure Cu is not concentrated only at the outer surface; require Cu depth gradient <2× across film thickness (unless intentionally designed otherwise).

Project decision points and timeline (high-level)
• Months 1–3: define LPE window + sequence fidelity (Go/no-go #1).
• Months 4–6: defect window mapping + bounded defect protocol (Go/no-go #2).
• Months 7–9: Cu selectivity regime + kinetics (Go/no-go #3).
• Months 10–12: adsorption + mechanistic controls + stability (Go/no-go #4).
Feasibility:
1) Making “pKa-programmed incorporation” operational and falsifiable: Asset 3 shows linker pKa correlates with SURMOF orientation/composition, but the reviewer correctly notes that LPE incorporation is governed by local deprotonation and surface coordination kinetics. The revised plan therefore specifies solvent composition, base-equivalent, concentrations, and exposure times, and it requires *independent per-cycle uptake quantification* (QCM mass-per-cycle) plus *absolute composition readout* (IRRA calibrated to digestion NMR/ICP). Sequence fidelity is no longer assumed from pKa; it is experimentally verified against explicit tolerances.

2) Defect pockets with bounded density and known defect type: The reviewer concern (uncontrolled missing-linker/missing-node chemistry) is addressed by a dose-controlled monocarboxylate pulse protocol and a multi-modal defect metrology stack: digestion NMR + ICP defines linker:metal stoichiometry (defect density), Zn K-edge XAS/XPS provides coordination-state evidence for defect type, and (optionally) PALS/ellipsometric porosimetry quantifies added free volume. A hard upper bound (fML ≤3% plus diffraction/orientation retention) ensures defects remain isolated and do not percolate into a mechanically fragile network. This directly resolves the “isolated, non-percolating” claim with a measurable criterion.

3) Explicit Cu2+ selectivity engineering to prevent Zn→Cu transmetalation and hydroxo/oxo deposition: Rather than exposing films to aqueous Cu2+ (high risk of Cu(OH)x and exchange), the protocol uses low-water-activity media (MeCN/EtOH with KF verification), weakly coordinating anions (OTf−/NO3−), and an optional moderate chelator (bpy at sub-stoichiometric ratio) to stabilize Cu2+ against carboxylate-driven exchange while still allowing substitution by pendant pyridyl donors on L3. Time-resolved XPS/XAS/EPR and Zn-leaching ICP provide direct evidence that metalation is diffusion-limited capture at L3/defect pockets, not global transmetalation or precipitation.

4) Decoupling transport/access from binding: Asset 3 indicates mesopores increase accessibility, which could inflate uptake without changing binding enthalpy. The revised plan adds required control films that independently match (i) mesoporosity without Cu and (ii) Cu loading without mesoporosity, and it normalizes adsorption by mass, thickness, and accessible pore volume (ellipsometric porosimetry). Only if uptake gains persist under these matched-access conditions and coincide with increased Qst and Cu site-efficiency can the cooperative bimetallic enthalpy mechanism be claimed.

5) Alignment with broader modification logic: Asset 1 supports the principle that chemical/surface modification and controlled assembly tune stability and functional interactions; here, L3 donor tags and bounded defect pockets are the chemical “handles” enabling controlled post-metalation without destabilizing the oriented film. Asset 2 underscores that adsorption enhancements in MOF composites depend on accessible surface area and controlled interaction sites; the revised plan explicitly quantifies accessibility and separates it from enthalpy-driven site effects.

Overall, the revised proposal converts each mechanistic lever into a controlled variable with quantitative thresholds and orthogonal readouts, directly addressing reviewer demands for process windows, defect/metalation metrics, selectivity rationale, and confound-free adsorption comparisons.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-engineered proposal that directly addresses common failure modes in mixed-linker SURMOF post-metalation (sequence ambiguity, uncontrolled defects, and Cu–Zn transmetalation). The strongest aspect is the conversion of qualitative concepts (pKa control, defect isolation, selective metalation) into operational windows with explicit tolerances and orthogonal measurements. Logical consistency is high: the Zn paddlewheel scaffold, low-fraction L3 donors, and bounded missing-linker pockets form a coherent kinetic/thermodynamic framework for Cu2+ capture without node exchange. Minor deductions arise from practical risk rather than conceptual weakness: (i) IRRA calibration across three chemically distinct linkers may suffer from orientation-dependent transition dipole effects, potentially complicating absolute mol-fraction assignment; (ii) distinguishing truly node-adjacent missing-linker pockets from surface-proximal defects in thin films remains experimentally challenging even with XAS/XPS; and (iii) the Cu–ligand (bpy or MeCN-solvated) strategy assumes substitution kinetics that may vary strongly with L3 identity, risking system-specific tuning rather than generality. These are execution risks, not logical flaws.

Hypothesis: A MIL-96(Al)-based QCM electronic-nose can achieve reproducible sub-ppm to ppb-class trace detection of diagnostically relevant breath VOCs and spoilage-marker headspace VOCs under high humidity (40–95% RH) if (and only if) the sensor stack is engineered and validated to (i) keep QCM operation in a quantified “near-Sauerbrey” regime (or corrected by a validated Voigt viscoelastic model) and (ii) ensure that analyte transport/partitioning through any humidity-buffering/calibration overlayer does not dominate adsorption kinetics. Mechanistically, MIL-96(Al) provides polar Al–OH/μ3-OH motifs whose Lewis/Brønsted acidity and hydrogen-bonding can selectively stabilize oxygenates and amines; deliberate defect/functional-site engineering creates two kinetically separable uptake channels: (a) fast, weak adsorption on external surfaces and intrinsic pores and (b) slow, strong binding at defect-associated Al–OH clusters and grafted functional motifs. This dual-site behavior produces concentration- and RH-dependent multi-time-constant QCM transients that add information content beyond equilibrium mass shifts, improving mixture deconvolution in an e-nose array as supported by thermodynamic+kinetic co-design principles in gravimetric sensor literature. To overcome the dominant real-world limitation—humidity-driven drift and viscoelastic artifacts—the “microencapsulation layer” is redefined as a mechanically-stiff, ultrathin, microporous humidity-buffering/calibration stratum with explicitly bounded viscoelastic loading and independently measured transport properties. The layer must (1) maintain a stable shear modulus across RH (minimizing ΔD and Δf artifacts), (2) provide high VOC diffusivity and low VOC partitioning into the binder (so MOF adsorption still sets kinetics), and (3) allow repeatable on-sensor calibration pulses without chemically aging MIL-96(Al) or the binder. Under these constraints, time-resolved uptake/desorption signatures can be confidently assigned to MOF adsorption (fast/slow site populations) rather than polymer swelling, enabling robust trace sensing in humid breath/headspace matrices.
Plan:
Step 1 — Define quantitative QCM viscoelastic-control architecture and go/no-go thresholds (mandatory)
1.1 QCM mode selection and readout: Use 5–10 MHz AT-cut QCM with multi-overtone acquisition (n = 1, 3, 5). Record both frequency (Δf_n) and dissipation (ΔD_n) at each overtone to diagnose viscoelasticity and solvent-like coupling.
1.2 Film-stack mechanical design targets:
- MOF layer thickness target: 200–600 nm (SEM cross-section), to ensure adequate uptake while maintaining rigid-film behavior.
- Overlayer thickness target (revised from 1–10 μm): 100–800 nm total (ellipsometry/profilometry), implemented as a microporous, mechanically stiff matrix; microcapsules (if used) must be nanoscale (100–400 nm) or sparse areal coverage (<5% surface fraction) to avoid large viscoelastic loading.
- Acceptance thresholds (“near-Sauerbrey” gate): For blank humid cycling (no VOC), require |ΔD_3| ≤ 1×10⁻⁶ and |ΔD_5| ≤ 0.7×10⁻⁶ across 40–95% RH; and overtone consistency |(Δf_3/3) − (Δf_5/5)| / |Δf_3/3| ≤ 10% under the same RH sweep. If thresholds fail, operate under Voigt modeling with independent thickness validation (1.4).
- Temperature coefficient constraint: under a 25–55 °C calibration-pulse range, require baseline drift |d(Δf)/dT| ≤ 1 Hz/°C (post-correction) and |d(ΔD)/dT| ≤ 0.2×10⁻⁶/°C.
1.3 Sauerbrey-validity/Voigt protocol:
- If dissipation and overtone scaling satisfy 1.2 thresholds, use Sauerbrey for mass interpretation.
- If not, fit Δf_n and ΔD_n simultaneously to a Voigt viscoelastic model to extract shear modulus (G′, G″) and viscosity; proceed only if the fitted RH-dependence of G′ changes by ≤20% between 40–95% RH for the blank layer (no VOC).
1.4 Independent mass–thickness cross-checks:
- Determine dry thickness by ellipsometry (on planar Au witness chips processed identically) and/or profilometry.
- Determine areal mass by quartz frequency (Sauerbrey/Voigt) and cross-check by microbalance of coated crystal (pre/post, controlled RH) when feasible.
- Go/no-go: QCM-derived areal mass must agree within ±15% of thickness×density estimate (density bounded from MOF crystal density and measured porosity).

Step 2 — Material mini-library: MIL-96(Al) defect/functional-site engineering with stability-by-design
2.1 Target analytes and interferents:
- Breath VOCs: acetone, ethanol, isoprene.
- Spoilage/headspace VOCs: trimethylamine (TMA), hexanal, 2-nonanone.
- Interferents: H2O (40–95% RH), CO2 (400–5,000 ppm).
2.2 MIL-96(Al) variants (6–8 channels total, each replicated ≥3):
A) Pristine MIL-96(Al) (baseline polar Al–OH sites).
B) Defect-enriched MIL-96(Al): modulated synthesis with formic/acetic acid (systematic modulator/linker ratios, e.g., 0, 10, 30, 60 equivalents vs Al) to tune missing-linker defects and Al–OH density.
C) Hydrophobically biased defect-capped variant: post-synthetic defect-site capping using fluorinated carboxylates (e.g., trifluoromethyl-benzoate) to reduce water affinity while preserving Lewis acidity at remaining Al sites.
D) H-bond donor/acceptor tuned variant: mixed-linker partial substitution of trimesate with amino- or hydroxyl-functionalized benzenetricarboxylate (kept ≤20 mol% to preserve phase purity), to bias interactions with carbonyl VOCs.
E) Acid–base tuned variant: sulfonate-terminated aromatic grafting at defect sites (low loading) to strengthen amine capture (TMA) while monitoring irreversible binding risk.
2.3 Chemical compatibility screen before QCM integration:
- Expose powders/films to (i) 95% RH, (ii) 10–100 ppm TMA, (iii) 10–100 ppm acetone/ethanol, and (iv) combined RH+VOC for 72 h. Track PXRD, FTIR, and N2 sorption (or vapor sorption proxy) for stability; eliminate chemistries that show phase change or irreversible site poisoning.

Step 3 — Sensor-stack fabrication: adherent MOF thin film + mechanically bounded “active packaging” layer
3.1 MOF film growth on Au QCM:
- Surface priming: form carboxylate-terminated SAM (e.g., 11-mercaptoundecanoic acid) to promote adhesion.
- Seed layer: layer-by-layer assembly (Al source + carboxylate linker cycles) to form a nanocrystalline anchoring layer.
- Secondary growth: solvothermal growth tuned for 200–600 nm thickness; verify by SEM cross-section and AFM roughness.
- Adhesion metric: tape test + ultrasonic immersion test (10 min in water/ethanol); acceptance: <5% area delamination by optical/SEM mapping.
3.2 Redefined humidity-buffering/calibration overlayer (mechanically stiff, transport-open):
- Matrix candidates: (i) thin organosilica (ORMOSIL) sol–gel with controlled microporosity, or (ii) crosslinked fluorinated poly(urethane-urea) with porogen to create interconnected pores; reject neat PDMS-like matrices if partitioning/swelling dominates (quantified in Step 4).
- Thickness: 100–800 nm.
- Optional calibration reservoirs: nanoscale cyclodextrin-in-organosilica domains or silica nanocapsules (100–400 nm). Loading kept low to meet ΔD gates.
3.3 Calibration-pulse actuation:
- Mild thermal micro-heating (≤55 °C at the crystal surface, confirmed by IR thermometry) or low-power IR LED.
- Calibrant choice: isotopically labeled VOC (e.g., acetone-d6) or tert-butanol (chemically orthogonal to target set), selected to avoid irreversible binding.
- Pulse schedule: e.g., 10–30 s pulse every 30–60 min during long runs; objective is to generate a stable “internal standard” transient used for drift correction.

Step 4 — Transport/partitioning study of the overlayer (mandatory): ensure it does not dominate kinetics
4.1 Effective diffusivity (Deff) of VOCs through overlayer:
- Use planar witness films (same deposition) on inert substrates; measure VOC uptake kinetics by QCM on bare Au coated only with overlayer (no MOF) and/or ellipsometric swelling kinetics.
- Extract Deff via Fickian diffusion model for thin films; conduct at 40%, 70%, 95% RH.
- Go/no-go: characteristic diffusion time through overlayer τ = L²/Deff must be ≤10% of overall sensor response time (t90) observed on MOF-only films. Practically, target τ ≤ 1–3 s for L ≤ 800 nm for small VOCs.
4.2 VOC/binder partition coefficient (Kfilm/gas):
- Determine K by equilibrium uptake on overlayer-only QCM versus gas concentration (dynamic dilution, ppm range) at multiple RH.
- Go/no-go: at target concentrations, predicted mass uptake in overlayer-only must be ≤20% of total uptake in MOF+overlayer stack for each VOC; otherwise overlayer chemistry/porosity is redesigned.
4.3 RH-dependent swelling/modulus shifts:
- Measure RH sorption and swelling by ellipsometry and/or QCM-D on overlayer-only films.
- Go/no-go: blank RH step (40→95%) produces |Δf| equivalent mass ≤10% of typical VOC signal at 1 ppm and meets ΔD thresholds in Step 1.

Step 5 — Definitive evidence for bimodal adsorption kinetics under humid dynamic conditions (mandatory)
5.1 Step-response relaxation analysis:
- Perform concentration steps (e.g., 0→50→200→1000 ppb; and 0→1→5→20 ppm where needed) at fixed RH (40, 70, 95%) for each VOC.
- Fit Δf(t) (and ΔD(t)) to a two-process model: (i) fast adsorption/transport (external + weak sites) and (ii) slow adsorption at strong/defect sites, explicitly including gas-to-film mass transfer and overlayer diffusion terms from Step 4. Require that two time constants are statistically separable (confidence intervals non-overlapping across ≥3 replicates) and that the slow component fraction increases with defect density/grafting in a chemically consistent way.
5.2 Pulse-response deconvolution (calibration + analyte):
- Use calibrant pulses in clean humid carrier to characterize purely overlayer-mediated dynamics; then apply identical pulses with MOF present.
- Compare impulse responses: if MOF introduces an additional slow component beyond overlayer-only response and this component scales with defect-engineering metrics, assign it to strong sites.
5.3 In situ assignment of binding motifs:
- QCM + MS outlet monitoring: connect downstream MS (or PTR-MS) to measure breakthrough during steps/pulses. A delayed outlet rise paired with QCM uptake indicates true adsorption rather than viscoelastic drift.
- In situ IR (DRIFTS/ATR-FTIR on analog films): under humid VOC exposure, track shifts consistent with defect-bound species (e.g., carbonyl red-shifts for acetone coordination/H-bonding; ammonium-like signatures for TMA protonation/strong acid sites). Correlate IR band evolution rates with QCM fast/slow kinetics.
- Go/no-go: must demonstrate at least one VOC (acetone or TMA) with reproducible two-time-constant behavior that (i) persists under 70–95% RH, (ii) is enhanced by defect engineering, and (iii) is corroborated by outlet monitoring and/or IR assignment.

Step 6 — Stability, compatibility, and drift control (mandatory accelerated aging matrix)
6.1 Aging matrix (stack-level on QCM):
- RH cycling: 40↔95% RH, 2 cycles/day for 30 days.
- Chemical exposure cycling: repeated exposures to 10–100 ppm ethanol/acetone and 1–10 ppm TMA (or relevant realistic ranges) with purge.
- Pulsing endurance: ≥10,000 calibration pulses (thermal/IR) with periodic performance checks.
6.2 Pre/post characterization and acceptance:
- MOF integrity: PXRD/SEM on sacrificial sister samples; ATR-FTIR/XPS for functional groups; quantify Al–OH/defect proxies (acid–base titration) before/after.
- Film adhesion: repeat adhesion metric (Step 3.1) and quantify mass loss from QCM baseline.
- Drift metrics: baseline Δf drift ≤ 5 Hz/day (after internal standard correction) at fixed RH; sensitivity loss ≤20% after aging.
- Failure analysis: if drift correlates with overlayer modulus changes (ΔD increase) redesign overlayer; if drift correlates with MOF chemical change (XPS/IR), adjust grafting chemistry or regeneration protocol.

Step 7 — E-nose modeling and benchmarking under realistic matrices
7.1 Feature engineering (explicitly separating MOF vs overlayer contributions):
- Use multi-overtone Δf_n and ΔD_n features, extracted fast/slow time constants and amplitudes, equilibrium uptake, and internal-standard pulse features (amplitude, decay) to correct drift.
7.2 Mixture inference:
- Concentration estimation: PLS regression (or Bayesian regression) using kinetic+equilibrium features.
- Classification: probabilistic classifiers for mixture labels; compare to models trained on equilibrium-only features.
7.3 Benchmarks:
- LOD/LOQ in humid breath-mimic and food headspace-mimic mixtures, validated vs GC–MS.
- Compare four architectures: (i) MOF-only, (ii) MOF + overlayer without calibration reservoirs, (iii) MOF + overlayer + calibration pulsing, (iv) non-defect-engineered MOF variants.
- Success criterion: improved accuracy and lower effective LOD under 70–95% RH for architectures (ii–iii) without violating viscoelastic/transport go/no-go constraints.
Feasibility:
1) Addressing viscoelastic confounding directly (reviewer point 1): The revised design constrains the overlayer to sub-micron thickness and enforces explicit ΔD and overtone-scaling gates to keep the response adsorption-dominated. If those gates fail, the plan mandates Voigt modeling with independent thickness/mass cross-checks (ellipsometry/profilometry), preventing misassignment of swelling/softening as adsorption. This turns “acknowledging dissipation” into a quantified acceptance workflow.

2) Preventing transport/partitioning from dominating kinetics (reviewer point 2): The proposal now includes a standalone transport-and-partitioning campaign (Deff, Kfilm/gas, RH swelling) on overlayer-only controls, with go/no-go criteria that cap overlayer uptake and ensure diffusion times are minor relative to the MOF response. This ensures the intended kinetic fingerprints originate in MIL-96(Al) adsorption rather than a PDMS-like sink or diffusion barrier.

3) Definitive validation of bimodal adsorption kinetics under humid dynamic conditions (reviewer point 3): Beyond –OH titration and initial heats, the plan adds step-response relaxation analysis across RH and concentration, pulse-response deconvolution using internal calibration impulses, and independent assignment via QCM+MS outlet monitoring and in situ IR signatures. Demonstrating defect-density-dependent emergence of a slow kinetic component under 70–95% RH provides decisive evidence for two kinetically separable site classes relevant under flow.

4) Chemical stability/compatibility and drift (reviewer point 4): The proposal adds an accelerated aging matrix spanning RH cycling, amine/oxygenate exposure, and ≥10,000 actuation pulses, with explicit pre/post defect-site proxies, adhesion metrics, and drift thresholds. This directly tests whether defect grafting, amine exposure (e.g., TMA), and pulsing alter site populations or binder chemistry—and ties observed drift to either MOF chemistry or overlayer mechanics for actionable redesign.

5) Overall plausibility of ppb-class operation: Literature on MOF-QCM arrays supports ppm-to-ppb discrimination when adsorption is selective and arrays exploit orthogonal responses; kinetic+thermodynamic co-design (including information-rich transients) is established as beneficial for mixture estimation. The revised proposal makes ppb-class claims conditional on passing the mechanical and transport gates and on demonstrating true bimodal kinetics under humid flow. That conditional structure de-risks the ambition while preserving the original concept chain (MIL-96(Al) defect engineering + time-resolved QCM e-nose + humidity-buffered/calibration-enabled layer).
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and technically mature proposal that directly confronts the dominant failure modes of MOF–QCM sensing under humidity. Engineering resolution is very high: dissipation thresholds, overtone consistency metrics, Voigt fallback rules, independent thickness/mass cross-checks, and transport time-scale caps are all explicitly defined and enforceable. Logical consistency is strong—the dual-site adsorption hypothesis is chemically credible for MIL-96(Al), and the proposal correctly recognizes that kinetic information is only meaningful if viscoelastic and transport artifacts are quantitatively bounded. Evidence grounding is solid and remains within gravimetric sensing, MOF chemistry, and e-nose literature; no speculative cross-disciplinary leaps are made. Minor deductions arise from (i) the practical risk that maintaining ≤20% RH-induced modulus variation in real microporous overlayers may be difficult across 40–95% RH, and (ii) the ambitious scope: multiple defect chemistries, multilayer stacks, QCM-D+MS+IR coupling, and long aging matrices could strain resources and timelines. These are feasibility, not conceptual, weaknesses.

Hypothesis:
A MOF-templated, peptide-imprinted double-hollow heterostructure—In2S3 hollow nanorods (HNRs) bearing a conformal, ultrathin In/Fe–MIL-101(BDC)-analog shell that is kinetically “arrested” during sulfidation into a nanometric Fe/In–Sx–(oxy)carboxylate–C interlayer—will deliver (i) photocurrent amplification from decoupled optical and electronic gain mechanisms (multi-light scattering in the hollow architecture + improved charge separation/transport from a type-II or quasi–type-II interfacial band gradient) and (ii) biosensing specificity enforced by an epitope-imprinted cavity whose binding-face presentation is *experimentally verified post-immobilization*, not assumed from solution NOE alone.

Mechanistic rationale addressing reviewer concerns:
1) Conformal MOF coating is enabled by a defined surface-priming nucleation strategy that converts the chemically “inert/defect-rich” In2S3 surface into a high density of carboxylate/phosphonate anchoring sites, thereby controlling heterogeneous nucleation, shell continuity, and thickness at the 5–20 nm scale.
2) Partial MOF-to-sulfide conversion is treated as a parameterized kinetic map (temperature, time, sulfur activity) with in situ/time-resolved phase/chemistry readouts. The interlayer’s carbon is hypothesized to originate from *BDC linker carbonization/graphitization under sulfidation* and to act as (a) a percolating electronic bridge and (b) a defect-stabilizer that suppresses macroscopic FeSx segregation by trapping Fe in mixed Fe–S–C/O coordination environments. The conversion is purposely stopped before complete collapse to dense sulfides, preserving mesoporosity and residual coordination handles (carboxylate/Fe sites) for recognition chemistry.
3) NOE defines the epitope’s solution contact map, but surface presentation is ensured through a *single-point, site-specific anchoring* design plus direct experimental verification (surface-sensitive/FRET/STD-NMR on immobilized peptide). Imprinting is performed under conditions that minimize peptide refolding and polymer shrinkage, and cavity fidelity is validated against scrambled-sequence and immobilization-geometry controls.

Together, these refinements make coating continuity, interlayer composition/porosity, and epitope face exposure measurable “control knobs,” enabling deconvolution of scattering vs junction vs recognition contributions to PEC performance.
Plan:
Step 0 — Define controls and normalization (pre-registered):
0.1 Build a full control matrix to deconvolute effects:
- Geometry controls: solid In2S3 rods (no void) with matched external dimensions; hollow In2S3 with collapsed void (post-anneal) to decouple scattering.
- Shell controls: (i) no shell, (ii) non-MOF-derived FeSx deposition (CBD or SILAR) with matched Fe loading, (iii) pure In–MIL-101 shell (no Fe), (iv) pure Fe–MIL-101 shell (no In) where possible.
- Recognition controls: non-imprinted polymer (NIP), scrambled epitope imprint, and altered anchoring geometry (multi-point vs single-point).
0.2 Normalization plan (mandatory for each PEC dataset):
- Fix catalyst mass loading on FTO (µg cm−2) by quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) during deposition or by gravimetric difference with replicate electrodes.
- Determine electroactive surface area (ECSA) by double-layer capacitance (Cdl) in non-faradaic window and report photocurrent normalized to ECSA.
- Measure optical absorption (integrating sphere UV–Vis DRS on films) and report incident-photon-to-current efficiency (IPCE) and absorbed-photon-to-current efficiency (APCE) to separate absorption/scattering from charge-separation.
- Report film roughness/thickness (profilometry/AFM) and keep within ±10% across comparisons.

Step 1 — In2S3 hollow nanorods with tunable cavity for scattering:
1.1 Synthesize In2S3 HNRs via hard-template route (AAO or polymer rods):
- Target outer diameter 150–300 nm; inner diameter 60–200 nm; shell thickness 10–30 nm.
- Acceptance criteria: TEM statistics on ≥200 rods: shell thickness CV ≤ 15%; void fraction 0.30–0.70; >90% rods hollow (no fully solid rods).
1.2 Quantify scattering potential:
- Integrating-sphere DRS on powder and on deposited films; extract scattering coefficient via Kubelka–Munk and fit with Monte Carlo photon transport using measured film thickness.

Step 2 — Surface priming for conformal MIL-101-like growth on sulfide (explicit nucleation protocol):
2.1 Clean/activate In2S3 surface without oxidation:
- Mild plasma (Ar, low power, short duration) or UV–ozone minimized; confirm In(III)/S(−II) states by XPS (no excessive sulfate).
2.2 Install an anchoring interfacial primer (choose one as primary, one as backup):
Primary (phosphonate primer; high affinity to In sites):
- Treat HNRs with 2-carboxyethylphosphonic acid (CEPA) or 11-phosphonoundecanoic acid (PUA) in ethanol/water (pH 4–5) to form In–O–P bonds; terminal –COOH presents carboxylate nucleation sites.
Backup (polydopamine–carboxylate co-primer):
- Deposit ultra-thin PDA (2–5 nm) followed by succinic anhydride ring-opening to enrich –COOH; preserves adhesion and increases nucleation density.
2.3 Verify priming density and uniformity:
- XPS: P 2p (phosphonate) and O 1s increase; attenuated In 3d consistent with sub-2 nm overlayer.
- ζ-potential shift to more negative at neutral pH.
- Acceptance: primer present on ≥95% particles (XPS survey across batches) and no aggregation (DLS, TEM).

Step 3 — Conformal bimetallic MIL-101(BDC)-analog shell growth with thickness control:
3.1 Use a “seeded, modulated” growth to force heterogeneous nucleation:
- Pre-seeding: expose primed HNRs to dilute Fe3+/In3+ solution (e.g., FeCl3 + In(NO3)3, total 1–5 mM) to form surface-bound metal–carboxylate/phosphonate complexes.
- Growth solution: BDC (terephthalic acid) + Fe3+/In3+ in DMF/EtOH/H2O with monocarboxylate modulator (acetic acid) to suppress homogeneous nucleation.
- Metal ratio series: Fe:In = 0.2:0.8, 0.5:0.5, 0.8:0.2 (molar in feed) to tune band alignment/Fe site density.
3.2 Thickness tuning knobs:
- Total metal concentration (e.g., 5–50 mM), modulator:BDC ratio (e.g., 10–50), temperature (80–120 °C), time (0.5–6 h).
- Apply a “stop-growth” wash with excess modulator to cap surfaces and limit secondary growth.
3.3 Quantitative acceptance criteria for conformality:
- TEM/STEM: shell continuity ≥ 90% of rod surface length with no pinholes >5 nm; thickness 5–20 nm with σ ≤ 3 nm across ≥50 rods.
- Porosity retention: N2 sorption (powder) shows measurable micro/mesoporosity; BET not necessarily MIL-101-level, but must exceed primed HNR baseline by ≥50%.
- Phase/structure confirmation: XRD/FTIR consistent with MIL-101-like coordination (carboxylate bands) while recognizing nanoshell broadening.

Step 4 — Controlled partial sulfidation: conversion map + operando/time-resolved characterization:
4.1 Define sulfidation parameter space (“conversion map”):
- Sulfur sources: thioacetamide (solution, 80–120 °C) and/or H2S/Ar (gas, 150–350 °C) as orthogonal methods.
- Variables: T (80–350 °C), time (5–240 min), sulfur activity (TAA concentration or H2S partial pressure), ramp rate.
- Goal window: convert outer MOF coordination network into mixed Fe/In–Sx while retaining (i) residual carboxylate/oxycarboxylate signatures and (ii) an sp2/sp3 carbon fraction from linker carbonization.
4.2 Carbon origin/role hypothesis and tests:
- Hypothesis: BDC linker partially carbonizes under sulfidation (especially in gas-phase at ≥200 °C), forming a thin amorphous/graphenic carbon that electronically couples Fe/In sulfide domains and suppresses FeSx crystallite coarsening.
- Tests: Raman (D/G bands), XPS C 1s (sp2/sp3), and elemental analysis; correlate carbon content with conductivity (four-point probe on films) and with FeSx domain size (STEM).
4.3 Time-resolved/operando readouts to avoid phase ambiguity:
- Time-resolved XRD during conversion (where feasible) to detect emergence of FeSx/In2S3 reflections.
- Raman mapping to track linker→carbon evolution and sulfide vibrational modes.
- XPS depth profiling (gentle Ar cluster) to map Fe/In/S/C vs depth and confirm interlayer rather than segregated outer FeSx crust.
- STEM-EDS/EELS mapping at nanometer resolution to quantify co-localization (Fe and S) and whether Fe concentrates at outer surface or is interdispersed.
4.4 Acceptance criteria for “partial conversion, porous, handle-rich interlayer”:
- No macroscopic FeSx crystallites >10–15 nm (STEM);
- Residual O/C signatures consistent with remaining carboxylate/oxycarboxylate at ≥10–20% of initial carboxylate signal (FTIR/XPS) to preserve coupling handles;
- Mesoporosity retained (hysteresis/uptake) and shell not densified into impermeable layer (electrochemical probe diffusion test with Fe(CN)6 3−/4−).

Step 5 — PEC electrode assembly and mechanism deconvolution:
5.1 Deposition onto FTO:
- Electrophoretic deposition (EPD) in low-water alcohol with iodine or Mg(NO3)2 charging agent; target uniform films of controlled thickness (e.g., 1–3 µm).
- Mild anneal under inert (e.g., 150–250 °C) only if needed for contact; verify hollows preserved by TEM on scraped film.
5.2 PEC testing:
- Chopped illumination, wavelength-resolved IPCE/APCE; mediator screening (ascorbate vs O2) selected to match band positions and avoid sulfide photocorrosion.
- Mechanism suite with controls: TRPL quenching, transient photocurrent, EIS, Mott–Schottky, UPS/XPS for band edges.
- Explicit deconvolution: compare (hollow vs solid) at constant composition to isolate scattering contribution; compare (MOF-derived interlayer vs non-MOF FeSx) at constant Fe loading to isolate junction/interlayer chemistry.

Step 6 — NOE-guided epitope design AND verified surface presentation (closing the “NOE-to-surface” gap):
6.1 Epitope selection/design:
- Choose CA15-3 (MUC1) epitope (10–20 aa) from solvent-exposed repeat region; incorporate a designed aromatic/cationic pair (Trp/Phe with Lys/Arg) to enable a C–H···π/cation–π signature.
- Prepare mutants disrupting the NOE contact: Lys→Nle and/or Trp→Cha (as per literature logic) while keeping overall hydrophobicity comparable.
6.2 Solution conformation validation:
- 2D NOESY/ROESY to define key intrapeptide distances for aromatic–Lys proximity and any β-turn propensity.
6.3 Site-specific single-point immobilization to preserve face presentation:
- Engineer a unique anchor handle at peptide terminus (e.g., N-terminal cysteine or azido-lysine) separated by a short spacer (PEG2–PEG6) to minimize surface-induced refolding.
- Surface coupling options:
  (i) Maleimide-functionalized carboxylate handle on interlayer (EDC/NHS to introduce maleimide-amine linker) for Cys anchoring;
  (ii) Click chemistry (surface alkyne/azide) if residual carboxylates are abundant.
- Avoid multipoint adsorption by passivating residual Fe sites with weak ligands (e.g., acetate) prior to peptide coupling, then selectively re-open sites post-coupling if needed.
6.4 Direct verification that the NOE-defined face is exposed after immobilization:
- FRET geometry test: label peptide with donor near aromatic and acceptor near anchor; compare FRET efficiency in solution vs immobilized; loss indicates surface-flattening.
- Surface-sensitive spectroscopy: PM-IRRAS or SFG to assess orientation changes (amide I/II and aromatic modes).
- Binding-site accessibility: antibody/lectin probing specific to the epitope segment as an orthogonal check.
- Optional high-rigor: STD-NMR on immobilized peptide with soluble “cavity monomer” or target protein fragment to confirm the same contact face participates.

Step 7 — Imprinting with cavity fidelity controls:
7.1 Form thin imprint layer with controlled shrinkage:
- Use a metal–ligand crosslinked imprint (PICN-like) or a low-shrinkage sol–gel/coordination polymer; keep thickness 5–30 nm (ellipsometry/TEM).
- Polymerization under buffered aqueous conditions approximating NMR conditions to reduce conformation drift.
7.2 Template removal:
- Competitive elution (high ionic strength + mild chelator) designed not to strip interlayer Fe excessively; confirm by ICP-MS of eluate.
7.3 Fidelity/negative controls:
- NIP on same substrate;
- Imprint using scrambled epitope;
- Imprint using mutant epitope (Lys→Nle / Trp→Cha);
- Immobilization geometry variants (single-point vs intentionally multipoint) to show specificity collapses when orientation is not controlled.

Step 8 — Biosensing validation in complex media:
8.1 Analytical figures of merit:
- Calibration in buffer and 10–50% serum; report LOD, linear range, slope, RSD (intra/inter-assay), and 2+ week storage stability.
8.2 Selectivity panel:
- Closely related glycoproteins and abundant serum proteins (albumin, IgG, transferrin); compute cross-reactivity factors and apparent Kd via SPR/QCM-D.
8.3 Structure–function maps:
- Hollow geometry (void fraction, shell thickness) vs scattering coefficient vs APCE.
- Conversion degree (XPS depth + Raman D/G + XRD) vs EIS Rct, band edges, and photocurrent.
- Imprint thickness vs mass transport (probe diffusion) vs specificity factor.
Feasibility:
1) Conformal MIL-101-like shell feasibility is converted into measurable process control: phosphonate/carboxylate surface priming creates deterministic nucleation sites on In2S3, while modulated solvothermal growth (acetic-acid modulation + pre-seeding) is a well-established route to suppress homogeneous MOF nucleation and enforce thin, continuous coatings. Quantitative acceptance criteria (shell continuity %, thickness σ, porosity gain) prevent “hand-wavy” conformity claims.

2) Partial conversion feasibility is addressed via a kinetic conversion map tied to multi-modal compositional/phase mapping (time-resolved XRD/Raman, XPS depth profiling, STEM-EELS/EDS). Rather than asserting an Fe/In–Sx–C interlayer exists, the proposal defines what counts as success (no large FeSx segregation; retained O/C handles; retained permeability) and how carbon is generated (BDC carbonization) and validated (Raman/XPS/EA). The interlayer is intentionally formed under kinetically limited conditions to avoid full collapse to dense sulfides and to retain porosity/handles.

3) The NOE-to-surface orientation gap is closed by design and verification: NOE is used to choose an epitope with a defined contact map, but face presentation is enforced by single-point, site-specific immobilization with spacers and is experimentally checked post-attachment (FRET/orientation-sensitive IR/SFG and/or STD-NMR). Imprint fidelity is proven with scrambled/mutant epitopes and immobilization-geometry variants, directly testing the reviewer’s concern that surface-induced folding or polymer shrinkage can scramble the contact map.

4) Mechanistic claims are deconvoluted with strict normalization and matched controls: APCE/IPCE separates absorption/scattering from charge separation; ECSA normalization and constant loading isolate intrinsic activity; solid vs hollow and MOF-derived vs non-MOF shells isolate scattering vs junction chemistry. This makes type-II/quasi-type-II alignment and scattering gains testable rather than inferred.

5) Empirical precedent supports the core concept chain: double-hollow heterostructures are known to enhance PEC via multi-light scattering and reduced recombination (Asset 1 logic), while aromatic/cationic contacts provide specificity that can be interrogated by NOE and mutant-cycle-like disruptions (Asset 2 logic). The revised plan adds the missing materials-chemistry and surface-biophysics rigor needed to reliably implement and validate those principles in a MOF-templated PEC biosensor.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and technically mature proposal that anticipates and directly addresses common reviewer objections in MOF-derived heterostructures and imprint-based biosensing. Engineering resolution is very high: nearly every speculative step is converted into a parameterized process with quantitative acceptance criteria and orthogonal characterization. Logical consistency is strong, particularly in the deconvolution of optical scattering, junction chemistry, and recognition effects through pre-registered controls and normalization. Minor score deductions arise from cumulative complexity and execution risk: the simultaneous optimization of conformal bimetallic MOF growth, partial sulfidation with controlled carbonization, and peptide orientation verification represents a very high experimental burden that could challenge timelines and reproducibility, even though each step is individually defensible. Evidence grounding is excellent, staying tightly within PEC, MOF chemistry, and surface biophysics, though some operando techniques (e.g., time-resolved XRD during sulfidation) may be aspirational rather than routine. The rationale quality is high, with genuine structural and conceptual innovation aimed at solving known bottlenecks (shell conformity, interlayer ambiguity, NOE-to-surface mismatch), rather than incremental application of known methods.

Hypothesis:
A ZIF67@ZIF8 core–shell can be converted into a visible-light-responsive, micropore-confined photocatalyst for selective C–C coupling of methanol-derived C1 intermediates to ethanol **only if** (a) the Ni chemical endpoint is explicitly constrained to a *defect-docked, imidazolate/N-donor coordinated Ni(II) single-site* within an intact ZIF8 shell (not “O-vacancies” in the ZIF lattice), (b) the shell is engineered to support *measurable* interfacial electronic communication with the Co-rich core via a deliberately introduced short-range electronic bridge, and (c) ethanol formation is validated by strict atom/redox balance closure with identified coproducts and electron sinks.

**Defined Ni-site/defect model (replaces ‘O-vacancy’):** Ni is installed post-synthetically into the ZIF8 shell as isolated Ni(II) bound to 2-methylimidazolate (mIm−) and nitrate-derived inner-sphere ligands at pre-existing or induced shell defects. The intended coordination is **Ni(II)(mIm)3–4(ONO2)0–1(H2O/ROH)0–1**, i.e., a mixed N/O donor environment where nitrate is a *labile spectator/charge-balancing ligand* rather than a lattice oxygen source. Upon mild activation (≤250 °C, inert), nitrate is **removed/converted** to volatile NOx (tracked by TGA-MS) leaving **coordinatively unsaturated Ni–Nx sites (Ni(II)–N3/4)** and/or **Ni–OH/Ni–OMe** after exposure to methanol—these are the chemically explicit, testable “defects”. No claim is made of true lattice O-vacancies, and no Ni–N4 ‘M–N–C’ motif is claimed unless partial carbonization is intentionally invoked as a separate, gated branch.

**Mechanistic rationale for ethanol plausibility (with redox/atom balance):** Under visible light, photoexcitation in the Co-containing core (or core–shell interfacial states) generates separated charges that are funneled to the shell Ni site, enabling a *two-step C1→C2 coupling sequence* that competes with over-oxidation because methanol is enriched inside micropores (Type I regime) and oxygen is excluded/limited.

Two operating regimes are explicitly proposed and will be distinguished by product closure:

(1) **Inert (no external oxidant) “acceptorless” coupling with H2 as coproduct (primary target):**
Overall target stoichiometry (carbon/oxygen balanced):
**2 CH3OH → C2H5OH + H2O + H2**
This is redox-neutral overall but requires photocatalytic charge separation to enable dehydrogenation/coupling steps at low temperature. The proposed elementary accounting is:
- Two sequential PCET-enabled dehydrogenations: CH3OH → HCHO + 2H+ + 2e− (occurs twice)
- C–C formation via confined coupling/hydrogenation cascade: HCHO + CH3OH → C2 oxygenate (e.g., HOCH2CH2OH or CH3CHO) followed by reduction/hydrogenation to ethanol.
- Electrons/protons are balanced by **H2 evolution** on Ni/Co interfacial sites: 2H+ + 2e− → H2.
**Pass/fail prediction:** If ethanol is truly formed under inert conditions, measurable H2 must be co-produced with a molar relationship consistent with closure (within experimental error after accounting for minor side products).

(2) **Trace O2 (controlled ppm–0.5%) “oxidant-assisted” coupling with H2O2/H2O as sinks (secondary regime):**
O2 functions as terminal electron acceptor to pull electrons away, suppressing recombination, but must not drive total oxidation.
Representative balanced variant (one admissible closure model):
**2 CH3OH + 1/2 O2 → C2H5OH + H2O**
Here, O2 accepts the net 2e−/2H+ equivalents that otherwise appear as H2. Alternative sink: H2O2 formation (to be measured), e.g., O2 + 2H+ + 2e− → H2O2.
**Pass/fail prediction:** In trace O2 runs, H2 yield should decrease; H2O2 (or increased H2O) must appear to satisfy electron balance, and COx must remain low if selectivity claim holds.

**Charge-transfer across shell—explicit constraint:** Meaningful Co(core)→Ni(shell) electronic communication is not assumed for 20–100 nm shells. Instead, the shell thickness is constrained to **≤5–15 nm** (primary design window) and/or an electronic bridge is introduced by **mixed-linker or redox-mediator doping** in the shell that creates through-bond/through-state hopping sites (quantitatively verified by thickness-dependent kinetics and action spectra). Thus, the revised hypothesis claims *distance-limited interfacial ET* rather than generic ‘junction’ behavior.

**Why the refined approach overcomes reviewer-identified limitations:** (i) the Ni endpoint is chemically explicit and verifiable (Ni–N/O defect-docked single site; no lattice O-vacancy claim), (ii) the activation window is chosen to preserve ZIF8 while enabling nitrate removal and Ni coordination unsaturation (≤250 °C, with PXRD/sorption gating), (iii) ethanol plausibility is enforced by strict atom/redox closure with explicit coproduct predictions (H2 under inert; H2O2/H2O under trace O2), and (iv) interfacial ET is engineered and quantified via shell-thickness limits and deliberate bridge states rather than assumed through an intact thick shell.
Plan:
Step 0 — Hard gating decision tree (mandatory): choose one of two Ni endpoints and lock conditions accordingly.
0A. **Endpoint A (primary): defect-docked Ni(II)–Nx/NO3 in intact ZIF8** with activation ≤250 °C, preserved crystallinity/microporosity.
0B. **Endpoint B (secondary, separate aim): Ni–Nx in partially carbonized shell (M–N–C-like)** requiring ≥500–700 °C and accepting loss of ZIF crystallinity. Endpoint B is optional and will only be pursued if Endpoint A fails ethanol selectivity/closure.

Step 1 — Core–shell synthesis with shell thickness in ET-relevant regime.
1.1 Synthesize ZIF67 cores in methanol (Co2+ + 2-methylimidazole) targeting 100–300 nm cores (monodisperse) to ensure resolvable core–shell gradients.
1.2 Overgrow ZIF8 shell in methanol to **5, 10, 15, 30 nm** thickness series (not 20–100 nm as default). Control via Zn2+ feed rate, mIm/Zn ratio, and growth time.
1.3 Characterize: STEM-EDS line scan (Co core/Zn shell), PXRD (ZIF67+ZIF8), N2 sorption (77 K) targeting Type I isotherm with preserved micropore volume after shelling.

Step 2 — Ni installation as defect-docked single sites (chemically specified).
2.1 **Solvent and hydrolysis control:** Perform Ni loading under rigorously anhydrous alcohol (absolute ethanol or methanol) with ≤0.05% H2O; N2 glovebox if needed. Maintain pH-neutral conditions (no added base) to suppress Ni(OH)2 precipitation.
2.2 **Defect-docking protocol (low driving force):** Suspend ZIF67@ZIF8 in EtOH/MeOH (1:1) containing Ni(NO3)2·6H2O at 1–10 mM, plus a controlled mIm co-feed (Ni:mIm = 1:4 to 1:8) to rapidly re-ligate transient Zn–N bond cleavage and prevent shell etching.
2.3 **Limit Ni to isolated sites:** Target Ni loading 0.1–1.0 wt% initially; iterate only after site proof. Short contact times (0.5–6 h), low temperature (20–40 °C).
2.4 **Post-treatment wash sequence (removes extraframework Ni nitrate):** alcohol washing → weakly coordinating wash (acetonitrile) → final alcohol wash. Collect wash liquors for ICP to quantify removable Ni.

Step 3 — Activation that is consistent with intact ZIF8 and explicit nitrate fate.
3.1 **Thermal window:** 180–250 °C under flowing N2 (or Ar), 1–4 h. This is chosen to drive partial nitrate dissociation/NOx evolution without ZIF8 decomposition/carbonization.
3.2 **Nitrate fate verification (no “O-vacancy” language):** TGA-MS/TPD-MS to quantify NO, NO2, N2O evolution; XPS N 1s/O 1s before/after to track nitrate removal and formation of Ni–OH/Ni–OMe after methanol exposure.
3.3 **Framework integrity gating:** PXRD peak retention + N2 sorption micropore volume retention ≥80% relative to parent ZIF67@ZIF8; failure triggers re-optimization or Endpoint B branch.

Step 4 — Engineering and verifying interfacial electronic communication (quantitative).
4.1 **Thickness-dependent kinetics:** Run identical photocatalysis on thickness series (5–30 nm). A monotonic decay of activity with thickness consistent with short-range ET supports interfacial communication; no dependence indicates shell-isolated chemistry.
4.2 **Electronic bridge (implemented if thickness dependence is weak):** Introduce a mixed-linker shell fraction (e.g., low % amino-functionalized imidazole derivative) to create mid-gap/hopping states while preserving ZIF topology; alternatively, incorporate a tethered redox mediator (e.g., viologen-like cation) confined in shell pores by ion-pairing. Selection is validated by DRS/Tauc shifts and increased transient photocurrent.
4.3 **Action spectra requirement:** Measure wavelength-dependent AQY and compare to absorption; matching trends are required to claim true photodriven chemistry.

Step 5 — Photocatalysis with strict atom/redox balance closure (pass/fail criteria).
5.1 Reactor: sealed batch photoreactor (quartz), temperature-controlled with internal thermocouple; parallel dark controls at matched temperature profile.
5.2 Feeds:
- Inert regime: methanol (neat or MeOH/H2O defined ratios), N2 purge; quantify dissolved gases.
- Trace O2 regime: controlled O2 addition (ppm–0.5%) using mass-flow mixing; verify by GC.
5.3 Analytics (mandatory closure):
- Liquid: GC-FID/GC-MS + 1H NMR (internal standard) for ethanol, formaldehyde (derivatize if needed), methyl formate, dimethyl ether, ethylene glycol, acetaldehyde.
- Gas: GC-TCD for H2, CO, CO2; GC for O2 consumption; quantify H2O2 in liquid (titration or colorimetric).
5.4 **Closure metrics:**
- Carbon balance ≥95% and O/H closure within defined tolerance.
- In inert regime: ethanol formation must correlate with H2 formation per proposed stoichiometry; otherwise ethanol claim is rejected or reinterpreted.

Step 6 — Decisive active-site proof and confounder controls (mandatory additions).
6.1 **Acid wash test (extraframework Ni removal):** mild acid in alcohol (e.g., acetic acid in EtOH) to strip exposed/weakly bound Ni without collapsing ZIF; re-test activity. Large activity loss implies extraframework Ni dominance.
6.2 **Chelator/poison tests:** introduce thiol/chelating agents (e.g., mercaptoethanol or EDTA in controlled minimal water) to selectively poison accessible Ni; compare to unpoisoned. Coupled with porosity data to infer whether Ni is internal vs external.
6.3 **Operando/quasi-operando XAS (Ni K-edge):** confirm absence of Ni–Ni scattering under working conditions and track Ni(II)↔Ni(I) signatures under illumination.
6.4 **EPR/spin trapping + in situ DRIFTS:** detect methoxy/*CH2OH, carbon-centered radicals, and C2 oxygenate intermediates.
6.5 **Photothermal exclusion:** dark thermal controls precisely matching the illuminated catalyst temperature (PID-controlled heating); additionally vary light intensity at constant temperature to demonstrate photochemical rate dependence.

Step 7 — Benchmarking and decision points.
7.1 Compare to: ZIF8, ZIF67, Ni/ZIF8 (no core), physical mixture (no junction), and NiO/ZnO/NC derived materials.
7.2 Normalize by Ni moles, photon flux, and illuminated area; report TOF (per accessible Ni from chemisorption/probe reaction) and selectivity at matched conversion.
7.3 If Endpoint A cannot meet closure/selectivity, proceed to Endpoint B (partial carbonization) as a clearly separated fallback with revised claims (no ‘intact ZIF8’ requirement).
Feasibility:
1) Chemical consistency of the defect model (addresses critique #1/#2): ZIF8 contains no lattice oxygen; the revised plan therefore treats nitrate exclusively as a removable/transformable ligand to Ni (inner-sphere NO3−) and an NOx precursor under mild activation. The structural endpoint is explicitly **defect-docked Ni(II) coordinated to imidazolate N donors with variable residual O-donor ligation** (Ni–NxOy), verifiable by XAS/XPS/DRIFTS and by the absence of Ni–Ni EXAFS. The activation window (≤250 °C) is chosen to preserve ZIF8 crystallinity/microporosity and is gated by PXRD+sorption retention thresholds.

2) Ethanol plausibility is made testable by redox/atom-balance closure (addresses critique #3): Two explicit regimes are defined with predicted coproducts and electron sinks. Under inert conditions, ethanol formation requires H2 co-production consistent with **2 CH3OH → C2H5OH + H2O + H2**; under trace O2, oxygen must appear in H2O/H2O2 with controlled O2 consumption. Carbon/hydrogen/oxygen closure is elevated to a pass/fail criterion rather than an interpretive afterthought, reducing the plausibility barrier to an experimentally decidable question.

3) Charge transfer is no longer assumed across thick shells (addresses critique #4): The shell thickness is constrained to 5–15 nm (primary), and charge/energy transfer is validated quantitatively by thickness-dependent kinetics plus action spectra (AQY vs wavelength). If communication is weak, an explicit electronic bridge (mixed-linker or confined mediator) is introduced and verified by optoelectronic metrics (TRPL, transient photocurrent, EIS) and by restoration/enhancement of thickness dependence.

4) Confounders are directly controlled (addresses critique #5): Hydrolysis/precipitation is suppressed by low-water alcoholic media and low Ni concentration with mIm re-ligation; extraframework Ni is tested by acid washing and chelator/poison experiments; operando EXAFS excludes hidden Ni–Ni aggregation during turnover; and photothermal artifacts are ruled out by matched-temperature dark controls and intensity/temperature decoupling.

5) Alignment with literature assets: The proposal retains the original concept chain—ZIF67@ZIF8 architecture prepared in methanol/ethanol (Asset 2), micropore-limited Type I adsorption as the confinement lever (Asset 3), and heterometal synergy/visible-light charge separation in mixed-metal MOF motifs (Asset 1)—but replaces chemically vague claims with explicit coordination chemistry and decisive validation gates.
Critique: This proposal is unusually rigorous and addresses, head-on, nearly all of the common failure modes in MOF-based photocatalytic C–C coupling claims. The explicit rejection of fictitious lattice O-vacancies in ZIF8 and replacement with a chemically defensible Ni–Nx/NO3 defect-docking model is a major strength. The atom- and redox-balance closure criteria elevate ethanol formation from a speculative claim to a falsifiable hypothesis, which is rarely enforced at this level. Shell-thickness-limited charge transfer is treated realistically, and the inclusion of an engineered electronic bridge as a conditional remedy demonstrates methodological maturity. Minor weaknesses remain: (i) the mechanistic sequence for C–C bond formation (formaldehyde–methanol vs. dual formaldehyde coupling) is acknowledged but not sharply discriminated experimentally beyond product analysis, and (ii) the reliance on nitrate removal ≤250 °C, while plausible, remains experimentally delicate and may lead to partial Ni migration that is difficult to fully exclude even with EXAFS. These are execution risks rather than logical flaws.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a *charge-balanced*, mixed-linker M2(m-dobdc) (M = Co, Ni) in which a controlled fraction of m-dobdc4− linkers is replaced by a mono-sulfonated analogue (m-SO3H–m-dobdc3−) will create an experimentally quantifiable *ensemble* of metal–anion proximities (rather than assuming perfect periodicity) that is nonetheless sufficiently narrow to enable cooperative two-point binding for terminal olefins: (1) π-complexation at open M2+ sites and (2) proximal electrostatic polarization/hydrogen-bond acceptor interactions from tethered sulfonate oxygens and their associated countercations. The mechanistic premise is that terminal olefins (e.g., 1-butene) can adopt a low-entropy, bidentate adsorption geometry—metal–C=C coordination plus field-stabilization of the olefinic quadrupole and/or C–H···O(SO3−) contacts—while internal olefins (cis/trans-2-butene) are penalized by steric/rotational constraints that prevent simultaneous optimal metal coordination and electrostatic stabilization. Crucially, we will *engineer and verify* (i) countercation identity/stoichiometry/location to ensure charge compensation without pore blocking, and (ii) sulfonate–metal distance *distributions* (not single distances) with acceptance criteria that preserve site accessibility. Inelastic neutron scattering (INS), supported by DFT-informed spectral assignment and loading/isotopic controls, will then distinguish whether the observed selectivity arises from true cooperative two-point binding (signature: loading-dependent splitting/softening of hindered-rotation/torsional modes correlated with the population of dual-site geometries) versus heterogeneous single-site adsorption across a disordered lattice.
Plan:
Step 1 — Charge-balanced materials design with explicit countercation strategy (risk-mitigated).
1.1 Linker set and targeted compositions: prepare a series M2(m-dobdc) : M2(m-SO3–m-dobdc) mixed-linker solids with nominal sulfonated-linker fractions x = 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30 (M = Co, Ni). Use the sulfonated linker as the monosulfonate/triacid form (H3[m-SO3–m-dobdc]) such that each substitution introduces −1 framework charge relative to m-dobdc4−.
1.2 Charge compensation: introduce monovalent countercations A+ (Li+, Na+, K+) in stoichiometry A+x per formula unit (i.e., A+ equals the sulfonated-linker fraction) during synthesis/ion-exchange to yield A_x[M2(m-dobdc)1−x(m-SO3–m-dobdc)x]. Rationale: monovalent alkali cations minimize strong specific π-binding that could masquerade as “secondary sites,” while allowing systematic tuning of field strength and mobility.
1.3 Intended countercation location/immobility engineering:
- Primary design: place A+ near sulfonate oxygens (inner-sphere ion pairing) rather than in the channel center. We will promote this by using solvothermal conditions and post-synthetic ion exchange in polar aprotic media (e.g., MeCN/DMF mixtures) followed by activation to encourage A+–SO3− contact pairs.
- Secondary design (if pore blockage observed): switch to smaller/harder cations (Li+) and/or partial replacement with organic cations of low mobility but compact size (e.g., tetramethylammonium, TMA+) at low fraction, explicitly tracked as a variable.
1.4 Metal-site accessibility preservation: implement activation protocols (solvent exchange → vacuum/heat) benchmarked by CO/NO probe IR (for open-metal-site quantification) and N2 adsorption (micropore volume retention). Acceptance criterion: ≥80% of open metal sites retained relative to parent M2(m-dobdc), as assessed by probe uptake/IR band integration.

Step 2 — Quantify linker sequence/disorder and define acceptance criteria for “distance distributions.”
2.1 Average structure confirmation: PXRD with Rietveld refinement to confirm topology retention; unit cell trends vs x used to flag framework distortion.
2.2 Local structure and sulfonate–metal distance distribution:
- Total scattering/PDF (neutron preferred; X-ray as complement) to extract M···O(SO3) and M···S pair correlations. Fit with small-box models spanning random vs clustered substitution to quantify distribution width.
- Diffuse scattering (where measurable) to identify substitutional short-range order vs clustering.
- Solid-state NMR sequence metrics: ^13C ssNMR on linker carbons (and ^23Na/^7Li where applicable) to quantify local environments; 2D correlation (e.g., ^1H–^13C HETCOR) to probe proximity of sulfonate-associated protons/cations to the pore interior.
2.3 Acceptance criteria (pre-registered): proceed to separation/INS only for samples meeting all:
(i) topology retained (no secondary phases by PXRD; Rwp within defined threshold vs parent),
(ii) micropore volume ≥70% of parent,
(iii) open-metal-site probe metric ≥80% of parent,
(iv) PDF-derived M···O(SO3) distribution: primary peak center 3.5–6.0 Å with full width at half maximum (FWHM) ≤ ~1.5 Å (or an empirically defined equivalent) and no dominant population <3.0 Å (which would indicate sulfonate occlusion/chelation of metal sites),
