(v) countercation predominantly associated with sulfonate (ssNMR shift/relaxation consistent with bound state) with limited evidence of freely mobile channel cations.

Step 3 — Demonstrate countercation stoichiometry, location, and immobility (explicit reviewer requirement).
3.1 Stoichiometry: ICP-OES/ICP-MS for A+/M ratio vs target x; elemental analysis for S content to confirm sulfonate incorporation.
3.2 Location and pairing:
- VT PXRD/neutron diffraction (where feasible) to detect ordered/partially ordered A+ positions; monitor thermal displacement parameters vs T.
- ^7Li/^23Na ssNMR (variable temperature): line narrowing and T1/T2 changes used as mobility indicators; bound cations should show limited motional averaging across the relevant temperature window.
- Impedance spectroscopy under dry conditions: low ionic conductivity supports immobile/paired A+; if high conductivity is observed, treat as a failure mode (mobile cations likely act as the true adsorption sites) and adjust cation identity/activation.
3.3 Mobility acceptance criterion: ionic conductivity under dry conditions below a pre-defined threshold (benchmarked against known ionic MOFs) plus ssNMR evidence of restricted motion (no dramatic VT line narrowing characteristic of fast hopping).

Step 4 — Separation validation upgraded to industry-relevant and mechanistically correlated tests.
4.1 Equilibrium adsorption (foundation for IAST): measure single-component isotherms for 1-butene, cis-2-butene, trans-2-butene (and optionally i-/n-butane as controls) at multiple temperatures (e.g., 298/313/333 K). Fit with dual-site Langmuir (or appropriate) models; compute IAST selectivities for relevant mixture compositions.
4.2 Calorimetry: microcalorimetry or variable-T isotherm-derived Qst to separate enthalpic from entropic contributions; compare trends vs x and vs countercation identity.
4.3 Dynamic separations:
- Breakthrough experiments on C4 cuts (ternary 1-butene/cis-2-butene/trans-2-butene; include butanes as industrially relevant contaminants when appropriate). Report productivity metrics, roll-up behavior (if any), and 99.5% purity feasibility.
- Cycling/regeneration: ≥50 adsorption/desorption cycles with mild regeneration (temperature/vacuum) to quantify capacity/selectivity retention.
- Impurity tolerance: test under controlled humidity (ppm–% RH brackets) and acid gas traces (CO2; and, if safe/available, low ppm H2S/CS2 surrogates) to evaluate sulfonate/countercation stability and metal-site poisoning resistance.
4.4 Independent site-population readouts correlated to selectivity:
- In situ IR spectroscopy: quantify π-complexation signatures at open metal sites (C=C interaction-induced shifts) and track any sulfonate-involved perturbations.
- If available, in situ PXRD under gas loadings to observe subtle lattice responses consistent with dual-site binding.

Step 5 — Pre-registered INS workflow robust to multiple adsorption environments.
5.1 DFT-informed spectral library: compute adsorption geometries and vibrational spectra for (a) metal-only binding, (b) sulfonate/countercation-only polarization, and (c) cooperative dual-site binding for each olefin. Include multiple local environments reflecting the measured sulfonate–metal distance distribution (from PDF) rather than a single idealized geometry.
5.2 Loading-dependent INS: collect spectra at a sequence of coverages (e.g., 0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0 molecules per open metal site) to separate strong-site occupation from secondary-site filling. Expectation: cooperative binding should manifest at low-to-intermediate loading with characteristic changes (e.g., hindered-rotation barriers, torsional mode shifts) that saturate as strong sites fill.
5.3 Isotopic labeling to deconvolute modes: where feasible, use selectively deuterated olefins (e.g., 1-butene-d8 vs protio; or partial deuteration) to shift internal vibrational bands and isolate rotational/torsional contributions most sensitive to confinement.
5.4 Site heterogeneity deconvolution: fit INS spectra as linear combinations of DFT-predicted components weighted by site populations constrained by independent measurements (open metal site count from probe IR; sulfonate fraction x; countercation stoichiometry). This constrains ambiguity: “mode splitting” must track the predicted fraction of cooperative geometries across x and loading.
5.5 Mechanistic decision rule (pre-registered): we will claim cooperative two-point binding only if (i) INS-derived hindered-rotation barriers and/or torsional mode splitting correlate monotonically with the independently quantified cooperative-site population proxy (x × accessible-OMS fraction), and (ii) the effect is significantly larger for 1-butene than for 2-butenes under matched loading and temperature, while (iii) control samples (x = 0 or samples failing immobility criteria) do not show the same signatures.

Step 6 — Controls and failure-mode branches.
6.1 Controls: parent M2(m-dobdc) (x = 0); a “cation-only” control where countercations are introduced without sulfonate (to test whether cations alone create secondary sites); and a “blocked OMS” control (partial metal-site passivation) to confirm that selectivity requires π-complexation.
6.2 If clustering/disorder is too high (PDF FWHM too broad): reduce x, adjust synthesis kinetics, or use modulated synthesis to discourage phase separation; alternatively pivot to a 3D-linker strategy to impose more uniform pore environments while retaining the ionic-site concept.
6.3 If cation mobility is high: change cation identity (Li+ → larger less mobile or more strongly paired organic cations) and/or introduce stronger ion-pairing conditions; re-verify with ssNMR/impedance before proceeding.
Feasibility:
Mechanistic feasibility grounded in known OMS selectivity and secondary-site physics: M2(m-dobdc) already separates C4 olefin isomers via open-metal-site π-complexation and charge density effects, providing the primary strong site. Introducing sulfonate functionalities adds a nearby, tethered electrostatic perturbation capable of stabilizing terminal olefin binding geometries via quadrupole-field coupling and C–H···O interactions, consistent with established concepts of secondary binding sites and polarized adsorption landscapes.

Reviewer-risk mitigation (determinism → measurable distributions): rather than asserting crystallographic periodicity, the revised plan treats mixed-linker substitution as an inherently statistical process and makes the central claim contingent on *quantified* sulfonate–metal distance distributions (PDF/diffuse scattering/ssNMR) with explicit acceptance criteria. This converts the “fixed distance” idea into a falsifiable engineering target: if the distribution is too broad or if sulfonate chelates/block OMS, the material is rejected or redesigned.

Charge balance/topology retention explicitly addressed: the framework charge introduced by the triacid sulfonated linker is compensated by a defined amount of monovalent countercations whose identity and stoichiometry are measured (ICP; S analysis). Their location and mobility are treated as first-order design variables and verified using VT diffraction, ^7Li/^23Na ssNMR, and impedance; this directly addresses the risk that mobile countercations become the true adsorption sites or block pores.

Separation relevance and artifact control: the plan adds IAST-validated single-component isotherms across temperature, calorimetry, and—critically—breakthrough separations on realistic multicomponent C4 cuts with cycling and impurity tolerance. Selectivity is correlated to independently measured site populations (OMS probe IR; sulfonate fraction; countercation pairing), reducing the likelihood that apparent selectivity is a calorimetric or heterogeneity artifact.

INS made unambiguous under heterogeneity: INS interpretation is pre-registered as a constrained multi-site analysis tied to DFT libraries spanning the experimentally measured disorder. Loading series and isotopic labeling further separate rotational/translational features from internal vibrations, allowing discrimination of terminal vs internal olefin dynamics even when multiple adsorption environments exist. The proposal therefore remains coherent with the original concept chain (OMS + ionic secondary site → dynamics → selectivity) while meeting the board’s requirement for charge-compensation control, disorder quantification, dynamic separation validation, and mechanistically decisive INS analysis.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-prepared proposal that directly addresses common reviewer concerns in mixed-linker and ionic MOF design, particularly charge balance, disorder, and mechanistic over-interpretation. The engineering plan is detailed, internally consistent, and realistically executable using state-of-the-art techniques (PDF, ssNMR, impedance, INS). The strongest aspect is the pre-registration of acceptance criteria and mechanistic decision rules, which sharply reduces the risk of post hoc rationalization. Minor score deductions arise from residual complexity risk: the simultaneous optimization of linker distribution, countercation immobility, and open-metal-site accessibility across two metals (Co, Ni) and multiple cations may dilute statistical power and extend timelines. Additionally, while the INS decision rule is well defined, successful deconvolution under real disorder remains experimentally fragile and may hinge on neutron beamtime availability and signal-to-noise constraints.

Hypothesis: Embedding carboxylic acid groups as geometrically constrained, hydrogen-bond-assisted “acid pockets” inside a hydrolytically robust Zr6-oxo MOF—followed by post-synthetic, site-specific conversion of a fraction of –COOH to acyl-sulfonamide (–C(O)NHSO2R) or acyl-urea (–C(O)NHCONR2) without disrupting node coordination—will increase the isosteric heat of adsorption for CO2 at low coverage while preserving structural stability under humid/thermal cycling. Mechanistically, (i) paired –COOH groups create cooperative quadrupole-stabilized binding via dual O···C(O) interactions and directional H-bonds to CO2; (ii) partial PSM introduces stronger local dipoles and polarizability, increasing the initial Qst without creating irreversible chemisorption; and (iii) the electron-withdrawing PSM functionality slightly lowers the framework band gap (ligand-centered), enabling optional photothermal/photocatalytic “self-regeneration” under visible light. Thermogravimetric analysis will quantify whether the introduced functionalities alter decomposition/defect chemistry and will be correlated to retained uptake/selectivity after repeated activation.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a Zr6-based platform with proven water stability and accessible linker sites: UiO-66-(COOH)2 (using 2,5-dicarboxyterephthalic acid derivative where one –COOH coordinates and one remains pendant) and a pore-expanded analogue (UiO-67 derivative) to tune confinement.
1.2 Synthesize MOFs with controlled missing-linker defect densities by modulator programming (formic/acetic acid ratio) to create a defined population of open Zr sites while keeping crystallinity; activate via solvent exchange (EtOH) and vacuum.
1.3 Baseline characterization: PXRD, N2 sorption (BET, pore size distribution), FT-IR (pendant –COOH), solid-state 13C NMR (carboxyl signatures), and water vapor isotherms to establish hydrolytic behavior.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation (PSM that preserves node integrity): perform diffusion-limited, pore-confined coupling of pendant –COOH with sulfonamide/urea precursors using mild carbodiimide chemistry optimized for MOFs (EDC/NHS in anhydrous acetonitrile or DMF with controlled water content <0.1%).
2.2 Achieve spatial and compositional control by (i) using bulky sulfonamide nucleophiles (R = iPr, tBu-phenyl) to preferentially modify near-pore-mouth sites, and (ii) using smaller nucleophiles (R = Me, Et) for deeper pore penetration; quantify functionalization gradients by microtomed IR mapping and XPS depth profiling (surface vs bulk).
2.3 Generate a “paired-acid pocket” motif: target ~30–60% conversion of pendant –COOH to acyl-sulfonamide/urea, leaving remaining –COOH to act as H-bond donors adjacent to strong dipoles; verify conversion by FT-IR (amide C=O stretch), 15N ssNMR (if labeled nucleophile), and elemental analysis.
2.4 Band gap tuning/verification: measure diffuse reflectance UV–vis (Kubelka–Munk) to extract optical band gaps before/after PSM; compare with DFT (cluster or periodic) calculations to connect functional group electronics with frontier orbital shifts.
2.5 CO2 adsorption thermodynamics: collect CO2 isotherms at multiple temperatures (e.g., 273/288/298 K) down to low pressures (<0.1 bar) and calculate isosteric heat of adsorption (Qst) via virial fitting/Clausius–Clapeyron at constant loading; separately quantify Henry’s constants and selectivity (CO2/N2, CO2/CH4) by IAST.
2.6 Mechanistic validation of binding: in situ DRIFTS under CO2 dosing to identify bound CO2 motifs (C=O shifts, bicarbonate exclusion), and microcalorimetry (if available) to directly measure differential heats at near-zero coverage; compare to simulated binding energies and preferred adsorption sites from GCMC/DFT.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural stability under realistic conditions: subject materials to (i) humid CO2 (e.g., 50–80% RH) cycling, (ii) thermal swing (ambient to 120–150 °C) activation cycles, and (iii) dilute acid gas contaminants (trace SO2/NOx at ppm levels) to probe robustness.
3.2 Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA): run TGA/DTG under N2 and air to (i) quantify residual solvent/PSM mass increments, (ii) determine decomposition onset shifts due to PSM/defects, and (iii) assess whether functionalization introduces labile groups; pair with variable-temperature PXRD to separate solvent loss from framework collapse.
3.3 Performance metrics for carbon dioxide sequestration: report working capacity under PSA/VSA-relevant windows (e.g., 0.15–1 bar, 298 K; and 0.01–0.15 bar for DAC-relevant tests), regeneration energy estimate from Qst and heat capacities, and long-term capacity retention over ≥50 cycles.
3.4 Comparative controls: (i) parent UiO-66/67, (ii) fully carboxylated without PSM, (iii) fully converted (near-quantitative amide) to test loss of cooperative H-bonding, and (iv) an amine-functional analogue to benchmark against conventional basic sites.
3.5 Decision criteria: success is defined as simultaneously achieving higher initial Qst (target +5–15 kJ/mol at low coverage vs parent), equal-or-better working capacity, <5% crystallinity loss after humid cycling, and no significant decrease in BET area beyond what is predictable from added mass/partial pore narrowing.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Carboxylic acid functionalities can enhance CO2 uptake and increase isosteric heat of adsorption by strengthening specific interactions beyond surface area effects (cf. acidic CMP networks). Zr6-oxo frameworks (UiO family) are among the most hydrolytically and thermally stable MOFs, providing a suitable scaffold for aggressive functional group chemistry while retaining crystallinity. Prior MOF studies link electronic structure (band gap) to light-driven reactivity, enabling a rational route to couple adsorption tuning with optional photo-assisted regeneration.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation is a controlled post-synthetic modification of pendant –COOH groups that explicitly avoids altering the metal–carboxylate coordination bonds responsible for framework integrity. By tuning the degree and spatial distribution of conversion, the design creates cooperative binding motifs (acid + dipole) inside confined pores—an explicitly supramolecular, structure-directed strategy consistent with MOF reticular chemistry.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to simple amine grafting (often moisture-sensitive and potentially chemisorptive), the proposed acid-pocket + partial acyl-sulfonamide/urea motif aims for high low-pressure CO2 affinity with reversible physisorption-dominant binding, improved tolerance to humidity, and quantifiable stability via TGA/PXRD cycling. Band gap modulation provides an extra handle to explore light-assisted desorption without adding external photothermal agents, while the defect/PSM control decouples stability from adsorption strength—addressing a common trade-off in CO2 sorbents.
Critique: This is a technically sophisticated and largely convincing proposal that demonstrates strong command of Zr-based MOF chemistry, post-synthetic modification strategies, and adsorption thermodynamics. The engineering plan is unusually detailed, with credible execution paths (EDC/NHS PSM, defect programming, low-pressure Qst determination, in situ spectroscopy) and appropriate controls. The central mechanistic logic—cooperative acid/dipole binding enhancing low-coverage CO2 affinity without irreversible chemisorption—is sound and well-aligned with current understanding. Minor deductions arise from two areas: (i) the band-gap/photothermal self-regeneration component is comparatively underdeveloped and risks appearing speculative without a clearer energy-balance or light–heat coupling argument; and (ii) the assumption that partial acylation will not significantly perturb pore accessibility or local acidity is plausible but not rigorously bounded by predictive modeling prior to synthesis. These issues do not undermine feasibility but slightly weaken logical closure.

Hypothesis:
A ZIF-90 coating can be engineered into a spatially segregated, dual-function architecture—(i) an outer, diffusion-limited hydrophobic “gatekeeping” shell that measurably suppresses H2O/Cl− ingress and underfilm delamination, and (ii) an internal, covalently immobilized, enantiopure imidodiphosphoric-acid (IDP) Brønsted-acid microenvironment that remains pore-accessible for asymmetric N,N-acetalization—provided that (a) ZIF-90 is operated within explicitly defined aqueous stability windows and (b) the depth distribution of post-synthetic modifications obeys a quantitatively validated reaction–diffusion functionalization model.

Mechanistic rationale (falsifiable): (1) Corrosion protection arises when the hydrophobic shell lowers effective water activity at pore mouths and increases ionic transport resistance, producing an order-of-magnitude retention in low-frequency impedance (|Z|0.01Hz) over immersion time relative to ungated ZIF-90. This is not claimed as “porosity elimination” but as a switch from continuous, water-wet percolation to intermittent/retarded wetting at the external microns, shifting the dominant EIS element from diffusion/Warburg to barrier capacitance with reduced water uptake. (2) Enantioselective catalysis persists because the IDP sites are placed predominantly beyond the shell thickness (depth-segregated) and remain accessible to organic substrates with kinetic diameters below the ZIF-90 aperture constraint, while water (and hydrated Cl−) transport is preferentially inhibited at the shell. The chiral outcome is predicted to scale with confinement: a measurable increase in ee (and/or inversion of selectivity relative to solution) that collapses when pores are blocked, when IDP is immobilized on a nonporous support, or when an enlarged-pore analogue removes confinement. (3) The entire concept is gated by MOF structural integrity: ZIF-90 crystallinity/porosity retention and Zn2+ release rates under chloride at defined pH are treated as go/no-go endpoints; failure triggers pivot to stabilization strategies (crosslinking density, shell thickness, polymer grading) rather than assuming chemical robustness.

Thus, the central claim is not merely that ‘hydrophobic gating + internal chiral acidity’ can coexist, but that spatial segregation can be quantitatively demonstrated and used to predict (and optimize) two coupled performance metrics—chloride-media barrier retention and site-normalized enantioselective turnover—within experimentally defined ZIF-90 stability boundaries.
Plan:
Step 0 — Define ZIF-90 stability windows and go/no-go endpoints (mandatory risk control).
0.1 Prepare powder and film analogues of baseline ZIF-90 (same linker/metal ratio, same modulator history as coating synthesis) to decouple intrinsic framework stability from adhesion/coating defects.
0.2 Stability matrix: immerse powders and films in (i) 3.5 wt% NaCl, (ii) pH 3 chloride (HCl/NaCl), (iii) pH 10 chloride (NaOH/NaCl), and (iv) deionized water as control, at 25 °C and 60 °C (accelerated). Timepoints: 1 h, 6 h, 24 h, 7 d, 28 d.
0.3 In situ structural endpoints (go/no-go):
  - In situ GI-XRD on films during immersion (time-resolved loss of characteristic ZIF-90 reflections; define failure as >30% drop in integrated intensity of main peaks within 24 h in any target medium).
  - In situ ATR-FTIR (monitor imidazolate ring modes + –CHO band evolution; define failure as emergence of broad Zn–OH/H2O features concomitant with linker loss).
  - Zn2+ release rate by ICP-MS of immersion media (define acceptable window as ≤1% of total Zn leached per day during first 72 h at 25 °C; adjust threshold as coating thickness is known).
  - Porosity/uptake retention on powder analogues (Kr/N2 uptake; define failure as >40% loss of uptake after 7 d in target medium).
0.4 If any medium fails go/no-go: implement stabilization levers before proceeding to dual-function testing: (a) increase external hydrophobe shell density/thickness (Section 2.2), (b) introduce graded polymer infiltration (Section 2.4) to suppress continuous wetting, and/or (c) shift corrosion testing emphasis to media where stability is demonstrated while reporting the boundary explicitly.

Step 1 — Coating architecture and baseline characterization.
1.1 Substrates: mild steel and AA2024 coupons (polished to defined roughness, e.g., Ra < 50 nm), then hydroxylated oxide formation via O2 plasma (controlled dose) or mild alkaline activation; record oxide chemistry by XPS (O 1s components) to standardize nucleation.
1.2 Primer compatibility screening (addresses reviewer concerns).
  - Candidate primers: (i) phosphonate-only (alkyl bisphosphonate), (ii) catechol-only (dopamine), (iii) catechol-phosphonate hybrid.
  - Electrochemical stability screen of primer-only films on metal in NaCl via OCP drift + EIS; oxidation sensitivity via cyclic voltammetry (catechol/quinone couple) and XPS after immersion.
  - Growth compatibility: test whether each primer perturbs ZIF-90 nucleation (GI-XRD texture, SEM continuity). Downselect primer that (a) survives immersion without severe redox degradation and (b) does not inhibit ZIF-90 crystallization.
1.3 Baseline ZIF-90 film growth: seeded or interfacial solvothermal growth targeting continuous 1–10 µm films with controlled thickness (profilometry/cross-sectional SEM). Characterize:
  - GI-XRD (texture, crystallinity), SEM/AFM (coverage/roughness), FIB-SEM cross-sections (defects, through-thickness continuity).
  - Quantify –CHO density and accessibility: DRIFTS/ATR-FTIR (–CHO stretch), solid-state 13C NMR on powder analogue, and derivatization titration using a small aminooxy dye probe (UV-vis or fluorescence quantification) to estimate accessible aldehydes.

Step 2 — Quantitative reaction–diffusion model for depth-functionalization + experimental validation (mandatory).
2.1 Model definition (falsifiable): treat aldehyde functionalization as pseudo-first-order in aldehyde with a reagent concentration field C(x,t) penetrating from the external surface into the film.
  - Governing equation: ∂C/∂t = D_eff ∂^2C/∂x^2 − k_app C (where k_app lumps intrinsic oxime/imine formation kinetics under given water activity/solvent; x is depth).
  - Predict functionalization fraction f(x,t) via ∂f/∂t = k_app C (1−f), with boundary condition C(0,t)=C0 (external reagent activity) and no-flux at metal interface.
  - Extract a dimensionless segregation number: Φ = (k_app L^2 / D_eff) where L is film thickness. Target regime for surface-biased gating: Φ >> 1 for bulky hydrophobe reagents (fast consumption near surface relative to diffusion).
2.2 Experimental parameterization:
  - Determine D_eff for representative reagents using uptake kinetics on powder analogues (gravimetric sorption or QCM on thin films) and/or time-dependent XPS signal evolution on thin films.
  - Determine k_app via solution-phase model reaction of imidazole-2-carboxaldehyde with each reagent under matching solvent/water content, then adjust for confinement using early-time film data.
2.3 Depth-profile validation (critical discriminant):
  - Perform time-series functionalization with isotope-labeled or fluorinated reagents to enable ToF-SIMS depth profiling (e.g., CF3-tagged aminooxy/alkylhydrazide for gating; 19F as tracer).
  - Acquire ToF-SIMS profiles after controlled reaction times; fit f(x,t) to model to back-calculate D_eff and k_app and predict shell thickness δ(t) defined as depth where f reaches 0.8 of surface value.
  - Acceptance criterion for “true spatial segregation”: demonstrate δ_gating ≤ 10–20% of total thickness while internal region retains ≥70% of accessible pore volume (from uptake) and ≥50% of internal –CHO available for IDP installation.

Step 3 — Install internal chiral Brønsted-acid sites with quantified loading and wet stability.
3.1 IDP tether design (chemical specificity): synthesize enantiopure IDP bearing (i) aminooxy tether for oxime linkage (IDP–(CH2)n–ONH2) and/or (ii) primary amine tether for reductive amination (IDP–(CH2)n–NH2). Choose n to balance sterics and pore access (screen n=2,4,6).
3.2 Linkage selection by hydrolytic robustness (explicit test):
  - Route A (preferred): oxime formation (–CHO + –ONH2) under low-water, mildly acidic catalysis (avoid framework attack), yielding hydrolytically robust C=N–O linkage.
  - Route B: imine then NaBH3CN reduction to secondary amine (evaluate whether reducing conditions perturb ZIF-90).
3.3 Loading control and verification:
  - Quantify IDP loading by elemental analysis/XPS (P 2p) and digestion + ICP-OES for P/Zn ratio on powder analogues.
  - Confirm linkage by FTIR (oxime/imine bands), solid-state 31P NMR (IDP environment), and XPS N 1s deconvolution.
  - Demonstrate immobilization: leaching tests under catalytic solvent and under NaCl immersion; quantify IDP in solution by LC-MS and P by ICP; pass criterion: <5% IDP loss over 24 h under each relevant condition.
3.4 Wet chloride survivability of IDP-functionalized films: repeat Step 0 immersion endpoints specifically tracking (i) P 2p retention profiles (angle-resolved XPS), (ii) persistence of chiral sites (31P NMR on retrieved powders), and (iii) maintained catalytic activity after exposure (see Step 6).

Step 4 — Hydrophobic pore-mouth gating engineered as a thin shell (spatially segregated, model-guided).
4.1 Gating reagents (size-controlled): bulky long-chain aminooxy or hydrazide reagents (C12–C18) and/or branched groups to maximize Φ and minimize deep penetration.
4.2 Implement diffusion-limited conditions:
  - Use solvent systems that reduce internal wetting (e.g., low-polarity/limited-swelling solvent compatible with ZIF-90) and short reaction times predicted by model to reach target δ_gating.
  - Apply sequential functionalization: (i) internal IDP installation first (with small/medium reagent and longer time), then (ii) gating second with bulky reagent and short time to avoid internal capping.
4.3 Verification:
  - ToF-SIMS depth profiles (hydrophobe tag), angle-resolved XPS (C enrichment gradient), contact angle mapping.
  - Transport proxy: water vapor uptake (DVS) and electrolyte uptake (capacitance from EIS) before/after gating. Target: significant reduction in water uptake with minimal loss of organic-probe uptake relevant to catalysis (Step 6).

Step 5 — Interfacial adhesion strategy with electrochemical compatibility checks.
5.1 Primer downselection outcome from Step 1.2 is enforced: reject catechol-containing primers if oxidation leads to loss of adhesion or increased galvanic activity.
5.2 Demonstrate primer does not perturb Zn nodes or accelerate Zn dissolution:
  - Compare Zn2+ release (ICP-MS) of primed vs unprimed ZIF-90 films under NaCl.
  - XPS at interface (if accessible via sputter depth profiling) for Zn–O–P signatures without excessive Zn depletion.
5.3 Adhesion and underfilm delamination tests:
  - Scratch adhesion (critical load), pull-off adhesion (ASTM), and wet adhesion after immersion.
  - Delamination kinetics by EIS fitting (two-time-constant models) and scanning Kelvin probe (if available) to track underfilm corrosion front.

Step 6 — Catalysis: substrate panel matched to ZIF-90 size constraints + confinement controls (mandatory).
6.1 Aperture/cage matching (explicit):
  - Determine accessible pore/aperture constraint experimentally using uptake of a calibrated probe set (e.g., aromatics/amines of increasing kinetic diameter) on powder analogues; fit a cutoff diameter.
  - Select N,N-acetalization substrates with kinetic diameters below cutoff (Panel S, “fits”) and above cutoff (Panel L, “excluded”).
6.2 Reaction selection: choose an established IDP-Brønsted-acid-mediated asymmetric N,N-acetalization (or closely related iminium/acetal-type transformation) that is water-sensitive, so hydrophobic gating provides a mechanistic lever; run under controlled low-water conditions with deliberate water spikes to quantify gating benefit.
6.3 Controls to prove confinement-driven ee:
  - (i) Dual-functional ZIF-90 (IDP internal + hydrophobe shell).
  - (ii) IDP on nonporous silica/alumina with similar P loading (tests whether ee arises without confinement).
  - (iii) Pore-blocked ZIF-90-IDP (complete capping with small reagent) to show activity/ee collapse with blocked access.
  - (iv) Enlarged-pore analogue (if accessible) or defect-enlarged ZIF via modulator route to reduce confinement; prediction: reduced ee if confinement dominates.
6.4 Metrics and normalization:
  - Quantify conversion, ee (chiral HPLC/GC), and site-normalized TOF (normalize to accessible P sites quantified by titration of acid sites and/or P content multiplied by accessibility factor from probe uptake).
  - Hot filtration and leaching tests: monitor Zn and P in filtrate (ICP-MS) and IDP by LC-MS; show catalysis is truly heterogeneous.
6.5 Mass transport vs catalysis disentanglement:
  - Measure substrate uptake kinetics into functionalized powders (time-resolved uptake) to correlate diffusion timescales with observed rates.
  - Demonstrate that gating decreases water uptake more strongly than organic substrate uptake for Panel S, explaining maintained catalysis with improved water tolerance.

Step 7 — Corrosion performance with mechanistic discriminants tied to the model.
7.1 Test matrix across media (NaCl neutral, pH 3, pH 10) but only within stability windows established in Step 0; explicitly report any excluded regimes.
7.2 Electrochemical endpoints:
  - Time-resolved EIS (|Z|0.01Hz, coating capacitance, pore resistance) up to 28 d; potentiodynamic polarization (icorr, Ecorr).
  - Localized mapping (SVET/SECM) at defects to quantify whether gating+primer suppress localized anode formation.
7.3 Direct transport/permeability tests:
  - Cl− permeability via diffusion cell + ion chromatography.
  - Water uptake via DVS and electrochemical capacitance; correlate to ToF-SIMS-derived shell thickness and model-predicted effective D_eff.
7.4 Post-exposure structural retention:
  - GI-XRD/ATR-FTIR after immersion, Zn2+ release totals, and ToF-SIMS profiles to see whether shell and IDP gradients persist or homogenize.

Step 8 — Design-space mapping and Pareto optimization (explicit tradeoff deconvolution).
8.1 Independent variables: IDP loading (P/Zn), shell thickness δ_gating, and primer type.
8.2 Responses: (i) |Z|0.01Hz retention at day 7/28, (ii) Cl− permeability, (iii) ee and site-normalized TOF for Panel S substrates, (iv) structural integrity (GI-XRD retention; Zn2+ release).
8.3 Outcome: identify Pareto-optimal region where δ_gating reduces water/Cl− ingress without pushing organic substrate diffusion below the catalytic timescale; validate with model predictions and depth profiles.

Milestones (go/no-go summary):
M1 (Stability): ZIF-90 retains ≥70% GI-XRD intensity and ≤1% Zn/day release in the target NaCl medium at 25 °C; otherwise pivot stabilization before proceeding.
M2 (Segregation): ToF-SIMS/XPS demonstrate δ_gating confined to outer ≤20% thickness and internal porosity retention ≥70%.
M3 (Catalysis): Dual-functional material delivers ee significantly above nonporous-IDP control and shows size-exclusion behavior (Panel L inactive/low ee) with negligible leaching.
M4 (Coupled performance): Compared to baseline ZIF-90, dual-functional coatings show sustained impedance improvement (≥10× |Z|0.01Hz at defined timepoint) while preserving ≥50% of catalytic TOF for Panel S substrates.
Feasibility:
1) De-risking ZIF-90 chemical stability (addresses critique i): The revised plan treats hydrolysis/ion exchange/defect evolution as a primary risk with explicit stability windows, accelerated endpoints, and quantitative go/no-go thresholds (in situ GI-XRD, in situ ATR-FTIR, Zn2+ release kinetics, and porosity retention). This prevents proceeding on assumptions and creates a clear pivot strategy (shell densification, graded polymer infiltration, or media boundary definition) if ZIF-90 fails under certain pH/chloride conditions.

2) Spatial segregation is no longer asserted; it is modeled and measured (addresses critique ii): A reaction–diffusion framework with measurable parameters (D_eff, k_app, Φ) is introduced to predict when bulky hydrophobe reagents will be consumed near the surface before penetrating deeply. The model is validated directly against ToF-SIMS depth profiles (with 19F/label tracers) to quantify shell thickness δ_gating and demonstrate internal aldehyde/porosity retention. This is falsifiable: if profiles homogenize or δ_gating grows too thick, the design fails and conditions/reagents are reformulated.

3) Catalysis claim is constrained by pore-size logic and proven by confinement controls (addresses critique iii): The catalysis plan explicitly matches a substrate panel to experimentally determined size cutoffs (uptake-based kinetic diameter screening), then uses mandatory controls (nonporous IDP support, pore-blocked ZIF-90, and enlarged-pore/less confined analogues) to test whether ee is confinement-driven rather than an intrinsic property of immobilized IDP. Site-normalized TOF/ee comparisons and leaching tests convert “high ee” into a mechanistically attributable, reproducible claim.

4) Primer compatibility and electrochemical side effects are explicitly screened: The primer is no longer assumed benign; it is downselected by growth compatibility, redox stability, and absence of accelerated Zn dissolution or galvanic effects. Adhesion and delamination are quantified (wet adhesion + EIS delamination modeling), and the interfacial chemistry is verified.

5) Coupled-function coexistence becomes a testable design space: By mapping IDP loading versus δ_gating (and primer type) against both corrosion and catalysis metrics, the proposal replaces a qualitative “dual function” promise with a Pareto optimization that can demonstrate the intended synergy or reveal unavoidable tradeoffs.

Overall, the revised proposal remains faithful to the original concept chain (ZIF-90 aldehyde chemistry enabling covalent chiral-acid immobilization plus surface-biased hydrophobization for corrosion media), but converts the key vulnerabilities—framework stability, gradient formation, and confinement/transport limits—into quantitative, experimentally verifiable discriminants that determine success or trigger defined pivots.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-structured proposal that anticipates most common failure modes in dual-function MOF coatings. Engineering resolution is very high: in situ GI-XRD/ATR-FTIR under immersion, Zn2+ leaching thresholds, ToF-SIMS depth validation, and model-guided functionalization represent state-of-the-art execution. Logical consistency is strong, with clear causal links between hydrophobic gating, transport suppression, confinement-driven enantioselectivity, and electrochemical signatures. Minor deductions arise from the cumulative experimental burden and interdependence of steps—success depends on maintaining ZIF-90 integrity under chloride while also performing multiple post-synthetic modifications, which may compress the practical design space more than acknowledged. Evidence grounding is excellent, though the catalytic example (IDP-mediated N,N-acetalization) remains somewhat specialized and may limit generality. Rationale quality is high: the proposal does not merely combine corrosion protection and catalysis but frames them as coupled, optimizable outputs governed by measurable transport and stability parameters. Overall risk is high but is explicitly managed rather than ignored.

Hypothesis: A staged “competitive coordination modulation → crystallographically guided oriented attachment → chemically plausible defect-generation” strategy can produce ZIF-71 mesocrystals with predictable transport acceleration without invoking chemically implausible carboxylate-for-imidazolate substitution. Mechanistically, (1) DABCO (or a closely matched tertiary diamine control) transiently lowers free Zn2+ activity via measurable Zn–DABCO complexation in the pre-nucleation window, delaying imidazolate-driven growth and enabling a high nuclei density (nano-regime) under linker-rich conditions; (2) the same transient capping alters the relative growth rates of crystallographic faces by preferential binding to undercoordinated surface Zn sites, creating a facet-dependent surface charge/termination pattern that can be mapped by zeta potential and selective probe adsorption, thereby rendering oriented attachment (OA) a testable, non-accidental outcome; (3) stable defectivity is introduced in ZIF-71 by routes known to be chemically accessible in Zn–imidazolate frameworks—(i) controlled linker-deficient synthesis (Zn-rich, ligand-poor) to embed missing-linker/missing-node defects during growth and (ii) calibrated, subcritical acid/base etching and/or halide/neutral-ligand competitive coordination that creates vacancies and mesoporous pathways while preserving the ZIF-71 topology—rather than by post-assembly carboxylate exchange. The resulting hierarchical architecture couples (a) mesocrystal order (low-angle grain boundary density and coherent crystallographic alignment) with (b) a tunable population of coordinatively unsaturated Zn sites and defect-derived mesoporosity, yielding faster guest uptake/release and improved bioavailability proxies (dispersion stability in protein media and accelerated payload release) versus non-modulated ZIF-71. The same rule set—quantified ligand competition, proton-coupled linker deprotonation control, and falsifiable OA metrics—translates to MIL-53(Al)-NH2 using established monocarboxylate modulation, while DABCO·2HCl is treated explicitly as a buffered ionic/acidic additive whose role is validated via time-resolved pH profiles and Al speciation (27Al NMR/ESI-MS), with pre-registered diagnostics to prevent phase diversion (MIL-68/MOF-235-like impurities) and to exclude DABCO framework incorporation.
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-registration of chemical windows, pass/fail criteria, and controls (addresses reviewer falsifiability).
0.1. Define solvent systems and water content explicitly:
- ZIF-71: (A) MeOH, (B) MeOH/H2O 95:5, and (C) EtOH as robustness checks; record water content by Karl Fischer (target ±0.05 wt%).
- MIL-53(Al)-NH2: DMF/H2O (typically 9:1 v/v) with controlled added acid.
0.2. Predefine “structural pass/fail” for ZIF-71 defect generation:
PASS requires all of: (i) PXRD matches ZIF-71 reference with no new crystalline impurity peaks and ≤10% loss of integrated peak area vs baseline after normalization; (ii) total scattering/PDF retains first-shell Zn–N and Zn–N–C correlations with <10% broadening vs baseline (local order preserved); (iii) 13C/15N solid-state NMR (if linker labeled or sensitivity sufficient) shows intact imidazolate environment without new dominant carboxylate/amide resonances; (iv) N2/CO2 sorption shows reproducible increase in mesopore contribution (e.g., hysteresis + NLDFT/QSDFT shift) without collapse in micropore signature.
FAIL triggers route change: if amorphization or topology loss is detected (PXRD/PDF), revert to purely in-growth linker-deficiency and abandon etch step.
0.3. Predefine “mesocrystal OA success” metric threshold:
- SAED: azimuthal spread of primary reflections across multiple regions ≤15° (target ≤10°);
- Texture/line broadening: synchrotron PXRD shows anisotropic broadening consistent with coherent domains and a March–Dollase texture parameter indicating preferred orientation beyond random aggregate controls (quantify vs control set);
- TEM: visible subunit boundaries with shared orientation (HRTEM lattice continuity across interfaces).
0.4. Control matrix (minimum set) for OA falsification:
C1 no DABCO (baseline nano-ZIF-71); C2 DABCO constant dose (no pulsing); C3 ionic strength ramp only (no DABCO); C4 polymer-only (DHBC or PEO-b-PMAA only); C5 DABCO + polymer (if polymer becomes essential, quantify its minimum effective concentration).

Step 1 — Quantitative ligand competition/speciation map for Zn2+–DABCO vs Zn2+–imidazolate (addresses reviewer point ii).
1.1. Measure Zn–DABCO association in the exact solvent window used for ZIF-71 nucleation:
- Prepare Zn2+ solutions (e.g., Zn(NO3)2 or ZnCl2 consistent with synthesis) at 1–20 mM in MeOH (and MeOH/H2O 95:5).
- Titrate DABCO (0–10 equiv vs Zn) and record:
  a) 1H NMR chemical shift changes (DABCO) and diffusion (DOSY if possible) to infer complexation;
  b) ITC (if feasible) for K and ΔH (use MeOH-compatible setup) or, alternatively, UV–vis with a competitive chromophore proxy ligand (e.g., pyridine derivative) to extract conditional stability constants.
- Fit to 1:1 and 1:2 Zn:DABCO binding models to obtain conditional β values.
1.2. Measure imidazolate competition under nucleation-relevant basicity:
- Generate linker base form in situ (e.g., using triethylamine) and titrate linker into Zn–DABCO solutions while monitoring:
  a) 1H NMR (disappearance/shift of linker resonances),
  b) time-resolved turbidity (onset of nucleation),
  c) stopped-flow DLS for early particle formation.
- Construct an operational “dominance map” plotting turbidity onset time and particle size vs [DABCO]/[Zn] and [linker]/[Zn] at fixed base equivalents.
1.3. Convert data into design rules and pulsing schedule:
- Define a target free-Zn activity suppression factor (e.g., 5–20× reduction) required to arrest growth at 20–80 nm.
- Set initial dosing where >50% Zn is DABCO-bound (from conditional β), then pulse additional DABCO to maintain this bound fraction during the first 1–5 minutes (nucleation/growth crossover) based on observed consumption/precipitation kinetics.

Step 2 — ZIF-71 nanocrystal formation with transient DABCO capping (mechanistically constrained size control).
2.1. Baseline ZIF-71 synthesis:
- Establish reproducible ZIF-71 nanocrystal synthesis (no DABCO) with documented size distribution (TEM, DLS), phase purity (PXRD), and yield.
2.2. DABCO-modulated nucleation (nano-regime):
- Use the speciation map to select 3 conditions (low/med/high Zn suppression) targeting mean sizes 20, 50, 80 nm.
- Keep linker:Zn high (e.g., ≥8:1 as starting point) while adjusting base to maintain consistent linker deprotonation kinetics.
- Collect aliquots at sub-minute resolution for time-resolved SAXS/PXRD (or lab SAXS if synchrotron not available) to extract growth rate constants.
2.3. Validate DABCO is transient and not incorporated:
- Post-synthesis exhaustive solvent exchange (MeOH → EtOH → water) and verify DABCO removal by:
  a) solution 1H NMR of washings,
  b) elemental analysis (N content vs expected),
  c) ATR-IR for DABCO signatures,
  d) XPS N 1s deconvolution (imidazolate N vs tertiary amine N).

Step 3 — Oriented attachment (OA) into ZIF-71 mesocrystals with explicit facet/charge rationale (addresses reviewer point iii).
3.1. Map facet-dependent surface termination/charge in nano-ZIF-71:
- Measure zeta potential as a function of pH/ionic strength for (i) no-DABCO particles and (ii) DABCO-pulsed particles.
- Use selective adsorption probes to infer facet chemistry (e.g., small anions/cations, or fluorescent probes with known charge) and correlate adsorption with morphology (SEM/TEM).
3.2. OA assembly protocol with falsifiable knobs:
- Start from purified nanocrystal sols at fixed solids concentration.
- Apply ionic strength ramp with a non-coordinating electrolyte (e.g., NaNO3) in a controlled microfluidic or syringe-pump addition mode to reach a defined Debye length window (predefine 3 final ionic strengths).
- In parallel, apply DABCO pulses timed to maintain partial surface coverage during the alignment window (timing derived from Step 1 kinetics).
- Optional polymer as a quantified variable, not a hidden reagent: if DHBC/PEO-b-PMAA is used, predefine a concentration series (e.g., 0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1 wt%) and require demonstration that OA metrics improve monotonically.
3.3. OA validation:
- SEM/TEM for hierarchical structure; SAED/HRTEM for shared orientation; synchrotron PXRD texture/anisotropic broadening; compare against controls C1–C5.

Step 4 — ZIF-71 defect chemistry: replace carboxylate ‘defect-writing’ with chemically plausible routes (addresses reviewer point i and mandatory directive 1).
4.1. Route A: In-growth linker-deficient defect introduction (primary, topology-preserving).
- Systematically lower linker:Zn ratio while keeping DABCO-based Zn suppression constant to decouple size from defectivity.
- Target a monotonic defect series (low/med/high) defined by digestion analysis + TGA/EA mass balance (missing linker equivalents per Zn).
- Confirm topology retention by PXRD + PDF (pass/fail criteria in 0.2).
4.2. Route B: Calibrated subcritical etching to open mesopores without phase loss (secondary, conditional on pass criteria).
- Apply mild acid vapor or solution etch compatible with Zn–imidazolate stability (pre-screen short exposures and low acid activity; strictly time-limited).
- Alternatively, use controlled base/solvent-assisted etch known to preferentially dissolve high-energy sites (e.g., grain boundaries) while preserving crystalline cores.
- After each etch, immediately quench and solvent-exchange; verify crystallinity and local order (PXRD/PDF).
4.3. Route C: Competitive neutral/halide ligation during growth (optional, hypothesis-driven).
- Introduce low equivalents of halide (Cl−/Br−) or neutral ligands with known Zn affinity (carefully chosen to avoid topology change) during nucleation to bias missing-node formation.
- Validate by XPS/EA (halide content), PDF, and porosimetry; fail-fast if new phases appear.
4.4. Defect quantification toolkit (pre-registered):
- PALS for vacancy/mesopore signatures;
- Total scattering/PDF for local disorder;
- TGA + elemental analysis for stoichiometry;
- XPS for surface composition and Zn unsaturation indicators;
- Gas sorption with NLDFT/QSDFT pore size distributions.

Step 5 — Translate rigorously to MIL-53(Al)-NH2 with explicit phase control and DABCO·2HCl role validation (addresses reviewer point iv).
5.1. Pre-nucleation Al speciation and pH-time profiling:
- Prepare precursor solutions (Al3+ + NH2-BDC + acetic acid ± DABCO·2HCl) and measure:
  a) pH vs time (room temp → heating ramp),
  b) 27Al NMR of pre-nucleation solutions (identify hydrolyzed/complexed Al species),
  c) ESI-MS (where feasible) to detect Al–carboxylate species distributions.
- Hypothesis test: DABCO·2HCl primarily shifts ionic strength and provides a controllable proton reservoir; it should not generate persistent Al–N complexes. Operational criterion: no new 27Al signatures consistent with stable Al–amine complexes; no DABCO incorporation detected by digestion 1H NMR.
5.2. Phase-control diagnostics during synthesis (pre-registered):
- In situ PXRD (where feasible) or time-resolved ex situ PXRD across heating to confirm MIL-53 formation trajectory.
- Define exclusion criteria for competing phases: presence of diagnostic peaks for MIL-68/MOF-235-like phases triggers condition elimination.
5.3. Modulation and defect control:
- Use acetic acid (and amine-compatible monocarboxylates) as the primary coordination modulator; vary equivalents to generate low/med/high defect series.
- Use DABCO·2HCl as an adjustable additive with a bounded range (predefine 0–2 equiv vs Al) based on speciation results.
- Quantify modulator incorporation and defects by digestion 1H NMR, TGA, ATR-IR (carboxylate termination), and variable-temperature PXRD to ensure breathing is retained.
5.4. Mesocrystal formation pathway:
- Two-step temperature program (low-T nucleation then higher-T growth) under controlled modulator speciation.
- Induce OA by solvent polarity shift (DMF → DMF/H2O → EtOH) with controlled ionic strength; apply the same OA metrics (SAED spread threshold, texture analysis) adapted to MIL-53 crystallography.

Step 6 — Bioavailability-relevant performance tests with normalization and mechanism linkage.
6.1. Payload selection and loading:
- Use one fluorescent model payload (e.g., rhodamine B) with standardized loading protocol; quantify loading by UV–vis/fluorimetry mass balance.
6.2. Release/transport kinetics:
- Measure release at pH 7.4 and 5.5 in PBS ± serum albumin; fit to diffusion/dual-porosity models; extract effective diffusivity and compare across defect series and OA metrics.
6.3. Colloidal stability and corona:
- DLS/zeta in PBS + albumin; protein corona profiling by SDS-PAGE (LC-MS optional) and correlate with surface chemistry (XPS) and defect level.
6.4. Mechanistic correlation:
- Multivariate correlation linking (i) OA orientation metric, (ii) defect metric (PALS/PDF/sorption), and (iii) transport/release parameters to test the central claim that OA + stable defectivity jointly accelerate kinetics.

Deliverables and decision gates (ensures predictability claims are earned):
- Gate G1: Speciation map yields a validated DABCO dosing regime (conditional β and turbidity/DLS onset shifts).
- Gate G2: OA metrics pass threshold versus controls.
- Gate G3: Defect routes A/B/C produce monotonic defect series while meeting topology-preservation pass criteria.
- Gate G4: Transport/release improvements correlate with defect+OA metrics rather than merely reduced size or amorphization.
Feasibility:
1) ZIF-71 defect chemistry is made chemically plausible by eliminating the unsupported premise of carboxylate substitution into a Zn–imidazolate lattice under mild conditions. Instead, defectivity is introduced via (A) linker-deficient growth (a direct, thermodynamically/kinetically consistent route to missing-linker/missing-node populations during framework formation) and (B) calibrated, subcritical etching/competitive coordination only under strict pass/fail crystallinity criteria. This directly addresses the reviewer’s concern that carboxylates would merely terminate surfaces or amorphize the ZIF rather than create stable, topology-preserving defects.
2) DABCO’s role is converted from qualitative to quantitative by requiring an experimentally measured Zn–DABCO conditional stability and a competition/speciation map against imidazolate in the exact solvent/base window used for nucleation. The pulsed-addition schedule is no longer heuristic; it is parameterized to maintain a target bound-Zn fraction during the nucleation/growth crossover, aligning with the literature principle that particle size is controlled by local metal-ion activity and metal–ligand competition (nano-MOF growth termination logic).
3) Mesocrystal assembly is made falsifiable and mechanistically constrained: OA is tied to measurable surface charge/termination changes (zeta potential and probe adsorption), explicit control sets are defined (no pulses, no ionic strength ramp, polymer-only), and a quantitative orientation threshold (SAED azimuthal spread and PXRD texture) is pre-registered. This prevents the polymer from becoming an unacknowledged critical reagent and distinguishes true mesocrystals from random aggregates.
4) MIL-53(Al)-NH2 translation is strengthened by treating DABCO·2HCl as a testable pH/ionic additive rather than an assumed ‘kinetic buffer’. Buffered pH-time profiles plus 27Al NMR/ESI-MS of pre-nucleation solutions are used to verify its effect on Al hydrolysis/speciation and to rule out unintended coordination pathways. In situ PXRD and digestion NMR are pre-registered to exclude competing phases and to quantify modulator incorporation, ensuring phase purity and breathing retention across a defined defect series.
5) The analytical plan is already strong; here it is explicitly coupled to decision gates that prevent over-interpretation (topology preservation criteria, OA metric thresholds, monotonic defect series requirement). This structure supports the proposal’s predictability claim with measurable constraints rather than aspirational control.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and methodologically dense proposal that directly addresses common reviewer objections in ZIF and MOF modulation literature. Strengths include (i) replacing chemically implausible carboxylate-for-imidazolate substitution with linker-deficient growth and calibrated etching grounded in known Zn–imidazolate chemistry; (ii) converting DABCO from a heuristic additive into a quantified coordination modulator via conditional stability constants and competition maps; and (iii) making oriented attachment falsifiable through pre-registered SAED and texture metrics with a clearly defined control matrix. Logical consistency is strong: each mechanistic claim is paired with a diagnostic that could disprove it. Minor score deductions arise from the sheer experimental breadth and coupling: the proposal assumes access to high-end infrastructure (PDF, PALS, synchrotron PXRD, in situ measurements) and flawless execution across multiple orthogonal techniques. While not logically flawed, this raises feasibility risk and dilutes focus. Additionally, the OA-to-transport acceleration linkage, though thoughtfully correlated, still relies on multivariate inference rather than a single decisive causal experiment.

Hypothesis:
A flame-resistant, humidity-tolerant, catalytically active MOF can be made deterministic (rather than asserted) by coupling (i) a carboxylate-reticulated, hydrolytically robust node chemistry with (ii) a pendant phosphorus chemistry that is *operationally proven* to remain largely non-coordinating after deprotection, and (iii) a quantitatively metered intrapore P–OH condensation that forms a confined polyphosphate nanophase while preserving crystallinity and transport. Mechanistically, the proposal hinges on two separable, testable modules:

Module A (Non-coordinating P–OH under MOF-relevant conditions): Pendant phosphinate/phosphonate groups are installed on a ditopic aromatic dicarboxylate such that carboxylates enforce reticulation and P groups project into pore space. After selective deprotection to P–OH, the pendant groups are designed to remain predominantly pore-facing (hydrogen-bonded and solvated) rather than node-binding. This is made chemically plausible by (1) steric/electronic shielding at phosphorus (bulky phosphinate substituents; optional α-aryl substitution adjacent to P to reduce oxyanion basicity), and (2) selecting a node/SBU family with demonstrably lower oxyanion “hard” binding competition than Mg/Al mixed SBUs if binding cannot be suppressed (go/no-go switch to Zr(IV) oxo/hydroxo SBUs with kinetically inert carboxylate bonding, or to Al(III)–oxo chains where oxyanion access is sterically constrained). The *reason* this overcomes reviewer risk (ii) is that we do not assume non-coordination; we quantify Mg/Al (or alternative node) affinity for pendant P–O(H)/P–O− using model-cluster competition experiments and in-MOF diagnostics, and only proceed to locking conditions when P–node coordination is below a defined threshold.

Module B (Gating-to-locking as a metered, nanoconfined condensation): Upon mild thermal treatment, a controlled fraction of pendent P–OH groups undergo dehydration/condensation to Q1/Q2 polyphosphate-like species confined to pore surfaces (a “glassy” nanophase) that (a) passivates defect-prone hydrolysis/acid sites and suppresses volatile fuel release during heating (condensed-phase flame retardancy), and (b) increases pore polarity and acid-gas binding under humidity through persistent P–O and P=O dipoles and H-bond networks. The key mechanistic refinement is that the extent of condensation is treated as a controllable state variable (Q0→Q1→Q2 distribution) governed by water activity and thermal ramp/hold, not as an assumed 10–30% target. By mapping quantitative 31P ssNMR speciation against crystallinity retention, pore metrics, and diffusion coefficients, we define a deterministic “locking window” where phosphate formation occurs without collapse or transport loss. This directly addresses reviewer risks (i), (iii), and (iv) by bounding the transformation with explicit strain/crystallinity/transport criteria.

Catalysis/pollutant conversion is integrated as a low-percentage Fe-porphyrin tetracarboxylate co-linker *only after* the material-risk modules are validated, and is protected by (1) spatial isolation (≤1–3 mol% to minimize defect-driven amorphization), and (2) diagnosing/mitigating demetalation/leaching under SO2/NOx + humidity via effluent ICP and Fe speciation (Mössbauer/XAS where available). The resulting material couples functional groups → gas separation/storage under humidity (CO2/SO2/NOx) → flame resistance (condensed-phase phosphate/char formation) → catalysis/pollutant conversion, with each link supported by quantified go/no-go constraints rather than assumed compatibility.
Plan:
Phase 0: Architecture selection and de-risking logic (Month 0–3)
0.1 Node/SBU down-select with explicit fallback: Start with Mg(II)/Al(III)-carboxylate only if it meets thermal and competition thresholds (below). In parallel, synthesize a benchmark Zr(IV)-oxo carboxylate analogue (UiO-type or NU-type topology) as the pre-defined contingency platform because Zr–carboxylate bonds are kinetically inert at 220–320 °C and tolerate acidic functionalities better. Decision gate: if Mg/Al system fails either (A) P–node non-coordination threshold or (B) crystallinity/transport retention at locking, switch to Zr platform while keeping identical linker logic.

Phase 1: Linker and control lattice set (Month 1–8)
1.1 Linker set (primary and variants):
- L-P(steric): aromatic dicarboxylate bearing a pendant phosphinate (e.g., aryl–P(=O)(OR)(tBu) or diaryl phosphinate) designed for steric shielding and reduced tendency to chelate nodes after deprotection.
- L-P(less shielded): pendant dialkyl phosphonate as a “worst-case” coordination propensity comparator.
- L-H (non-P parent): isoreticular dicarboxylate without P (e.g., terephthalate analogue).
- L-P(protected): the permanently protected ester version of L-P(steric) (non-condensable control).
- Optional: L-P(electronic) variant with electron-withdrawing aryl substituent near P to reduce basicity.
1.2 Hard control lattices (mandatory set):
C1: non-P analogue MOF (L-H only).
C2: P-ester/protected analogue MOF (L-P(protected) only).
C3: P-only/no-Fe MOF (L-P only).
C4: Fe-only/no-P MOF (L-H + 1–3 mol% Fe-porphyrin co-linker).
C5: P+Fe MOF (L-P + 1–3 mol% Fe-porphyrin co-linker).
1.3 Crystallization constraints for SCSC feasibility: Grow single crystals (target ≥50–150 µm) under diffusion/slow-cooling conditions; in parallel produce microcrystalline powders for Rietveld/PDF. Record defect proxies (thermogravimetric linker/node ratios; modulator incorporation if used) to set allowable defect fraction.

Phase 2: Mandatory de-risking study A — P–OH coordination/competition quantification (Month 4–10)
2.1 Model-cluster competition (quantifies assumption #1):
- Prepare soluble Mg(II) and Al(III) carboxylate clusters or appropriate salts with carboxylate ligands that mimic node environment.
- Titrate deprotected L-P (P–OH) versus L-H into metal solutions under MOF-relevant solvent/water activities.
- Readouts:
  (i) Solution/solid-state 31P NMR: coordination-induced shifts/broadening; quantify bound vs free fraction.
  (ii) IR: P=O and P–O bands; monitor appearance of metal–O(P) signatures.
  (iii) Metal uptake/leaching: ICP-OES of supernatant after contact with L-P (P–OH), giving conditional stability constants/extent of complexation.
- Go/no-go criterion A1 (non-coordination threshold): Under conditions matching planned deprotection/locking (same solvent, ionic strength, and water activity), ≤10% of P sites show node-binding signatures (combined NMR/IR/ICP mass balance). If >10%, implement redesign:
  Redesign option A: increase steric bulk (phosphinate > phosphonate; bulky OR/aryl substituents).
  Redesign option B: enforce larger P–node separation (longer spacer/ortho substitution that blocks approach).
  Redesign option C: switch node to Zr(IV)-oxo platform with sterically constrained, kinetically inert SBUs.
2.2 In-MOF verification of P–node binding (post-deprotection):
- Perform deprotection on C3 (P-only/no-Fe) under mild conditions.
- Readouts:
  (i) 31P ssNMR: appearance of strongly shifted/broadened resonances consistent with immobilized metal phosphonates/phosphinates.
  (ii) VT-PXRD/Rietveld: detect topology change or new phase formation.
  (iii) Metal environment probes: 27Al ssNMR (if Al present) or XPS to detect new M–O(P) environments.
- Go/no-go criterion A2: No new crystalline phase by PXRD; unit-cell parameters change smoothly without symmetry breaking; absence of a dominant bound-P resonance.

Phase 3: Mandatory de-risking study B — Deterministic locking window (Month 8–18)
3.1 Define controlled extent-of-condensation “knob” (quantifies assumption #2):
- Perform locking as a designed experiment varying:
  (i) water activity aw (dry inert; controlled humid inert; trace water dosing),
  (ii) heating ramp (0.5–5 °C/min),
  (iii) hold temperature/time (200–320 °C; 0.5–8 h),
  (iv) optional mild acid catalysis/scavengers (only if non-coordination is proven; otherwise excluded).
3.2 Quantify phosphate speciation (extent-of-reaction):
- Quantitative 31P ssNMR deconvolution into Q0/Q1/Q2 (and Q3 if present). Primary conversion metric: Xcond = (Q1+Q2+Q3)/(Q0+Q1+Q2+Q3).
- FTIR: P–O–P growth (supporting evidence).
- PDF: detect short-range phosphate network correlations without long-range order.
3.3 Explicit locking success metrics (Rietveld + strain + pore/transport):
- Crystallinity retention: Rietveld refined scale factor / crystalline fraction ≥80% of pre-treatment.
- Unit-cell strain: |ΔV/V0| ≤2.0% and no peak splitting indicative of symmetry loss.
- Porosity: N2(77 K) and CO2(273/298 K) derived pore volume loss ≤25% and BET loss ≤30% vs pre-locking.
- Transport: transient uptake kinetics for CO2 and H2O (and SO2 where safe) to extract effective diffusion coefficients (Deff) via Fickian uptake models; require Deff(post)/Deff(pre) ≥0.5 for CO2 and ≥0.3 for H2O.
- Go/no-go criterion B: Only conditions meeting all four thresholds constitute the “locking window”; catalytic integration proceeds only within this window.

Phase 4: Gas separation/storage validation under humidity (Month 12–24)
4.1 Equilibrium + humid breakthrough (all controls C1–C5):
- Isotherms: CO2, N2, CH4, SO2, NO2 (where feasible) at 273/298 K.
- Qst via Clausius–Clapeyron; correlate increases with P microdomain density (Xcond, Q-distribution).
- Dynamic breakthrough: CO2/N2, CO2/CH4, SO2/CO2 under dry and 40–60% RH; multicycle regeneration.
4.2 Stability benchmarking informed by ZIF humid-CO2 degradation literature: long-term humid CO2 aging (weeks) and acid-gas exposure; track PXRD/Rietveld crystallinity, ICP leaching (Mg/Al/Zr), and capacity retention; compare C1 vs C2 vs locked C3 to prove that improvements require *condensed* phosphate, not just pendant polarity.

Phase 5: Flame resistance as a function of Xcond (Month 18–30)
5.1 Composite fabrication with fixed loading (e.g., 10–20 wt% MOF) in at least two polymer matrices (epoxy + polyolefin).
5.2 Metrics:
- LOI, microscale combustion calorimetry (heat release capacity), TGA/DTG char yield and residue analysis.
- Correlate LOI/char yield with Xcond and P speciation (Q1/Q2). Key control: C2 (protected P ester) must show weaker flame retardancy than locked C3 at similar loading to attribute effect to condensed-phase phosphate formation.

Phase 6: Catalysis/pollutant conversion with explicit leaching/demetalation diagnostics (Month 20–36)
6.1 Integration rules to minimize defect chemistry: introduce Fe-porphyrin co-linker at 1–3 mol% only after a locking window is established in C3. Prepare C4 and C5.
6.2 Benchmark reaction + targets:
- Primary: catalytic NO oxidation to NO2 (or an established Fe-porphyrin oxidation surrogate) under controlled O2/H2O; specify target TOF and stability: TOF within literature range for MOF-porphyrin analogues and ≤20% activity loss over 10 h under humid feed.
- Secondary (if safe/available): SO2 oxidative conversion or nitrosyl binding/release cycling.
6.3 Deactivation and integrity diagnostics:
- Effluent ICP-OES for Fe (and node metals) every cycle; go/no-go: Fe loss ≤5% over 10 h test.
- Fe speciation: Mössbauer or XAS pre/post exposure to detect demetalation/reduction/oxidation; UV–vis diffuse reflectance for porphyrin integrity.
- Framework damage: VT-PXRD, N2/CO2 uptake recovery, DRIFTS during exposure to identify irreversible sulfate/nitrosyl accumulation.
6.4 Decoupling controls: compare C3 vs C5 to isolate Fe effects; compare C4 vs C5 to test whether phosphate locking improves Fe retention and humidity/acid-gas tolerance.

Decision summary (explicit milestones):
M1 (Month ~10): Non-coordination validated (A1/A2). If failed → linker shielding redesign or node switch.
M2 (Month ~18): Locking window established with quantified Xcond–structure–transport map meeting criterion B.
M3 (Month ~30): Demonstrated flame retardancy correlation with Xcond (locked C3 outperforming C2/C1 in LOI/MCC).
M4 (Month ~36): Catalysis meets Fe retention and stability targets in humid/acid-gas relevant streams with diagnostic closure.
Feasibility:
1) The proposal now treats the two highest-risk assumptions as *measured variables with thresholds*, not as design intentions. Pendant P–OH coordination is explicitly quantified by model-cluster competition (31P NMR/IR/ICP) and verified in-framework (31P ssNMR + Rietveld). This directly addresses the hard-acid affinity concern for Mg/Al and provides a pre-defined, chemistry-consistent escape route (sterically shielded phosphinates; node switch to kinetically inert Zr carboxylate SBUs) if coordination cannot be suppressed.

2) The “locking” step is made deterministic by defining an operational control knob (water activity + thermal ramp/hold) and by quantifying extent-of-condensation via Q0/Q1/Q2 integration in quantitative 31P ssNMR. Correlating Xcond with Rietveld crystallinity, unit-cell strain, pore-volume loss, and diffusion coefficients produces a bounded locking window rather than a speculative 10–30% target. This directly de-risks SCSC/thermal stability and nanoconfined polyphosphate formation.

3) Transport preservation is substantiated beyond equilibrium adsorption by adding transient sorption kinetics (CO2/H2O/SO2) and explicit Deff retention criteria. This addresses the reviewer’s concern that partial pore-wall glass could catastrophically reduce diffusivity even if isotherms look acceptable.

4) Multifunctionality is decoupled with hard controls (non-P, protected-P, P-only/no-Fe, Fe-only/no-P, P+Fe). These controls isolate (i) polarity-only effects vs condensed phosphate effects, and (ii) catalytic-site-driven defect/stability risks vs phosphate-locking benefits.

5) Acid-gas catalysis risks (Fe demetalation/leaching, redox damage) are addressed by explicit effluent ICP mass balances and Fe speciation (Mössbauer/XAS where available), with clear stability/retention go/no-go criteria. The catalytic element is staged after the material locking window is established, ensuring the program cannot be derailed by secondary functionality before the core transformation is validated.

6) The refined approach remains coherent with the original concept chain (functional groups → gas separation/storage under humidity → flame resistance → catalysis/pollutant capture), while integrating stability lessons from humid CO2 sensitivity in imidazolate systems by making long-term humid-CO2/acid-gas aging a central benchmark rather than an afterthought.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-engineered MOF proposal that explicitly converts its two highest-risk assumptions (pendant phosphate non-coordination and controlled intrapore condensation) into measured state variables with predefined thresholds. The phased structure, hard controls, and explicit decision gates significantly reduce technical risk. Engineering resolution is very high due to the integration of quantitative ssNMR speciation, Rietveld strain limits, diffusion coefficients, and effluent ICP diagnostics. Logical consistency is strong: Module A and Module B are mechanistically separable, falsifiable, and correctly staged before multifunctional integration. Minor deductions arise from residual uncertainty around Mg/Al cluster models faithfully reproducing in-framework coordination thermodynamics, and from the ambitious breadth (flame retardancy, gas separation, catalysis) which may strain execution even with gating. Evidence grounding is excellent; the proposal stays entirely within MOF, phosphate chemistry, and gas-adsorption science without conceptual drift. Rationale quality is high, as the confined polyphosphate 'locking window' is a genuinely creative solution to the long-standing stability–transport tradeoff, though it builds incrementally on known phosphate and Zr-MOF stability paradigms rather than redefining them.

Hypothesis: A MOF membrane that couples (i) sub-nanometer, low-flexibility channels tuned to the ion dehydration diameter (optimal pore size) with (ii) a permanently charged, spatially patterned internal surface will outperform conventional ZIF-90-type pores in ionic permselectivity and high-salt rectification because electrostatic Donnan exclusion and dehydration barriers will act cooperatively and directionally, while suppressed framework breathing preserves a time-invariant free-energy landscape for ion transport. Methodological adaptation: convert a ZIF-90-derived sub-nanometer channel network into a 'Janus-charged, rigidity-locked' architecture by (a) postsynthetic covalent anchoring of zwitterionic/ionic groups on the aldehyde sites to impose fixed surface charge density gradients along the transport axis and (b) intraframework crosslinking (imine/oxime bridging) to reduce linker mobility and pore flexibility without collapsing porosity.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select ZIF-90 as the parent due to its aldehyde handle and established sub-nanometer ion-transport behavior; prepare nanopipette-supported ZIF-90 (GNS-ZIF-90 geometry) and, in parallel, prepare continuous thin-film membranes on porous alumina for macroscopic flux tests.
1.2 Establish baseline structure–transport: quantify pore aperture distribution (PXRD + Rietveld/total scattering, CO2/N2 sorption for microporosity proxy, PALS if available) and baseline I–V curves in KCl/NaCl/CaCl2 across pH 3–12.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Janus surface-charge patterning inside sub-nanometer channels (directional electrostatics):
- Use a diffusion-limited postsynthetic modification (PSM) strategy exploiting ZIF-90 aldehydes: expose only one side of the membrane (or nanopipette tip exterior) to an amine reagent under controlled time so that reaction fronts create an axial gradient.
- Reagents: (i) quaternary-ammonium-terminated primary amines (introduce permanent positive charge), (ii) sulfonate-terminated primary amines (permanent negative charge), and (iii) zwitterionic betaine amines (high hydration, antifouling). Build three variants: uniformly charged, axially graded (Janus), and charge-inverted (positive-to-negative).
- Verify spatial charge gradient by depth-profile XPS/ToF-SIMS on planar films and by confocal mapping using charged fluorophore probes where applicable.
2.2 Rigidity-locking to preserve optimal pore size under operation (flexibility suppression):
- Perform intrapore crosslinking by converting remaining aldehydes to (a) oximes using diamino-oxy linkers or (b) imines using rigid diamines (e.g., p-phenylenediamine) to form interlinker bridges; tune crosslink density to maintain crystallinity.
- Confirm reduced dynamics via variable-temperature PXRD, DMA/nanoindentation on films, and comparing gas sorption hysteresis; ensure pore accessibility is retained.
2.3 Mechanistic transport quantification and modeling:
- Measure ionic permselectivity (transference numbers) and rectification in symmetric/asymmetric electrolytes (0.01–3 M; mono/divalent series) across pH, extracting surface charge density via Poisson–Nernst–Planck (PNP) fits augmented with ion dehydration free-energy terms.
- Use EIS to separate pore resistance vs charge-transfer artifacts; use streaming potential/zeta (where feasible) to corroborate surface charge.
- Run MD/DFT-informed calculations: DFT cluster models to estimate binding/dehydration penalties near functional groups; MD in sub-nanometer pores to quantify residence times and effective diffusion coefficients under different charge patterns.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Benchmark against controls: pristine ZIF-90, uniformly functionalized (no gradient), gradient-only (no crosslink), and crosslink-only (no charge modification).
3.2 Define success metrics: (i) rectification ratio at 1 M KCl exceeding the pristine benchmark, sustained over 30-day soaking; (ii) permselectivity for monovalent over divalent ions under mixed-salt conditions; (iii) stability of I–V characteristics over pH cycling (3↔12) and high ionic strength.
3.3 Establish causal mechanism: correlate performance to (a) measured axial charge gradient magnitude, (b) crosslink-induced reduction in flexibility (VT-PXRD/indentation), and (c) computed free-energy profiles (electrostatic + dehydration). Demonstrate that the best-performing samples require both the gradient (directional electrostatics) and rigidity-locking (fixed optimal pore size).
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 3 shows ZIF-90 sub-nanometer channels yield extreme pH-dependent rectification governed by surface charge/electrostatic interaction; thus deliberate, permanent charge engineering should directly program ion selectivity. Asset 1 indicates optimal pore size benefits are undermined by flexibility; suppressing breathing should stabilize the transport landscape. Asset 2 demonstrates charged frameworks can gain exceptional chemical robustness via electrostatic effects, supporting the idea that designed charge can improve stability and function.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): ZIF-90 uniquely enables covalent PSM via aldehydes, allowing molecularly precise installation of ionic/zwitterionic groups and crosslink bridges inside a crystalline MOF while preserving topology—an explicitly coordination-polymer/MOF-native strategy rather than generic polymer coating.
3. Comparative Advantage: Conventional MOF ion channels rely on pH-tunable charge and uncontrolled defect chemistry, yielding variable selectivity and drift. The proposed Janus-charged, rigidity-locked channels create a deterministic axial electrostatic potential (built-in diode) plus a fixed, optimally sized dehydration gate, enabling higher permselectivity at high salt and improved long-term operational stability compared to pristine ZIF-90 or uniformly functionalized pores.
Critique: This is a technically sophisticated and largely coherent proposal that addresses a real bottleneck in MOF-based ion transport—namely, the instability and non-determinism of electrostatic landscapes due to framework flexibility and pH-dependent charging. The engineering plan is unusually detailed for a proposal, particularly in the use of diffusion-limited PSM to generate axial charge gradients and the pairing of crosslinking chemistry with transport measurements. Minor deductions arise from (i) partial under-specification of how charge-gradient sharpness will be quantitatively related to rectification strength (the causal mapping risks being correlative rather than predictive), and (ii) some optimism regarding the preservation of crystallinity and percolated porosity at higher crosslink densities, which is not yet convincingly bounded by preliminary data or contingency pathways. Additionally, while MD/DFT modeling is well-motivated, the proposal does not fully clarify how simulation length scales will faithfully capture experimentally relevant high-salt, low-dielectric sub-nanometer regimes.

Hypothesis: A reversible, adsorption-triggered phase transition (α↔β) can be engineered in an open-metal-site MOF without sacrificing the CO2 enthalpic driver by replacing inner-sphere phosphonate anchoring and speculative dobdc aromatic PSM with a chemically defensible, low-occupancy, outer-sphere “molecular gate” that (i) is tethered to the linker (not the metal), (ii) is geometrically constrained to modulate the 1D channel bottleneck, and (iii) is designed to be non-chelating toward Mg2+/Co2+ (no phosphonate inner-sphere binding) so that >80–90% of open metal sites remain accessible. Mechanistically, CO2 first binds strongly and selectively at the native open metal sites (as established for Mg2(dobdc) and high-selectivity MOFs), raising local CO2 chemical potential and generating a loading-dependent electrostatic field/steric pressure in the channel. This shifts the conformational free-energy landscape of a nearby crown-ether rotor (through CO2 quadrupole–ether interactions and crowding), promoting a cooperative reorientation of a sub-stoichiometric population of gates that collectively changes the channel’s effective free volume and elastic state, yielding an α (open) to β (constricted or reconfigured) transition with stepped isotherms and enhanced PSA-relevant working capacity. The refined approach overcomes prior feasibility concerns by: (1) using a prefunctionalized linker handle (isoreticular dobdc-analog or BDP-analog) to place the gate with known chemistry rather than modifying framework-forming phenoxides; (2) eliminating competitive metal poisoning by using a non-coordinating tether/anchor architecture (outer-sphere only) and by quantifying accessible open-metal fraction via direct titration/IR probes; (3) abandoning partial-occupancy SCSC claims and instead building a disorder-aware structural picture from operando PXRD plus total scattering/PDF; and (4) de-risking computation by first proving phase coexistence/steps with a minimal two-state Hamiltonian coupled to adsorption before adding polarization and atomistic detail.
Plan:
A. Minimal, chemically defensible material system (de-risking site poisoning + crystallography)
A1. Primary scaffold selection and narrowing
