- Primary target: Mg2(dobdc) (MOF-74/Mg) due to dominant CO2 binding at open Mg2+ sites and well-documented challenges for generic force fields (motivating QM-derived interactions).
- Comparator: Co(BDP) retained only as Phase-II generalization after the minimal Mg system demonstrates: (i) preserved open-metal accessibility and (ii) reversible adsorption-induced cooperativity. This directly reduces disorder/topology risk.

A2. Replace speculative aromatic PSM with a proven, prefunctionalized linker handle
- Strategy: synthesize an isoreticular dobdc-analog that preserves Mg2(dobdc) topology but carries a pendant, non-coordinating tether on the aromatic ring introduced prior to framework formation (mixed-linker approach). The tether terminus is an ether-rich crown rotor; the tether backbone is chemically inert to Mg2+ (no phosphonate/carboxylate/amine chelators).
- Design constraints (chemical parameters):
  (i) Gate density: 2.5–10% of linkers functionalized (target 5% as the primary point) to minimize pore blockage/disorder while enabling cooperative bottleneck statistics.
  (ii) Tether: short (≈3–6 heavy atoms) and rigid/semirigid (e.g., aryl–(CH2)n–O–) to position the crown near the channel wall but avoid direct coordination to Mg.
  (iii) Rotor: 18C6-like or 24C6-like macrocycle chosen to be large enough to modulate the pore aperture yet not to fully occlude; install a single-point attachment to permit hindered rotation rather than free translation.
  (iv) “Non-poisoning” rule: exclude phosphonate, catechol, pyridine, imidazole, or carboxylate motifs from the tether/rotor architecture; if an anchor is required, use a neutral aryl/ether linkage only.

A3. Mandatory negative controls that isolate gating from site blocking/added heats
- Control 1 (site-blocking/mass control): same linker substitution level with a non-rotor pendant of similar mass and polarity (e.g., a short PEG-like chain) that cannot sterically gate the bottleneck.
- Control 2 (rotation-locked control): crown present but conformationally immobilized (e.g., by intramolecular tethering/cyclization to restrict dihedral freedom) while keeping chemistry and substitution level constant.
- Control 3 (parent): unfunctionalized Mg2(dobdc).

B. Experimental workflow (structural evidence without SCSC; explicit open-metal accessibility metrics)
B1. Synthesis and activation
- Mixed-linker solvothermal synthesis to incorporate functionalized dobdc-analog at 2.5%, 5%, 10% feed ratios; verify incorporation by digestion NMR and/or LC-MS of digested linkers.
- Activation protocol ladder to probe α (solvated) vs β (activated/CO2-loaded) states without assuming SCSC:
  (i) solvent exchange (MeOH) → (ii) mild vacuum/temperature ramp (e.g., 80–150 °C) → (iii) CO2 dosing steps.

B2. Quantify and cap open-metal-site blockage a priori (mandatory)
- Accessible open-metal fraction metrics (apply to all samples including controls):
  (i) CO probe + IR: quantify Mg–CO band intensity relative to parent as a direct measure of accessible Mg2+ sites.
  (ii) H2 isotherms at 77 K: use low-pressure uptake as a proxy for open-site accessibility and compare to parent.
  (iii) CO2 isosteric heat vs loading (microcalorimetry): verify preservation of the characteristic high-Qst initial binding signature of Mg2(dobdc); a strong reduction at low loading flags site poisoning.
- Acceptance criterion to proceed to “gating” claims: ≥85% of parent open-metal signature retained by CO-IR and consistent low-pressure H2 uptake.

B3. Structural characterization centered on disorder-aware methods (no SCSC dependence)
- Operando/in situ PXRD under CO2 pressure (and temperature where needed): track unit-cell metrics/peak shifts/peak splitting indicative of α↔β transformation.
- Total scattering/PDF (synchrotron if available): detect local structural rearrangements and distinguish genuine framework transition from mere adsorption swelling; fit with small-box models representing α and β local environments with partial gate occupancy.
- Rietveld refinement with disorder models: treat the gate as partially occupied, using rigid-body restraints for the crown and refining occupancy against known linker incorporation values.
- Complementary spectroscopy:
  (i) VT solid-state NMR on selectively labeled rotor segments (e.g., 2H or 13C labels) to quantify mobility changes across α↔β and upon CO2 loading.
  (ii) IR for CO2 binding mode shifts (metal-bound vs secondary ether interactions).

B4. Adsorption performance + PSA-relevant metrics
- CO2 isotherms at relevant temperatures (e.g., 298–313 K) + hysteresis mapping; identify steps/cooperativity windows.
- Measure working capacity in pre-defined PSA windows (explicitly pre-registered, e.g., 1→10 bar and/or 0.15→1 bar depending on application framing) and compare to parent and negative controls.
- Selectivity: CO2/H2 (as in Asset 1 context) using IAST from single-component isotherms and/or mixed-gas breakthrough (if available); ensure any gains are not solely due to reduced H2 uptake from blocked pores.
- Cycling: ≥50 adsorption/desorption cycles with retention of step position and capacity (defines reversibility).

C. Simulation workflow (minimal two-state model first; pre-registered CVs; then atomistic refinement)
C1. Stage-1: Rigorously defined two-state Hamiltonian to prove phase coexistence/stepped uptake
- Build a coarse-grained model with two framework states (α, β) characterized by different accessible free volume and elastic penalty ΔG0(α→β).
- Couple adsorption via state-dependent Langmuir-type site energies:
  (i) strong open-metal CO2 sites (retained from parent energetics),
  (ii) weaker secondary ether sites near the gate.
- Gate variable: rotor dihedral state (open vs constricted) coupled to the α/β free-volume parameter; include a cooperative term that scales with gate density (occupancy-dependent coupling) to enable collective transitions.
- Fit/validate against minimal experimental observables without assuming crystal endpoints: step pressure, hysteresis width (if present), and Qst vs loading trends.
- Pre-registered collective variables (CVs) and acceptance criteria:
  CV1: framework state variable s∈{α,β}; CV2: average rotor “open fraction” f_open; CV3: CO2 loading N.
  Acceptance: the model must reproduce (within uncertainty) the presence/absence of steps across parent vs controls and the directionality of step shifts with temperature.

C2. Stage-2: Atomistic, phase-aware adsorption with restrained disorder representation
- Construct atomistic supercells with randomly distributed functionalized linkers at experimentally measured incorporation (2.5–10%) to represent disorder explicitly.
- Use dual-structure sampling rather than assuming crystallographically solved α and β: generate candidate α-like and β-like cells guided by operando PXRD lattice metrics; constrain via elastic network or cell-parameter restraints consistent with diffraction.
- Adsorption: hybrid GCMC/MD in an extended ensemble where cell parameter (or a proxy strain coordinate) is biased between α-like and β-like basins; rotor dihedral included as an explicit coordinate with torsional potential from QM scans.

C3. Interaction model: prioritize correctness at open metal sites before polarizability
- Start with QM-derived, site-specific CO2–open-metal interactions (per Asset 2 logic): compute binding energies/geometries on cluster models representing Mg2+ site + local linker environment; calibrate charges/parameters to match heats and low-loading isotherms.
- Add rotor–CO2 interaction parameters from QM (CO2 with ether-rich fragments) to capture the gating bias without introducing inner-sphere artifacts.
- Only if Stage-1/2 reproduce cooperative trends, introduce explicit polarization (Drude/induced dipole) for Mg site to refine Qst and loading dependence—this is a performance upgrade, not a prerequisite for demonstrating gating.

D. Decision gates / down-selection (explicit, reviewer-aligned)
D1. Chemical viability gate
- Proceed only if open-metal accessibility ≥85% of parent by CO-IR/H2(77 K) and initial Qst remains within a pre-set tolerance (e.g., ≤15% reduction vs parent at near-zero loading).

D2. Mechanistic gating gate (must beat negative controls)
- Claim “gate-induced cooperativity” only if: (i) stepped/hysteretic CO2 uptake appears or is significantly sharpened in the rotor sample vs all controls, and (ii) the step correlates with operando PXRD/PDF evidence of a reversible α↔β structural change, not just sorbate-induced swelling.

D3. Performance gate
- Success criterion: ≥20% increase in CO2 working capacity in the pre-registered PSA window relative to parent, while maintaining cyclic reversibility and without losing more than 15% of open-metal accessibility.

E. Phase-II generalization to Co(BDP) (only after Mg system is validated)
- Implement the same design rules (prefunctionalized linker; non-chelating tether; explicit disorder modeling). Use operando PXRD + PDF as primary structure tools due to expected disorder; replicate the same control set and accessibility metrics (metal-site probe adapted to Co).
Feasibility:
1) Chemical realism of modification (addresses critique i): The revised design eliminates speculative electrophilic substitution/etherification on framework-forming dobdc phenoxides and instead uses prefunctionalized linker synthesis with mixed-linker assembly, a standard and controllable route for introducing low-density functionality while retaining topology. This directly de-risks crystallinity loss and makes functional group identity/stoichiometry quantifiable by digestion analytics.

2) Avoiding open-metal-site poisoning (addresses critique ii): The anchoring concept is redesigned to be outer-sphere and non-chelating—explicitly excluding phosphonates (and other strong donors) from the tether/rotor architecture so the enthalpic driver (CO2 binding to open Mg2+/Co2+ sites) remains intact. Feasibility is enforced by an a priori, quantitative cap on site blockage using CO-IR titration, 77 K H2 uptake, and low-loading calorimetric Qst; these metrics are built into decision gates before any gating claims.

3) Structural characterization without SCSC (addresses critique iii & iv): The proposal no longer depends on single-crystal-to-single-crystal behavior at partial occupancy. Operando PXRD provides reversible lattice/phase signatures under CO2 stimulus, while total scattering/PDF supplies local-structure sensitivity compatible with disorder and partial functionalization. Rietveld refinement is performed with explicit disorder/rigid-body models and occupancies constrained by measured linker incorporation, providing a defensible α/β structural narrative despite heterogeneity.

4) Disorder and “mere blocking” disentanglement (addresses critique v and mandatory negative control): A matched-mass/polarity pendant control (no rotor gating) and a rotation-locked rotor control isolate true volume-modulation cooperativity from trivial loss of adsorption sites or added heats. The mechanism is considered supported only if stepped uptake/phase switching occurs uniquely in the mobile-rotor case while open-metal accessibility remains high.

5) Computational scope is staged and testable (addresses critique v): Rather than starting with a fully polarizable, high-dimensional osmotic ensemble on a disordered rotor system, the simulation plan is explicitly hierarchical. Stage-1 proves that a two-state Hamiltonian coupled to adsorption can generate phase coexistence/steps consistent with experiment and controls, with pre-registered CVs and acceptance criteria. Stage-2 then adds atomistic disorder supercells and restrained phase switching, while interaction accuracy is prioritized first at open-metal CO2 binding using QM-derived, site-specific parameters (consistent with the demonstrated necessity in open-metal-site MOFs) before optional polarizability upgrades.

6) Alignment with the concept chain and literature assets: The refined hypothesis preserves the original logic that strong CO2 binding at open metal sites (Asset 1) provides the thermodynamic lever, while the accuracy limits of generic force fields motivate QM-derived interactions (Asset 2) and simulation-based free-volume/adsorption coupling (Asset 3). The phase-change/gated-free-volume concept remains, but is translated into a chemically and structurally defensible minimal system consistent with the phase-change precedent in dynamic MOFs (Asset 4) without over-claiming crystallographic resolution at partial occupancy.
Critique: This is a technically mature and unusually well-defended proposal that directly addresses known failure modes in dynamic MOF design (metal-site poisoning, overreliance on SCSC, and uncontrolled disorder). Engineering resolution is very high due to explicit decision gates, mandatory negative controls, and disorder-aware characterization. Minor deductions arise from the synthetic risk inherent in producing an isoreticular dobdc analog with pendant crown ethers at controlled low occupancy without degrading crystallinity or channel uniformity; while defensible, this remains nontrivial. Logical consistency is strong: the thermodynamic lever (CO2–open-metal binding) is clearly separated from the gating mechanism, and the cooperative transition is mechanistically argued rather than asserted. A small logical vulnerability remains in assuming that a sub-10% population of rotors can generate a sufficiently collective elastic response in MOF-74 without long-range framework distortion—this is plausible but not yet demonstrated in closely analogous systems. Evidence grounding is excellent, with disciplined adherence to the concept chain and avoidance of speculative crystallographic claims. Rationale quality is high: the proposal does not merely apply known techniques but restructures both chemistry and modeling to overcome a recognized bottleneck in adsorption-driven phase-change MOFs.

Hypothesis:
A reproducible, stereochemically biased enantiodiscrimination response toward histidine can be generated in an otherwise achiral Zn(II) MOF by enforcing (before any chiral exposure) a crystallographically ordered, compositionally verified dimethylammonium (Me2NH2+) counterion sublattice within 1D channels, then converting that pre-registered ion lattice to L- or D-histidinium through a demonstrably topotactic, single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) counterion exchange that preserves unit-cell continuity and excludes dissolution–recrystallization.

Mechanistic rationale (explicit symmetry-breaking pathway):
(1) **Pre-organization and registry**: An ordered Me2NH2+ array provides a periodic set of electrostatic minima and directional H-bond donors/acceptors (N–H···O(carboxylate)/O(solvent)) that defines discrete, symmetry-related binding microenvironments along the channel. This converts “guest inclusion” from a statistically disordered adsorption problem into a lattice substitution problem (ion A → ion B at mapped crystallographic sites).
(2) **Chiral amplification upon substitution**: Replacing an achiral, orientationally ordered Me2NH2+ with a *chiral, multifunctional* histidinium introduces an orientational preference (imidazolium/imidazole + α-NH3+ + COO−) that can select one of two enantiomorphic arrangements (or generate enantiomorphic domain populations) because each substituted site must satisfy an overdetermined H-bond/ion-pairing set to the framework oxygens and to adjacent counterions/solvent. This creates a coherent, non-centrosymmetric (or domain-coherent) chiral counterion lattice rather than random, locally chiral but globally cancelling configurations. L vs D is predicted to produce either (i) enantiomorphic guest packings (opposite handedness; opposite-sign CD with comparable magnitude at matched loading) or (ii) identical framework symmetry but opposite-sign oriented guest CD that is axis-dependent in single-crystal CD.
(3) **Isolation from metal-node chemistry**: By selecting a Zn-carboxylate/azole host with saturated Zn coordination (no open-metal sites under exchange conditions) and by directly testing for Zn/linker leaching and Zn–histidine binding, the optical readout is constrained to counterion exchange-driven chiral field formation (not Zn-node cation exchange, defect coordination, or etching).
(4) **Causally linked dual transduction**: (a) solid-state CD reports on long-range chiral order (guest lattice coherence and symmetry), while (b) fluorescence quenching constants extracted primarily from lifetime Stern–Volmer (τ0/τ) report on excited-state microenvironment changes near an integrated luminophore. Enantiodiscrimination is claimed only if L and D give matched uptake/partitioning and matched optical artifact controls, yet distinct lifetime-based quenching behavior consistent with the crystallographically verified chiral arrangement.
Plan:
A. Platform pre-registration (mandatory go/no-go gates)

A1. Select/engineer a cationic Zn(II) framework that admits crystallographically ordered counterions in 1D channels
- **Design constraint**: Zn nodes must be coordinatively saturated in the as-synthesized and exchanged states (no persistent open Zn sites). Prioritize Zn-carboxylate/azole nets known to be robust under alcohol/MeCN exchange and to crystallize with ordered counterions.
- **Topology/geometry constraint**: 1D channels with repeating ionic pockets spaced ~6–12 Å (to allow site-resolved counterion positions by SCXRD) and sufficient aperture for histidinium transport.

A2. Counterion composition control: avoid relying solely on DMF decomposition
- **Primary route (preferred)**: Deliberately introduce Me2NH2+ during solvothermal growth using Me2NH2Cl (or Me2NH2NO3) as the only added salt, while using a solvent system that minimizes competing decomposition products (e.g., DMF/MeCN or DEF/MeCN mixtures; avoid long high-T soaks that generate formate).
- **Secondary route (if in situ generation used)**: Use isotopically labeled DMF (e.g., d7-DMF) only as a diagnostic tool, not as the compositional source of Me2NH2+.

A3. Hard go/no-go #1: demonstrate ordered Me2NH2+ as the sole counterion in ≥2 independent batches
Required evidence (all must pass):
1) **SCXRD** (two separate syntheses): locate Me2NH2+ sites with reasonable ADPs/occupancies; low residual electron density in the channels; no unmodelled peaks consistent with alternative cations.
2) **Independent stoichiometry**: quantify Me2NH2+ per formula unit by (i) digestion 1H NMR with an internal standard and (ii) ion chromatography (IC) or quantitative 1H qNMR of the supernatant after complete framework dissolution. Agreement within ±10%.
3) **Rule out mixed counterions**: specifically assay for formate and monomethylammonium by (i) ion chromatography/formate calibration and (ii) digestion 1H NMR for HCOO− and MeNH3+ signatures; acceptable threshold: each <5 mol% of total counterion equivalents.
If any criterion fails: iterate synthesis (salt identity, solvent, temperature ramp, time) or switch to an alternative cationic Zn framework.

B. Integrate an emissive linker without perturbing ion order

B1. Reporter linker choice and loading
- Use 0.5–2 mol% of an isoreticular emissive dicarboxylate (e.g., naphthalene-2,6-dicarboxylate or a benzothiadiazole-dicarboxylate) chosen to (i) substitute into the same coordination motif, (ii) remain rigid (minimize nonradiative decay), and (iii) place emissive sites on the pore wall.

B2. Validate reporter incorporation and unchanged counterion order
- **Digestion 1H NMR**: quantify reporter/linker ratio.
- **PXRD**: confirm phase purity.
- **SCXRD spot-check**: verify that Me2NH2+ ordering persists (no symmetry change attributable to reporter insertion at this dilution).
Go/no-go #2: reporter-loaded crystals must retain the same space group (or a clearly understood subgroup) and comparable counterion site occupancy.

C. Topotactic SCSC counterion exchange with histidinium: discriminate from dissolution–recrystallization

C1. Exchange conditions engineered to suppress Zn–histidine coordination and etching
- **Histidine speciation control**: perform exchange using pre-protonated histidinium salts (L-His·HCl and D-His·HCl) at controlled pH 4.5–6.0 (buffered with non-coordinating buffers at low concentration if needed; avoid phosphate and strong chelators). This keeps histidine predominantly cationic, discouraging Zn binding by deprotonating donor sites.
- **Solvent**: MeCN/iPrOH/H2O micro-mixtures tuned to maintain crystallinity; water kept minimal but sufficient for ion mobility (screened empirically).
- **Stepwise osmotic protocol**: sequential soaks with increasing histidinium concentration (e.g., 1 mM → 10 mM → 50 mM → 100 mM) while monitoring crystal integrity.

C2. Hard go/no-go #3: prove exchange is topotactic (not recrystallization)
Required discriminating experiments:
1) **Time-resolved SCXRD on the same crystal**: collect partial datasets at multiple timepoints during exchange; require unit-cell parameters to evolve continuously (no discontinuous jump), preserved mosaicity within defined limits, and retention of crystal habit.
2) **Solution leaching analysis**: at each timepoint, analyze soak liquors by ICP-MS for Zn and by HPLC/UV (or LC-MS) for linker; thresholds: Zn loss <0.5% of total Zn per exchange step; linker signal below detection or <0.1%.
3) **Defect/metal-site probe post-exchange**: XAS (Zn K-edge) or solid-state NMR proxy plus ICP of combined soak solutions to verify no new Zn–N coordination signatures consistent with histidine binding and no significant Zn removal.
Failing any of these triggers redesign (lower ionic strength, different solvent, lower temperature, shorter steps, stronger protonation, alternative MOF).

C3. Quantify exchange fraction and ensure matched loading between enantiomers
- **Digestion 1H NMR**: Me2NH2+ vs histidine integrals.
- **Elemental analysis/IC**: released Me2NH2+ in solution mass balance.
- Run L and D exchanges to matched fractional replacement (e.g., 25%, 50%, 75%, ~100%) by adjusting time/concentration; enantiodiscrimination claims are made only at matched loading ±5%.

D. Make symmetry-breaking explicit and test crystallographic consequences

D1. Determine space group and absolute structure before/after exchange
- **Before exchange**: space group assignment with validation (systematic absences, refinement statistics).
- **After exchange**: attempt non-centrosymmetric refinement; if non-centrosymmetric, report Flack parameter and/or Parsons quotient where applicable.
Go/no-go #4 (symmetry criterion):
- Pathway A (strong): post-exchange structure refines in a non-centrosymmetric space group with acceptable absolute-structure metrics and identifiable histidinium ordering.
- Pathway B (allowed alternative): framework remains centrosymmetric, but histidinium forms oriented, long-range coherent domains; must be demonstrated by oriented single-crystal CD anisotropy and/or domain-sensitive measurements (see D2).

D2. Domain coherence and artifact rejection (if centrosymmetric average structure)
- **Oriented single-crystal CD**: collect CD along at least two defined crystallographic orientations; require reproducible axis dependence and sign inversion between L and D at matched loading.
- **Polarized absorption/linear dichroism controls**: separate LD contributions from true CD (appropriate baselines and rotation/orientation controls).

E. Chiroptical readout + orthogonal chiral verification

E1. Solid-state CD (DRCD + single-crystal)
- DRCD on microcrystals with matched particle size distributions (sieved fractions) and matched loadings; include scattering correction protocols and reference standards.
- Single-crystal CD on oriented plates when possible to confirm intrinsic chirality vs scattering.

E2. Orthogonal chiral readout (mandatory)
Choose at least one (prefer two):
1) **Vibrational CD (VCD) in the solid state** focusing on histidine vibrational bands; compare L vs D exchanged materials at matched loading.
2) **Chiral HPLC of desorbed guests from single crystals**: gentle back-extraction of histidinium (or complete digestion with immediate chiral derivatization) to confirm enantiopurity retention and rule out racemization; correlate desorbed amount with SCXRD occupancy.
3) **ROA (if available)** for complementary vibrational chirality.
Go/no-go #5: CD sign/intensity differences must be corroborated by an orthogonal chiral method not relying on electronic CD alone.

F. Stern–Volmer causality tightened to enantiodiscrimination

F1. Primary metric: lifetime-based Stern–Volmer (τ0/τ)
- Measure time-resolved emission (TCSPC or equivalent) to obtain τ0 and τ under quencher titration; define KSV,τ from τ0/τ = 1 + KSV,τ[Q]. Use steady-state I0/I only as secondary with inner-filter corrections.

F2. Enforce equal quencher partitioning and correct artifacts
- **Quencher uptake isotherms**: for each exchanged material (L, D at matched loading), measure quencher adsorption/partitioning (e.g., by UV–vis quantification of supernatant) to ensure identical [Q]in-pore vs [Q]bulk relationship; only compare KSV,τ when uptake isotherms overlap within error.
- **Inner-filter/scattering controls**: match crystal size distributions; measure diffuse reflectance/absorbance at excitation and emission wavelengths; apply standard inner-filter corrections; verify no systematic difference in turbidity between L and D suspensions.

F3. Optional stronger causality: chiral-sensitive excited-state reporter
- If ΔKSV remains ambiguous, implement an excimer-capable reporter pair at very low probability (statistical) or a linker known to show environment-sensitive circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) response; interpret only after confirming unchanged topology and counterion order.

G. Discriminating controls (expanded vs artifacts)

G1. Counterion-order controls
- Prepare isostructural analogues using alternative counterions introduced during growth (Et3NH+, NH4+, or bulky TBA+).
Prediction: weaker/absent counterion order → exchange may occur but CD and enantiodifferential KSV,τ should diminish.

G2. Dissolution/recrystallization positive control
- Deliberately perform an exchange under conditions known to partially dissolve MOF (e.g., higher water fraction or higher pH) to generate a “recrystallized” sample; demonstrate that it yields different diffraction signatures (loss of unit-cell continuity) and potentially spurious CD/fluorescence signals, thereby validating the discriminating tests.

G3. Metal-site binding control
- Expose Me2NH2+-MOF to histidine under identical conditions but with competitive non-coordinating cation present (e.g., excess Me2NH2Cl) to suppress exchange; test that no CD emerges if exchange is blocked.

G4. Loading-matched L vs D control
- For every CD/KSV comparison, enforce matched histidinium occupancy; report CD g-factor and KSV,τ as a function of occupancy to separate “loading” from “handedness.”

H. Success metrics and decision points
- **Milestone 1 (Month 1–3)**: Ordered Me2NH2+ confirmed in ≥2 batches + counterion purity thresholds passed.
- **Milestone 2 (Month 3–6)**: SCSC exchange demonstrated with unit-cell continuity + Zn/linker leaching below thresholds.
- **Milestone 3 (Month 6–9)**: Space-group/absolute structure (or domain coherence via oriented CD) established; L vs D yields reproducible opposite-sign CD at matched loading.
- **Milestone 4 (Month 9–12)**: Lifetime-based KSV,τ differences observed *only* when quencher uptake isotherms overlap and artifact controls pass; orthogonal chiral readout confirms enantiospecific arrangement.
Feasibility:
1) Addressing the highest feasibility risk (ordered Me2NH2+ as sole counterion): The plan no longer depends on uncontrolled DMF decomposition. Me2NH2+ is introduced deliberately (Me2NH2Cl/NO3) during crystal growth to preserve the “intrinsic during growth” requirement while enabling strict compositional control. Two-batch SCXRD reproducibility plus independent counterion stoichiometry (digestion qNMR + IC) and explicit assays for formate/MeNH3+ provide a hard pre-registration gate that prevents over-claiming an “ordered array” when mixed counterions are present.

2) De-risking SCSC exchange with histidine: Exchange conditions are engineered around histidine speciation (histidinium salts; mildly acidic pH window) to suppress Zn–histidine coordination and framework etching. Topotactic character is not assumed: it is *proven* via time-resolved single-crystal diffraction on the same crystal (unit-cell continuity), crystal habit retention, and quantitative solution-phase leaching limits (ICP-MS for Zn; LC/HPLC for linker). These discriminating experiments directly exclude dissolution–recrystallization as an alternative explanation.

3) Constraining the symmetry-breaking mechanism: The revised proposal commits to explicit crystallographic outcomes (space group assignments pre/post) and absolute structure validation (Flack/Parsons) when non-centrosymmetric structures emerge. If the average structure remains centrosymmetric, the proposal provides an alternative, testable mechanism (coherent oriented chiral guest domains) and requires oriented single-crystal CD anisotropy to demonstrate domain coherence—preventing misinterpretation of DRCD scattering artifacts as intrinsic chirality.

4) Tightening Stern–Volmer causality: Enantiodiscrimination claims are anchored to lifetime-based Stern–Volmer constants (τ0/τ) to decouple absorption/scattering and static quenching. Quencher uptake isotherms are measured and must overlap for L and D materials before KSV,τ is compared; this removes the major ambiguity that different partitioning, residual solvent, or particle size could dominate ΔKSV. Inner-filter and turbidity corrections are built in as required acceptance criteria.

5) Orthogonal chiral verification: Electronic CD alone is insufficient; the plan mandates an additional chiral-specific method (solid-state VCD and/or chiral HPLC of desorbed/digested guests) to confirm enantiospecific arrangement/retention, ensuring that opposite-sign CD is not attributed to uncontrolled differences in loading, defects, or scattering.

Together, these go/no-go gates and discriminating controls convert the original concept chain (pre-ordered counterion lattice → topotactic substitution → chiral ordering → CD + enantiodifferential quenching) into a falsifiable, artifact-resistant workflow that is realistic for MOF single-crystal chemistry while preserving the core novelty: counterion-lattice exchange as the driver of chiral field formation in an otherwise achiral Zn(II) framework.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and technically mature proposal that anticipates nearly all common failure modes in claims of chiral induction and enantiodiscrimination in achiral MOFs. The strongest aspect is the explicit conversion of a vague 'chiral adsorption' idea into a crystallographically mapped lattice-substitution mechanism with falsifiable symmetry outcomes. Engineering resolution is very high due to the mandatory SCXRD reproducibility, counterion purity assays, time-resolved single-crystal exchange, and quantitative leaching thresholds. Logical consistency is likewise strong: the symmetry-breaking pathway is explicit, alternative outcomes (non-centrosymmetric refinement vs. chiral domain coherence) are pre-defined, and artifact rejection is built into every optical claim. Minor deductions arise from cumulative experimental risk: the simultaneous requirement of ordered counterions, preserved single crystallinity, emissive linker tolerance, and clean histidinium exchange makes the overall workflow demanding and potentially slow, with several sequential hard gates that could stall progress. Evidence grounding is solid and stays within chemistry/MOF physics, though the Stern–Volmer → enantiodiscrimination link remains empirically contingent on the reporter–quencher geometry rather than guaranteed by the lattice model alone. Rationale quality is high: the proposal genuinely addresses a known bottleneck (false-positive chirality from disorder, dissolution, or uptake differences) with a structurally novel counterion-lattice strategy rather than repackaging standard chiral MOF sensing.

Hypothesis: A Ni(II) MOF built from preorganized, redox-innocent metalloligand nodes that enforce a near-degenerate five- vs six-coordinate landscape will exhibit guest-dependent, single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) coordination-geometry switching at the nickel active site, producing a measurable, cooperative structural transformation of the host lattice. Methodological adaptation: instead of introducing hemilabile pendant donors (rejected approach), we will hard-wire geometric frustration into the primary node by using a rigid tetradentate N2O2 metalloligand (salen/salophen-type) that locks Ni(II) into a square-planar basal plane, while the framework topology positions a crystallographic ‘apical pocket’ (defined by proximal noncoordinating O/F atoms and pore field) that can reversibly stabilize either (i) a true octahedral Ni site via guest axial ligation (six-coordinate) or (ii) a square-pyramidal Ni site via single axial binding (five-coordinate). Mechanistically, specific guest molecules with appropriate donor strength, steric profile, and dipole moment modulate the axial ligand binding free energy and local electrostatic field at Ni, tipping the equilibrium between 5C and 6C states; because the apical pocket is part of the repeating lattice, this local coordination change propagates as a collective lattice strain (hinge-like distortion of metalloligand–pillar angles), giving a crystallographically resolvable SCSC structural transformation and step-like sorption/selectivity.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Metalloligand synthesis (primary adaptation element): synthesize a dicarboxylate-functionalized salophen (or salen) ligand, H2L-2CO2H, where the salophen N2O2 pocket binds Ni(II) to give a square-planar Ni(L) unit, and the periphery bears two (or four) carboxylates positioned for framework assembly (e.g., 5,5'-dicarboxy substituents on the salicylidene rings for linear connectivity).
1.2 Node premetalation: prepare crystalline Ni(L-2CO2H) (Ni(II) inserted prior to MOF formation) to ensure the nickel active site identity is preserved during solvothermal assembly and to avoid mixed Ni-carboxylate SBUs.
1.3 Framework topology design to create an apical pocket: assemble Ni(L-2CO2) metalloligands with Zr6O4(OH)4 (or Hf6) clusters as robust carboxylate connecters to yield a 3D framework with large pores; select a topology (e.g., ftw/pcu-derived) where the Ni centers line the pore walls and the axial direction is unobstructed, while nearby cluster μ3-OH/terminal OH (or linker substituents such as –F on the salophen aryl rings) define a consistent apical electrostatic environment.
1.4 Single-crystal growth: optimize modulated solvothermal growth (benzoic/acetic acid modulators; DMF/DEF mixtures) to obtain 50–200 μm single crystals suitable for SCXRD; verify phase purity by PXRD and confirm metalloligand integrity by digestion NMR and ICP.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Baseline SCXRD and coordination-geometry metrics: solve the as-synthesized structure (guest-filled) by SCXRD to confirm (i) square-planar NiN2O2 basal geometry, (ii) presence/absence of weak axial solvent occupancy, (iii) apical pocket dimensions (Ni···O/F distances, void volume above Ni), and (iv) framework connectivity (Zr6–carboxylate binding mode).
2.2 Guest set rationalization (mechanistic contrast): choose guests that selectively favor 5C vs 6C and probe field/steric effects: (a) strong monodentate donors: MeCN, pyridine, THF; (b) bidentate/bridging candidates that could enforce 6C: 4,4'-bipyridine, pyrazine (size-limited to avoid framework binding elsewhere); (c) polar noncoordinating guests to test electrostatic stabilization without direct ligation: CH2Cl2, nitromethane; (d) weak donors/controls: CO2, N2, Ar.
2.3 In situ single-crystal guest exchange under controlled chemical potential (method adaptation): implement a fixed-crystal, variable-guest chemical potential protocol using sealed capillaries with saturated vapor reservoirs (or a microfluidic single-crystal cell) to avoid crystal handling. Collect serial SCXRD datasets on the same crystal after stepwise dosing (incremental vapor pressure or solution exchange) to capture intermediate occupancies and possible order–disorder transitions at the axial site.
2.4 Quantify coordination switching and lattice response: compute continuous shape measures (CShM) and τ5 for Ni (square-pyramidal index), track Ni–N/O axial bond formation and occupancy factors, and map unit-cell strain tensors and pore-limiting diameter changes. Identify whether switching is local (partial occupancy) or cooperative (symmetry change, abrupt cell change).
2.5 Correlate structure with thermodynamics/kinetics: measure adsorption isotherms (volumetric) for key guests showing switching; use microcalorimetry to extract differential enthalpies at the uptake step. Perform time-resolved PXRD during dosing/evacuation to obtain kinetic barriers and hysteresis corresponding to SCXRD-resolved states.
2.6 Electronic-structure readout at nickel active site: collect Ni K-edge XAS (XANES/EXAFS) on matched guest-loaded states to confirm average coordination number changes; use IR to detect coordinated MeCN/THF signatures (shifted ν(C≡N), ν(C–O)). If accessible, perform variable-temperature magnetic susceptibility to detect ligand-field changes associated with 5C/6C switching.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Causality controls (prove adaptation, not incidental flexibility):
- Control A (no apical pocket): synthesize an isoreticular analog with sterically blocking substituents above Ni (e.g., ortho-alkyl on salophen rings) predicted to prevent axial binding; test for absence of SCSC switching.
- Control B (electrostatics-only): replace Zr6(OH) termini by post-synthetic capping (e.g., sulfate/phosphate binding to Zr) to attenuate local H-bond/electrostatic field; evaluate whether guest thresholds/hysteresis shift.
- Control C (metal identity): prepare Co(L) or Cu(L) analog frameworks (same topology) to test whether switching is specific to Ni(II) axial lability.
3.2 Reversibility and fatigue: perform ≥20 guest adsorption/desorption cycles (e.g., MeCN ⇄ CO2 or THF ⇄ Ar) while tracking single-crystal integrity (mosaicity), PXRD crystallinity, and retention of switching step positions.
3.3 Mechanistic modeling across length scales: (i) periodic DFT (or DFT+U) to compute free-energy differences between 5C and 6C states as a function of guest and local field; (ii) compute elastic response (framework hinge angles) to link local coordination change to macroscopic strain; (iii) grand-canonical Monte Carlo with two-state site model parameterized from DFT/SCXRD to reproduce stepped isotherms and predict selectivity windows.
3.4 Structural transformation mapping: build a transformation diagram (guest chemical potential vs temperature) identifying phase boundaries (5C-dominant, 6C-dominant, mixed) and correlate with SCXRD-determined symmetry/unit-cell changes, establishing a mechanistic ‘coordination geometry → lattice transformation’ relationship.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Square-planar Ni(II) in salen/salophen environments is well established, and axial ligation to form 5C/6C adducts is a classic, tunable equilibrium controlled by donor strength/sterics and local electrostatics. SCSC transformations in MOFs under guest exchange are documented, and SCXRD can directly resolve axial ligand occupancy and unit-cell strain, enabling a structure-first mechanism.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The approach uses rational, modular MOF design: a premetalated metalloligand fixes the nickel active site identity and basal coordination geometry, while robust Zr6-carboxylate connectivity ensures crystallinity and chemical stability during repeated guest exchange. The ‘apical pocket’ is created by topology and local functional group placement rather than secondary-sphere hemilability, aligning guest molecules with a defined coordination direction.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional flexible MOFs where transformations arise mainly from linker torsions or solvent loss, this design couples a chemically explicit event (Ni coordination-number change) to a cooperative lattice response, enabling unambiguous SCXRD mechanistic assignment. Relative to the rejected pendant-donor toggle strategy, the adaptation eliminates tether conformational entropy and kinetic ambiguity by embedding the switch into a preorganized, rigid metalloligand node, improving crystallographic tractability, reversibility, and predictive tunability via apical-pocket electrostatics and steric design.
Critique: This is an unusually strong and technically mature proposal. The engineering plan is detailed down to crystallographic metrics (CShM, τ5, strain tensors), in situ SCXRD methodology, and multiscale modeling that directly interrogates the stated hypothesis. The logical arc—from enforced square-planar Ni(II), to guest-modulated axial ligation, to cooperative lattice strain—is internally consistent and chemically well founded. Minor score deductions arise from two points of risk: (i) the reliance on Zr6 cluster hydroxyls or proximal F/O atoms to provide a sufficiently uniform and strong electrostatic apical field may be overly optimistic without preliminary electrostatic mapping or spectroscopic validation; (ii) the assumption that axial ligation equilibria will remain sufficiently slow and ordered to permit clean SCSC switching under repeated guest exchange is nontrivial and may be system-specific. These are feasibility risks rather than conceptual flaws.

Hypothesis: Solvent-free, redox-programmed mechanosynthesis can lock in a non-equilibrium, percolating mixed-valence semiquinoid network that exhibits higher and temporally tunable electronic conductivity than solution-synthesized analogues, because controlled mechanochemical generation and trapping of semiquinone radicals increases metal–ligand covalency and intervalence charge-transfer (IVCT) pathways while suppressing insulating counterion/solvate trapping. Methodological adaptation: replace conventional ball-milling MOF synthesis with an in situ ‘redox-buffered LAG’ protocol (liquid-assisted grinding with a redox buffer + conductive-matrix milling) that (i) meters electron count during framework formation, (ii) imposes anisotropic microstrain to increase orbital overlap between M(d) and dhbq(π*) manifolds, and (iii) enables time-resolved conductivity tracking during formation to directly correlate electron motion/relaxation with emergent conductivity.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select the 2D metal–semiquinoid platform (H2NMe2)2M2(Cl2dhbq)3 as a conductivity benchmark and expand metals to a covalency series (V, Ti, Cr plus Fe, Co) while keeping topology constant; prepare Cl2dhbq ligand and define electron-count targets (quinone:semiquinone:catecholate ratios) via independent chemical titration.
1.2 Design a redox-buffered LAG additive set: (a) mild one-electron reductant (e.g., cobaltocene derivative or tetrathiafulvalene, TTF), (b) mild oxidant (e.g., ferrocenium salt), and (c) ion-pairing modulator (bulky ammonium) to minimize pore-blocking; calibrate redox potentials against dhbq couples in the milling microenvironment using ex situ EPR/UV–Vis–NIR on aliquots.
1.3 Prepare a conductive milling matrix (5–15 wt% carbon black or graphite) to form reproducible pressed pellets directly from the milled powder, enabling in situ/ex situ conductivity without solvent exposure; confirm the matrix does not dominate conduction by running blank matrix controls and percolation-threshold checks.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Execute mechanosynthesis under ‘electron-count control’: mill metal precursor + ligand + dimethylammonium source with sub-stoichiometric redox buffer (oxidant/reductant pair) and minimal LAG solvent (DMF or MeCN, η = 0.05–0.20 μL mg−1). Systematically vary (i) redox buffer ratio, (ii) milling frequency/energy, and (iii) η to map formation windows where semiquinone fraction is maximized while crystallinity/topology is retained.
2.2 Couple time-resolved monitoring to synthesis: (a) collect time-resolved PXRD (stroboscopic sampling) to capture phase evolution and crystallite growth, (b) acquire time-resolved EPR to quantify semiquinone radical concentration vs milling time, and (c) collect time-resolved diffuse-reflectance UV–Vis–NIR to track IVCT band emergence (signature of mixed valency and delocalization).
2.3 Implement time-dependent conductivity measurements during and after formation: rapidly press pellets from time-aliquots (e.g., 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60 min) under inert atmosphere and measure σ(t) by four-probe DC plus frequency-dependent impedance (10−1–10^6 Hz) to separate electronic vs ionic contributions; repeat σ(t) after controlled aging (minutes to days) to quantify relaxation/reorganization of electron pathways.
2.4 Mechanistic perturbations to isolate the electron-motion origin: (i) isotopic/protic perturbation (dry vs controlled humidity) to rule out protonic conduction, (ii) counterion variation (dimethylammonium vs bulky ammonium) to test pore/charge-compensation effects on IVCT, and (iii) microstrain annealing (gentle thermal anneal below decomposition) to observe whether conductivity decreases as non-equilibrium orbital overlap relaxes.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structure/composition validation: Rietveld refinement of PXRD for topology retention; XPS/XANES for metal oxidation state distribution; elemental analysis/ICP for stoichiometry; gas sorption to confirm porosity and check pore blocking by additives.
3.2 Quantify delocalization and mixed valency: correlate (a) EPR intensity/linewidth (spin concentration and exchange), (b) NIR IVCT energy and bandwidth (Hush analysis for electronic coupling), and (c) magnetic susceptibility (exchange pathways) with σ and activation energy (Arrhenius/VRH fits).
3.3 Benchmark against solution synthesis: prepare solution-grown analogues with matched composition and compare (i) σ at room temperature, (ii) temperature-dependent transport mechanism (band-like vs hopping/VRH), and (iii) time-dependent σ relaxation. Success criterion: mechanosynthesized, redox-buffered samples show ≥10× higher σ than solution analogues at matched topology, and exhibit controllable σ(t) evolution attributable to semiquinone fraction and IVCT coupling.
3.4 Establish causality: use multivariate models linking milling parameters → microstrain/crystallite size (Williamson–Hall) → IVCT coupling (Hush) → σ(t) and relaxation constants; confirm that removing redox buffer collapses IVCT signatures and reduces σ, demonstrating the adaptation—not merely milling—drives conductivity gains.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Metal–semiquinoid frameworks already show conductivity strongly dependent on electron delocalization and metal–ligand covalency, with V phases markedly more conductive than Ti/Cr analogues; mixed valency and IVCT bands are established hallmarks of enhanced transport. Time-resolved MOF studies demonstrate that transient states during formation and framework dynamics influence electron motion and measured conductivity, motivating direct time-domain coupling of synthesis and transport.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Mechanosynthesis provides access to solvent-free, kinetically trapped states; adding a redox buffer converts milling from a purely structural method into an electron-count-controlled assembly route, directly targeting the semiquinone/mixed-valence motif responsible for conductivity. Conductive-matrix milling enables reproducible pellet formation from air-sensitive, non-equilibrium powders for rapid σ(t) acquisition without solution processing.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to solution synthesis, the adapted method (i) prevents over-solvation/counterion trapping that can localize charge, (ii) enables deliberate semiquinone fraction tuning during crystallization rather than post-synthetic doping, (iii) creates microstrain-enhanced orbital overlap for stronger electronic coupling, and (iv) uniquely resolves time-dependent conductivity formation/relaxation, allowing mechanism-based optimization rather than endpoint screening.
Critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and technically mature proposal that demonstrates deep command of metal–semiquinoid MOF chemistry, mixed-valence physics, and mechanochemical synthesis. The engineering plan is detailed, internally consistent, and largely executable with advanced infrastructure. Minor score deductions arise from two areas: (i) the practical complexity and risk of synchronizing time-resolved EPR, PXRD, and conductivity with milling—while conceptually sound, it may strain throughput and reproducibility; and (ii) the assumption that mechanically induced microstrain will systematically enhance orbital overlap without introducing disorder that counteracts IVCT is plausible but not guaranteed. These are manageable risks, but they temper claims of determinism. Overall, the proposal exceeds the norm in rigor and originality and avoids speculative leaps or irrelevant conceptual imports.

Hypothesis:
We hypothesize that a defect-engineered, fluorinated Zn4O-carboxylate framework in the IRMOF/MOF-5 family—targeting Zn4O(F4-bdc)3 (F4-bdc = 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoro-1,4-benzenedicarboxylate) as the primary topology—can be reproducibly tuned to couple (i) CO2-selective transport (aperture constriction to the ultramicropore regime) with (ii) elevated density of chemically verified Lewis-acid Zn sites for CO2 activation, while (iii) maintaining persistent antifouling chemistry via covalently installed hydrophilic/zwitterionic moieties rather than relying on solvent history.

Mechanistic rationale resolving reviewer concerns:
(1) Defect placement is not assumed to “self-localize” at windows by ethanol alone. Instead, we enforce kinetically biased defect formation at external crystal surfaces and near pore mouths via a competitive-ligand/modulator strategy (monocarboxylate + controlled water content) during solvothermal growth, combined with a diffusion-limited post-synthetic treatment that preferentially accesses near-surface regions. This creates a core–shell (defect-rich shell / defect-lean core) architecture that functionally behaves as an “aperture bottleneck” layer without claiming atomically perfect window-only vacancies.
(2) The bottleneck claim is reframed from a narrow, absolute 3.3–3.6 Å window assertion to a quantitatively validated shift in the ultramicropore fraction and transport selectivity. Partial missing-linker defects and Zn–X (X = OH/OR/NO3) termination, plus controlled partial pore narrowing by grafted hydrophilic groups at/near the shell, jointly increase the population of ultramicroporous constrictions detectable by CO2 sorption/NLDFT and by diffusion/uptake kinetics.
(3) CO2 catalysis is attributed only after deconvolution: intrinsic turnover frequency (TOF) will be normalized to independently measured coordinatively unsaturated Zn (CUS) density (XAS/EXAFS + probe-DRIFTS), while transport/sieving contributions will be assessed through size-varied epoxide substrates and diffusion metrics.
(4) Antifouling is made chemically persistent by installing stable PEG/zwitterionic functionality (mixed-linker or post-synthetic grafting onto defect-terminating –OH) and validated under realistic aqueous cross-flow with ionic strength controls. This aligns antifouling to durable surface chemistry (hydrophilic/charge-neutral) rather than transient ethanol templating.

This integrated design leverages established MOF surface area and molecular sieving concepts (Assets 1–3) while grounding catalysis in Zn-derived Lewis acidity and defect-generated active sites (Assets 4–5) and explicitly introducing enforceable synthetic “knobs” (modulator, water activity, nitrate/alkoxide balance, and shell-functionalization) to replace over-claimed defect localization.
Plan:
Step 0 — Target selection, controls, and study design (DoE):
• Target topology: cubic IRMOF/MOF-5-type Zn4O(L)3 (L = F4-bdc; optional parallel arm with bdc for baseline). Rationale: Zn4O-carboxylate nodes provide a clear platform for CUS generation and comparability to MOF-derived porous materials; pore sizes are in the microporous regime where ultramicropore fractions can be tuned by defects/surface functionalization.
• Controls (minimum set):
  C1: Defect-lean Zn4O(F4-bdc)3 synthesized without modulator and with minimal water.
  C2: Defect-engineered sample(s) with increasing modulator equivalents.
  C3: Functionalized (antifouling) versions of C1 and C2.
  C4: A “transport-only” control where CUS are passivated (pyridine or phosphate treatment) but pore structure retained, to separate acidity from sieving.
• DoE variables (factorial/response surface; at least 2–3 levels each):
  V1 modulator type: formic acid vs acetic acid vs benzoic acid (monocarboxylate competitive ligand).
  V2 modulator:linker molar ratio (e.g., 0, 10, 30, 60 equiv vs linker).
  V3 water activity: added H2O equivalents (e.g., 0, 2, 10 equiv vs Zn) to tune Zn–O(H)/Zn–OR termination.
  V4 ethanol fraction in solvent (EtOH/DMF or EtOH/DEF blends) to modulate kinetics and nitrate/alkoxide balance; ethanol is retained as a variable but not the sole causality.
  V5 activation/anneal protocol: temperature and time to tune termination and stability.
• Primary responses: missing-linker concentration, CUS density, ultramicropore fraction, CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4 kinetic selectivity, intrinsic TOF.

Step 1 — Synthesis of Zn4O(F4-bdc)3 with tunable defects (enforceable defect-control knob):
• Precursors: Zn(NO3)2·6H2O; H2F4-bdc; solvent system DMF/EtOH (or DEF/EtOH) to balance solubility and ethanol-derived alkoxide possibility; monocarboxylate modulator (HCO2H/HAc/HBz).
• Strategy:
  – Competitive coordination: modulator competes with F4-bdc at Zn during nucleation/growth to generate missing-linker defects capped by modulator-derived carboxylates and/or –OH/–OR depending on water/ethanol content.
  – Water dosing controls node hydrolysis/termination (Zn–OH vs Zn–OEt) and influences defect compensation.
• Implementation details (example starting window; finalized by DoE):
  – Zn:linker ≈ 4:3 stoichiometry for MOF-5-type, with modulator 0–60 equiv (vs linker).
  – Reaction at 80–120 °C for 12–24 h in sealed reactors; crystal size tracked (SEM) to support core–shell diffusion arguments later.

Step 2 — Post-synthetic treatments to bias defects toward near-surface “bottleneck shell” (without over-claiming atomic localization):
• Solvent exchange: DMF → ethanol (multiple cycles) to remove high-boiling solvent and set a consistent chemical baseline.
• Diffusion-limited shell enrichment (two options, compared):
  (A) Mild, short-time acid/modulator wash in ethanol (e.g., dilute acetic/formic acid in EtOH) to promote near-surface linker labilization/partial vacancy creation; limited penetration depth yields defect-rich shell.
  (B) Controlled humid-ethanol anneal (EtOH with defined water activity) to re-terminate exposed Zn with –OH/–OEt and stabilize CUS precursors.
• Passivation control: selective capping of CUS (pyridine/phosphate) for transport-only control (C4).

Step 3 — Persistent antifouling chemistry installation (replace “ethanol polarity” claim):
• Route 1 (mixed-linker): incorporate a small fraction (e.g., 2–10 mol%) of functionalized dicarboxylate bearing short PEG chain or zwitterionic group (e.g., sulfobetaine-like) compatible with Zn-carboxylate assembly; confirm incorporation by digestion NMR.
• Route 2 (defect-site grafting): exploit defect-terminating –OH groups for covalent attachment (e.g., silane-PEG if surface silanol can be introduced, or carbonate/urethane coupling if an –OH termination is present and chemistry is compatible). Primary goal is stable, hydrophilic/charge-neutral interface.
• Stability check: repeated aqueous soaking + activation cycle; verify retention of functional groups by FTIR/XPS and digestion NMR where applicable.

Step 4 — Quantitative defect and chemical-state verification (mandatory loop):
• Missing-linker quantification:
  – Acid digestion + 1H/19F NMR (for F4-bdc and modulator counting) to quantify linker/modulator ratios.
  – ICP-OES for Zn content; combine with NMR to obtain Zn:(linker+modulator) and vacancy fraction.
  – TGA to cross-check organic/inorganic ratios and termination species.
• Zn coordination and CUS verification:
  – XAS/EXAFS at Zn K-edge to quantify coordination number changes vs defect-lean control.
  – DRIFTS of probe molecules: CD3CN (Lewis acid sites) and CO (where applicable) to quantify Lewis acidity and distinguish from Brønsted sites.
  – XPS to assess residual nitrate/ethoxide/oxygen environments; ensure ethanol-derived species are measured, not presumed.

Step 5 — Proving ultramicropore/bottleneck behavior by structure + transport (mandatory loop):
• Sorption/Pore analysis:
  – N2 isotherms at 77 K (BET; meso/micropore contributions).
  – CO2 isotherms at 273 K (and 298 K if possible) for ultramicropore sensitivity; NLDFT/QSDFT PSD extraction with explicit reporting of ultramicropore fraction (<7 Å) and any constriction peak.
• Diffusion/kinetics:
  – Uptake kinetics comparison for CO2 vs N2/CH4 at matched pressures; fit to diffusion models to extract apparent diffusivities.
  – Zero-length column (ZLC) diffusion measurements as primary kinetic proof; optional PFG-NMR if feasible.
  – In situ PXRD under CO2 to check adsorption-induced lattice changes and to rule out collapse.
• Success criterion (quantitative, not over-specific): a statistically significant increase in ultramicropore fraction and CO2 kinetic selectivity relative to defect-lean control, correlated with defect metrics.

Step 6 — CO2 catalytic conversion testing with deconvolution of active sites vs transport:
• Reaction: cycloaddition of CO2 with epoxides to cyclic carbonates (solvent-free or defined solvent), using standardized conditions (CO2 pressure, temperature) and ensuring catalyst activation state is controlled.
• Substrate size series: epichlorohydrin < propylene oxide < styrene oxide < bulkier epoxides to test size/sieving contribution.
• Intrinsic activity metrics:
  – Report TON/TOF normalized to measured CUS density (from DRIFTS/XAS quantification), not per gram only.
  – Compare defect-rich vs defect-lean and CUS-passivated controls to isolate Lewis acidity contribution.
  – If Brønsted/basic termination suspected (–OH/–OR), include base/acid poisoning tests and correlate with probe-DRIFTS signatures.

Step 7 — Antifouling evaluation under realistic aqueous flow (mandatory improvements):
• Membrane/coating format: grow MOF layer on porous support (or form composite) to enable cross-flow testing; alternatively, packed-bed particle tests with controlled shear.
• Tests:
  – Protein adsorption (BSA, lysozyme) across ionic strength (e.g., 1–100 mM NaCl) and pH range; quantify via QCM-D or depletion assays.
  – Microorganism adhesion (algae/bacteria) under flow; quantify surface coverage and flux decline.
  – Benchmark: defect-lean and non-functionalized controls to show that antifouling arises from persistent PEG/zwitterion chemistry, not ethanol history.
• Coupled performance: evaluate whether antifouling functionalization compromises CO2 uptake/catalysis; use DoE response trade-off analysis.

Step 8 — Iteration/optimization loop:
• Use DoE model to identify the defect/functionalization window that maximizes (i) CUS-normalized TOF, (ii) CO2 kinetic selectivity, (iii) antifouling performance at constant crystallinity/porosity.
• Gate criteria: crystallinity retention (PXRD), stable porosity after aqueous exposure, and reproducibility (≥3 synthesis replicates at optimum).
Feasibility:
Topology realism and stability: Choosing an IRMOF/MOF-5-type Zn4O-carboxylate framework provides a concrete, literature-grounded Zn-MOF node/linker paradigm where missing-linker/termination chemistry can be quantified by digestion NMR + ICP/TGA and where Lewis-acid Zn behavior is chemically testable (probe-DRIFTS, XAS). Using F4-bdc strengthens CO2 affinity and can amplify size/interaction-based selectivity consistent with molecular sieving concepts.

Enforceable defect control (addressing “spatial localization” over-claim): Defect formation is driven by explicit, tunable variables—monocarboxylate modulator identity/loading and water activity—which are known levers for vacancy/termination formation in carboxylate frameworks. Rather than claiming defects form exclusively at windows, the proposal implements a diffusion-limited post-treatment to bias defects toward near-surface regions (core–shell), creating an experimentally defensible bottleneck-shell concept verifiable by kinetics and sorption.

Mechanism validation (active site vs transport): The plan includes mandatory quantification of missing-linker density and Zn CUS by orthogonal methods (digestion NMR/ICP/TGA + XAS/EXAFS + probe-DRIFTS) and explicitly normalizes catalytic TOF to measured CUS density. Size-varied epoxides and CUS-passivated controls separate diffusion/sieving effects from intrinsic Lewis acidity.

Antifouling persistence: Antifouling is no longer attributed to transient “ethanol-templated polarity.” Instead, stable hydrophilic/charge-neutral functionality is introduced via mixed-linker or defect-site grafting and verified after aqueous exposure. Performance is tested under cross-flow and ionic-strength controls to meet realistic fouling conditions.

Alignment with literature assets: High accessible surface area and pore architecture are leveraged for both mass transfer and antifouling-relevant flux behavior (Asset 1), MOF selectivity via molecular sieving and pore tuning is explicitly quantified (Asset 2), and solvent effects (including ethanol) are treated as measurable contributors to porosity/phase behavior rather than assumed causal determinants (Asset 3). Zn-derived active site generation and catalytic relevance are addressed with direct chemical-state proof, consistent with Zn-based MOF-derived catalytic materials and CO2 conversion frameworks (Assets 4–5).
Critique: This is an unusually thorough and self-aware proposal that directly addresses common reviewer objections in defect-engineered Zn-MOF chemistry. Engineering resolution is high due to explicit DoE variables, orthogonal characterization loops, and enforceable synthetic knobs. Logical consistency is strong: the proposal carefully retracts over-claims about atomic defect localization and replaces them with a defensible core–shell bottleneck concept validated by kinetics and sorption. Evidence grounding is solid, with the concept chain preserved and no excursions into irrelevant domains; however, ethanol’s role, while treated more rigorously than typical, still occupies a somewhat overloaded position as solvent, kinetic modifier, and termination source, which slightly weakens conceptual sharpness. Rationale quality is high: the work does not merely apply known defect chemistry but structurally re-frames how transport, catalysis, and antifouling are decoupled and then recombined through quantification and controls. Minor score deductions reflect residual ambition risk (complexity and interdependence of variables) rather than conceptual flaws.

Hypothesis: A proton-activity–programmable Janus tandem-photocatalyst can be realized as a bilayer MOF-on-MOF flow-through membrane in which (i) an upstream, permanently cationic dye-gating/bleaching layer concentrates anionic azo dyes and hosts an ultrathin HxMoO3 plasmonic laminate whose free-carrier density (and thus LSPR-assisted ROS yield) is governed by *local* proton activity at the oxide/MOF interface, while (ii) a downstream Au@Zr-oxo MOF nanoreactor selectively oxidizes aromatic alcohols with minimal dye exposure. This architecture overcomes the reviewers’ risks by: (1) enforcing *quantified* transport decoupling (≥99% azo-dye rejection at defined permeance) via a pinhole-free, interfacially sealed bilayer validated by tracer permeation and through-plane conductivity mapping; (2) replacing bulk-pH assumptions with an explicit Donnan-buffer-transport model and *independent* in situ interfacial pH proxies to establish a uniquely invertible calibration from LSPR/photoconductance → local aH+ under the same ionic strength and dye loading; (3) using a falsifiable energetic/kinetic discriminant matrix (action spectra, intensity/temperature dependence, transient absorption/photothermal readouts, and scavenger controls) to distinguish plasmonic hot-carrier/field effects from photothermal heating, semiconductor-like charge transfer, and dye-sensitized artifacts; and (4) demonstrating robustness in realistic water matrices with explicit thresholds for fouling, Mo/Au leaching, and retention of reversible Hx modulation over ≥100 proton-activity cycles. Mechanistically, local aH+ sets x in HxMoO3, shifting EF and carrier density to tune LSPR amplitude/position and interfacial band bending; these jointly modulate the rate and identity of ROS (•O2− vs •OH) generated at/near the oxide surface and therefore the dye bleaching kinetics and the membrane’s self-referencing response factor, while Layer A’s fixed charge and controlled defect/pinhole density prevent dye transport to Layer B, preserving Au catalytic selectivity for benzyl alcohol oxidation.
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-registered go/no-go criteria (hard acceptance thresholds)
G0.1 Bilayer integrity/gating: methyl orange (MO, ~327 Da, −1) and Congo red (CR, ~697 Da, −2) rejection R ≥ 99.0% at water permeance ≥ 1.0 L m−2 h−1 bar−1 (LMH/bar) in 10 mM Na2SO4, pH 7, 25 °C; and R ≥ 97.0% in 1–10 mM NaHCO3 + 5 mg/L humic acid.
G0.2 Pinhole ceiling: ionic tracer (Cl−/Na+) through-plane conductivity indicates defect-area fraction fdefect ≤ 10−5 (operationally: through-plane conductance ≤ 2× that of a thickness-matched defect-free reference film); fluorescent neutral tracer permeation (rhodamine B base or fluorescein neutral form) shows ≤ 1% breakthrough over 2 h.
G0.3 Local aH+ calibration: under fixed ionic strength (I = 10, 50 mM) and defined dye loading (0, 10, 50 mg/L MO), the mapping {LSPR peak position λp, LSPR extinction magnitude, photoconductance ΔGph} → local pH at the oxide/MOF interface yields R2 ≥ 0.95 and hysteresis ≤ 0.2 pH units over 10 cycles.
G0.4 Mechanism discriminants: action spectrum of bleaching matches LSPR absorption profile (not dye absorption) within ±10 nm; apparent activation energy for rate constant kbleach < 15 kJ/mol (rules out purely thermal); and scavenger/EPR signatures satisfy predefined ROS dominance criteria (see Step 3.3).
G0.5 Stability: Mo leaching ≤ 50 ppb (ICP-MS) after 100 h continuous flow and ≤ 5% loss in LSPR amplitude modulation after ≥100 pH cycles (pH 2 ↔ 9); Au leaching ≤ 10 ppb; Zr leaching ≤ 100 ppb.

Step 1 — Materials selection with epitaxy/compatibility constraints
1.1 Choose lattice-compatible Zr-MOF pair to minimize interfacial mismatch: Layer B = UiO-66-NH2 (or UiO-67 if larger pores needed for Au precursor ingress), Layer A = UiO-66-derived mixed-linker film (BDC/BDAc or BDC-NH2) followed by post-synthetic quaternization to install permanent cationic groups while retaining the *same inorganic Zr6O4(OH)4 node topology* to enable quasi-epitaxial intergrowth rather than true heterotopological epitaxy.
1.2 Define Layer A fixed-charge density target: ≥ 0.5 mmol cationic sites per g film (quantified by elemental analysis/XPS N 1s deconvolution and dye titration), ensuring Donnan exclusion of anionic dyes and controlled local proton partitioning.

Step 2 — Fabrication of a pinhole-minimized Janus bilayer with interfacial sealing
2.1 Support and primer layer: anodic alumina (AAO) or porous alumina/ceramic with pore size 50–200 nm; apply carboxylate-terminated SAM or polydopamine primer (≤ 5 nm) to improve nucleation density.
2.2 Grow Layer B (support-facing) UiO-66-NH2 thin film (target thickness 200–400 nm):
- Seeded solvothermal growth with modulator control (acetic acid/formic acid) to tune defect density; target missing-linker defect concentration 5–15% (from TGA/1H NMR of digested film) to create Zr–OH anchoring sites without collapsing crystallinity.
- Go/no-go: GIXRD indicates preferred orientation (e.g., (111) enhancement) and continuous coverage (no substrate peaks in grazing incidence mapping across area).
2.3 Confine Au nanoparticles exclusively in Layer B (target 1–3 nm, 0.3–1.0 wt%):
- Infiltrate HAuCl4 (ethanol) under vacuum-assisted impregnation; rinse; reduce by CO (25–60 °C) or mild H2 (80–120 °C) to avoid external Au nucleation.
- Verify spatial confinement: HAADF-STEM/EDX line scans across cross-section show Au only in Layer B (Au signal in Layer A < 5% of Layer B integrated intensity). XPS surface Au < detection limit.
2.4 Grow Layer A (feed-facing) cationic UiO-66-derived film (target thickness 100–250 nm) atop Layer B via secondary growth:
- Use same Zr precursor chemistry to promote node continuity; mixed-linker growth to incorporate reactive handles (e.g., BDC-NH2).
- Post-synthetic quaternization to permanent cationic sites (e.g., grafting imidazolium/trimethylammonium via alkylation or amidation + quaternization).
2.5 Interfacial sealing strategy (activated only if G0.1/G0.2 fail):
- Apply an ultrathin “microporosity-preserving seal” at the Layer A/Layer B interface: vapor-phase infiltration (VPI) of alumina (1–3 cycles) or sol–gel silica (≤ 2 nm equivalent) targeted to grain boundaries; acceptance requires <10% loss of micropore volume (ellipsometric porosimetry) and ≥10× reduction in ionic conductance anisotropy.

Step 3 — HxMoO3 nanosheet lamination and definition of local proton activity
3.1 Laminate ultrathin MoO3·xH2O nanosheets onto Layer A with controlled thickness (3–10 nm equivalent):
- Electrostatic assembly driven by Layer A cationic surface; no polyelectrolyte unless needed (if used, ≤ 1 nm PEI/PSS bilayer, verified by QCM-D).
- Confirm retained porosity: ellipsometric porosimetry and Kr adsorption on scraped films; acceptance: ≥70% of Layer A microporosity retained.
3.2 Convert to proton-intercalated HxMoO3 under controlled buffers and quantify x:
- Use buffered solutions (pH 2–9) at fixed ionic strength (I = 10, 50, 100 mM) to reach steady x; quantify Mo5+/Mo6+ by XPS/operando XANES (if available) and correlate with NIR LSPR extinction (UV–Vis–NIR).
3.3 Explicit local-aH+ model (Donnan + buffer + transport) and independent local pH proxy:
- Model: solve coupled Nernst–Planck–Poisson (or electroneutral Donnan approximation) for a cationic microporous film with fixed charge Xf, including buffer species (e.g., phosphate/acetate/carbonate) and salt; outputs: local [H+]int, Donnan potential ΔψD, and partitioning of dye anions.
- Independent measurement: anchor a ratiometric pH fluorophore (e.g., SNARF-derivative) covalently to Layer A linkers at low loading (<1% of linkers) to report local pH within the MOF near the MoO3 interface; validate with confocal microscopy under flow. Alternative/backup: SECM pH microelectrode mapping at the membrane surface under illumination.
- Calibration protocol: for each (I, dye loading), acquire {λp, ExtLSPR, ΔGph} vs fluorophore-reported local pH; require G0.3.

Step 4 — Transport gating characterization with quantitative leakage diagnostics
4.1 Dye rejection/breakthrough:
- Measure rejection for MO and CR at 1–3 bar transmembrane pressure; define flux J and rejection R; target G0.1.
4.2 Multi-tracer pinhole assay:
- Use a panel: (i) anionic fluorescein, (ii) cationic rhodamine 6G, (iii) neutral dye (coumarin), and (iv) 3–10 kDa fluorescent dextrans; quantify selectivity and identify pinhole signatures (simultaneous passage of all tracers indicates defects).
4.3 Through-plane ionic conductivity mapping:
- Perform scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) or micro-4-point mapping across the membrane to spatially resolve high-conductance spots; acceptance: no hotspots exceeding mean + 3σ, consistent with fdefect ≤ 10−5.

Step 5 — Mechanistic discriminant matrix for ROS generation and charge-transfer directionality
5.1 Action spectrum:
- Measure apparent quantum yield (AQY) of dye bleaching vs wavelength (bandpass filters) and compare to (i) MoO3 LSPR absorption, (ii) MOF absorption, (iii) dye absorption. Validation: AQY tracks LSPR, not dye.
5.2 Intensity dependence:
- Determine rate vs photon flux: hot-carrier/photochemical pathways show near-linear at low flux; thermal shows superlinear with temperature rise. Fit k ∝ I^n (n ~ 1 expected for single-photon ROS generation).
5.3 Temperature control / photothermal exclusion:
- Use IR thermography and embedded microthermocouple; run isothermal controls matching any observed ΔT in dark; require G0.4 (Ea and isothermal mismatch).
5.4 ROS identity and location:
- Operando EPR (DMPO for •OH/•O2−, TEMP for 1O2), plus probe assays (terephthalic acid for •OH, NBT for •O2−) under identical conditions.
- Predefined discriminants: 
  (D1) If superoxide is dominant: strong DMPO-OOH signal, NBT reduction correlates with bleaching, SOD suppresses kbleach ≥ 70% while tert-butanol suppresses ≤ 30%.
  (D2) If hydroxyl is dominant: terephthalic fluorescence correlates with bleaching, tert-butanol suppresses ≥ 70%, SOD suppresses ≤ 30%.
5.5 Hot-carrier vs defect-mediated semiconductor-like transfer:
- Transient absorption (TA) or time-resolved photoconductance on MoO3-laminated Layer A: look for sub-ps–ps carrier signatures and their dependence on x (carrier density).
- Photocurrent polarity and Mott–Schottky/Kelvin probe: test band bending direction vs protonation state; require consistency with electron transfer to O2 at the interface.
5.6 Dye-sensitization artifact exclusion:
- Repeat bleaching with (i) colorless anionic pollutant analogs, (ii) dyes with different absorption maxima, and (iii) dark adsorption controls.
- Critical test: excite at wavelengths where dye absorbs but LSPR does not; bleaching should not accelerate significantly if not dye-sensitized.

Step 6 — Tandem operation in flow with orthogonal catalysis
6.1 Device: feed contacts Layer A first; permeate contacts Layer B. Visible illumination 420–700 nm with calibrated photon flux; dissolved O2 monitored (optode).
6.2 Layer A function (dye bleaching + self-referenced sensing):
- Establish kbleach and response factors RFopt = (−dAdye/dt)/C and RFelect = Jph/C under standardized flux; apply pH renormalization using calibrated local pH from {λp, ΔGph}.
6.3 Layer B function (benzyl alcohol oxidation):
- Quantify conversion/selectivity to benzaldehyde; test effect of any dye leakage by deliberate spiking; acceptance: ≤10% loss in activity at dye concentrations corresponding to ≤1% breakthrough.

Step 7 — Realistic water matrices, fouling, regeneration, and durability thresholds
7.1 Matrix challenges: humic acid (2–10 mg/L), carbonate (1–10 mM), chloride (1–100 mM), mixed ions (Ca2+/Mg2+ at 0.5–2 mM), variable O2 (air-saturated vs O2-depleted).
7.2 Fouling metrics and regeneration:
- Track flux decline, rejection loss, and LSPR modulation amplitude. Regeneration protocol: mild alkaline wash (pH 9–10) + low-ionic-strength rinse; optional short H2O2 pulse if organic fouling persists (verify no loss of cationic functionality).
- Acceptance: after 5 fouling/regeneration cycles, retain ≥90% of initial rejection and ≥80% of initial kbleach.
7.3 Stability/retention:
- 100 h continuous operation + ≥100 pH cycles; apply G0.5 leaching thresholds; confirm crystallinity (GIXRD), chemical state (XPS), and preserved Au confinement (post-mortem TEM).
Feasibility:
Heteroepitaxial compatibility and pinholes: The revised plan avoids claiming strict epitaxy between different topologies; instead it uses node/topology-matched UiO-66-derived films on both sides (Layer A and B), enabling coherent intergrowth via secondary growth while controlling mismatch through thickness limits (≤250 nm for Layer A) and defect management. Quantitative, spatially resolved leakage diagnostics (multi-tracer breakthrough + SECCM/through-plane conductance mapping) and a pre-defined interfacial sealing contingency (sub-2–3 nm VPI/sol–gel targeted to grain boundaries with <10% porosity loss) directly address the risk that pinholes defeat dye-gating.

Local proton activity under fixed charge: Cationic MOFs create Donnan potentials that can decouple bulk pH from interfacial aH+. The proposal now includes (i) a coupled electrostatic/transport model incorporating fixed charge, buffer equilibria, and ionic strength and (ii) independent measurement of local pH via an anchored ratiometric fluorophore (or SECM), performed under the same ionic strength and dye loading used for catalysis. This creates a falsifiable calibration that tests whether {LSPR, photoconductance} uniquely reports local aH+ (with explicit R2 and hysteresis criteria), thereby making the self-referencing response-factor claim experimentally accountable.

Mechanistic clarity for plasmonic ROS generation: The LSPR-tunable HxMoO3 concept is grounded in degenerately doped MoOx literature showing carrier-density-dependent NIR/visible plasmon resonance and enhanced visible absorption. The revised workplan adds an energetic/kinetic discriminant matrix (action spectra, intensity scaling, isothermal controls, TA/photothermal readouts) plus pre-registered scavenger/EPR outcome criteria to distinguish hot-carrier/field-assisted O2 activation from photothermal heating, defect-mediated semiconductor charge transfer, and dye-sensitization (a known confound for azo dyes). This makes the ROS pathway assignment (•O2− vs •OH) and directionality testable and rejectable.

Transport/performance tradeoffs and real-water robustness: The membrane is treated as a selective reactor with explicit targets for rejection and permeance, measured by flux-based rejection and breakthrough curves, and interpreted with transport modeling (Donnan partitioning + diffusion/convective flow). Realistic matrices (humics, carbonate, hardness ions, chloride, variable O2) are built into the validation with explicit regeneration protocols and stability/leaching thresholds, ensuring the claimed functionality persists beyond ideal laboratory water.

Overall, the revised proposal transforms the prior asserted assumptions (epitaxy quality, local pH control, ROS identity, and dye gating) into quantitative go/no-go criteria with independent measurements, contingency sealing chemistry, and mechanistic discriminants—while preserving the original concept chain: cationic dye capture + proton-tunable HxMoO3 plasmonic bleaching upstream, and Au@Zr-MOF aromatic alcohol oxidation downstream.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-pre-registered proposal that converts nearly every high-risk assumption into a quantified go/no-go criterion. Engineering resolution is very strong: bilayer MOF-on-MOF growth, Au confinement, HxMoO3 lamination, and interfacial sealing are all described with thickness, defect-density, and analytical acceptance thresholds that are realistic for advanced MOF membrane laboratories. Logical consistency is also high; the causal chain from fixed charge → Donnan potential → local proton activity → HxMoO3 carrier density → LSPR modulation → ROS identity → dye bleaching is mechanistically coherent and explicitly tested rather than assumed.
